title: IT Purge Leaves Asok Abacus-Bound

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I asked the I.T. department to upgrade my computer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They're coming here??!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We must hide our non-standard equipment!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zip!!

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: So-o-o... this den of non-standardization must be your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: This non-standard printer is coming with me. And I don't remember that monitor on our list.

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: I must cleanse your cubicle of non-conformance so the healing can begin.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Surely my upgraded computer will arrive soon.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Months later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Abacus?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please shut up.

situation: Asok has asked IT to upgrade his computer, but Dilbert and Alice warn that IT is coming to inspect and they hide their non-standard gear. The IT technician arrives and confiscates Asok's printer and monitor in the name of standardization. Months later Asok still has no computer and is using an abacus.
punchline: The IT department's zeal for standardization means a request for an upgrade results in Asok losing his equipment entirely, leaving him with an abacus instead of a computer.
summary: A request for a better computer ends with the IT enforcer stripping a worker's desk bare, leaving him to count on a bead frame.

file: 2005/2005-12-24_power point zone_real wolrd_bullet points_imaginary prodcutivity_eight lsides.gif
title: Dilbert's Imaginary PowerPoint Productivity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am entering the PowerPoint zone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I no longer feel the need to change the real world as long as I can change these bullet points.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How much imaginary productivity did you have today?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eight slides!

setting: Office cubicle and Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer thinking about entering the PowerPoint zone, then realizes he no longer cares about changing the real world as long as he can tweak bullet points. At home, Dogbert asks how much imaginary productivity he had, and Dilbert proudly reports he made eight slides.
punchline: Making PowerPoint slides feels like accomplishment but produces no real-world results, so Dilbert's proud tally of eight slides is only imaginary productivity.
summary: A worker gets so absorbed in editing presentation slides that he mistakes slide counts for genuine achievement.

title: Why Must We Talk In Your Office

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, come to my office for a minute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's in your office?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You and I will be there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you just want to talk, we can do it right here and save us both some time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we need privacy. Did you ever think of that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do we need it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. That was just an example. There are many, many reasons why we should talk in my office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be fascinated to find out what kind of information is geographically dependent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now, do you have the results from the benchmark tests?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup. In my cubicle.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss summons Dilbert to his office for a chat, but Dilbert asks what is in the office that justifies the trip and offers to talk on the spot. The Boss can't come up with a real reason, so Dilbert sarcastically predicts he'll learn what information depends on location. In the office, the Boss asks for the benchmark test results, which are back in Dilbert's cubicle.
punchline: Dilbert gets dragged to the Boss's office for no good reason, only to be asked for something that is in his own cubicle, proving the trip was pointless.
summary: A manager insists on relocating a simple conversation to his office without any justification, and the move turns out to require data stored back at the employee's desk.

file: 2005/2005-10-19_delete incriminating email_witness to crime_no good plan.gif
title: Deleting Emails Requires Killing Witness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to delete all of our incriminating e-mails before the court sees them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That plan is no good because I'd be a witness to the crime... unless you had me killed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Phase two is none of your concern.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It has a phase???

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to delete incriminating company e-mails before a court can see them. Dilbert points out that he would then be a witness to the cover-up, unless the Boss planned to have him killed. The Boss says the next phase of the plan is not Dilbert's concern, which alarms Dilbert.
punchline: The Boss's evasive reply that 'phase two' is none of Dilbert's concern implies he does intend to have Dilbert killed to eliminate the witness.
summary: A manager asks his employee to destroy evidence, then casually hints that the employee himself will be eliminated afterward.

title: Infinite Capacity, Zero Quality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to pick up Ted's function.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I have infinite capacity to do more work as long as you don't mind that my quality approaches zero.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or are you asking me to do something that's logically impossible?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I hate you.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to take over the duties of a coworker named Ted. Dilbert replies that he can absorb unlimited extra work only if the quality of everything he does collapses toward zero. He then asks whether the boss is requesting something logically impossible, and the frustrated boss says he hates him.
punchline: Dilbert uses deadpan logic to expose that piling extra work onto one person without extra resources must wreck quality, and the boss's only answer is resentment at being shown his request is unreasonable.
summary: Handed a departed coworker's duties, an engineer calmly explains the arithmetic of overload, leaving his manager with nothing to say but a petty insult.

file: 2005/2005-10-16_take the chair_don't sell chairs_sell hope_hope of chairs_ship in 2 months_call and yell_buy a chair.gif
title: Selling the Hope of Chairs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take that chair.

transcript.speaker: Saleswoman
transcript.text: Excellent choice.

transcript.speaker: Saleswoman
transcript.text: Now sit there quietly and try not to ask the one question that will kill this sale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the chair in stock?

transcript.speaker: Saleswoman
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Saleswoman
transcript.text: The truth is that we don't sell chairs at all. We sell the hope that a chair will someday be made for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How long will that take?

transcript.speaker: Saleswoman
transcript.text: If I could answer that question, it would be the same as selling you an actual chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about if I tell you it will ship in two months, and you call and yell at me every three months for eternity?

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: Did you buy a chair?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no way to know.

setting: A furniture store showroom and the saleswoman's desk, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert picks out a chair at a furniture store, and the saleswoman coaches him to stay quiet so he won't ask whether it is in stock. When he asks anyway, she admits the store only sells the hope that a chair will someday be made, with no delivery date. Dilbert offers to be called and yelled at regularly, and at home a ghost asks if he bought a chair.
punchline: Dilbert pays for a chair that may never exist, so he can't even say whether he made a purchase, which mocks vendors who sell vaporware and promise delivery that never comes.
summary: A furniture shopper learns that the store's chairs are only a promise, leaving him unsure whether he bought anything at all.

title: Mugging the CFO in Self-Defense

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I hate walking to work in this high-crime area.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Take this, you fiduciary misconducting *#@!%!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was our C.F.O.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I know.

setting: City sidewalk outside an office building
situation: A woman thinks aloud about how much she dislikes walking to work through a high-crime neighborhood. A man in a suit approaches and she attacks him, cursing him as a 'fiduciary misconducting' offender. Dilbert then points out the man was the company CFO, and she calmly says she knows.
punchline: She isn't being mugged or paranoid; she deliberately assaulted the CFO because she blames him for financial wrongdoing, turning the 'high-crime area' worry into her own crime.
summary: An employee pummels a passing executive in the street, fully aware that he is the finance chief she resents.

file: 2005/2005-03-06_catbert_evil director_human resources_assistant manager_simialr_slightly worse_wouldn't be threat_data base_both hideous_criminally insane_hate cats_business.gif
title: Hiring a Slightly Worse Assistant

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to hire an assistant manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want someone similar to me, but slightly worse in every way.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Worse than you???

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but only slightly.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hmm...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The ideal candidate wouldn't be a threat to replace me.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll check my database of applicants who are both hideous and criminally insane.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I said slightly worse.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Exactly. I found one.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: I can pretend to read in five languages.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate cats.

setting: The Boss's office and Catbert's HR office
situation: The Boss asks Catbert, the evil HR director, to find an assistant manager who is similar to him but only slightly worse, so the hire can't threaten his job. Catbert searches his database of hideous, criminally insane applicants and says he found a match. The interviewee turns out to be a wild-haired, tongue-lolling oddball who can only pretend to read, while the Boss thinks about hating cats.
punchline: Catbert's idea of 'slightly worse' than the Boss is a hideous, criminally insane candidate, implying the Boss is already so bad that a lunatic is only a small step down.
summary: A manager wants a subordinate just a bit inferior to himself, and the HR cat delivers a deranged candidate, insulting the manager in the process.

title: Credit Check Meets Acorn Payments

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to do a credit check on your company before we do any work. It's our policy.

transcript.speaker: Small Businessman
transcript.text: I resent that! Just because I'm a small businessman, that doesn't mean I'm a deadbeat!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't mean to imply...

transcript.speaker: Small Businessman
transcript.text: Do you know if the parking garage accepts acorns?

setting: Dilbert's office, with a tiny client sitting in a chair across the desk
situation: Dilbert tells a very small prospective client that company policy requires a credit check before work begins. The client angrily protests that being a small businessman doesn't make him a deadbeat. As Dilbert backpedals, the client asks whether the parking garage takes acorns as payment, revealing his finances really are unconventional.
punchline: The indignant client undermines his own creditworthiness by asking if the parking garage accepts acorns, implying he pays with nuts rather than money.
summary: A touchy tiny client insists he is no financial risk, then wonders aloud whether he can pay for parking with acorns.

title: All Internet Spam Traced to Dilbert's House

transcript.speaker: FBI Agent
transcript.text: FBI. We need to talk to you.

transcript.speaker: FBI Agent
transcript.text: We've traced the source of all Internet spam to your house.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...the revolutionary new pill that turns your body fat into Rolex watches!

situation: Two FBI agents in sunglasses and suits show their badges to Dilbert and tell him all Internet spam has been traced to his house. Dilbert is incredulous that it could be all of it. In the last panel, Dogbert is revealed happily typing a spam message at a computer, humming to himself.
punchline: Dilbert's own dog is the source of the world's spam, cheerfully writing absurd come-ons like a pill that turns body fat into Rolex watches.
summary: Federal agents blame a man for the world's junk email, but the real spammer is his pet dog gleefully typing away.

file: 2005/2005-05-01_complaints_badering manager_deciosn on issue_emails phonecalls_insist on the job_overpaid.gif
title: Alice Demonstrates Badgering to Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've received some complaints that you've been badgering managers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hmm... Badgering, you say.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let me see if I understand this "badgering" concept.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's say that I need a manager's decision on a critical issue...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And the manager in question ignores my e-mails and phone calls...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Shouldn't I insist that this manager do the job for which he is overpaid?!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Huh? Shouldn't I? What do you say? Huh? Huh? How about it? Huh?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll say I talked to her.

situation: The Boss tells Alice that managers have complained about her badgering them. Alice responds by hypothetically describing a manager who ignores her e-mails and calls, then works herself into a rage and demonstrates badgering by shouting questions in the Boss's face. The Boss, cowed, decides his only way out is to claim he has already spoken to her.
punchline: Alice proves the complaints right by badgering her own boss in the act of defending herself, and he is so intimidated that he gives up and plans to say he has dealt with her rather than actually confront her.
summary: Accused of harassing managers, a fierce engineer acts out exactly what she's accused of, leaving her frightened boss to simply pretend he handled it.

title: Showing Interest In Alice's Mood

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, what's it like to be in a bad mood all of the time?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: Alice glares with clenched teeth while Dilbert stands beside her.)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Something tells me that showing interest isn't working.

setting: Outdoors on a path beside a hedge
situation: Dilbert walks alongside Alice and asks her what it is like to be in a bad mood all the time. Alice answers with a silent, teeth-gritting glare. Dilbert concludes in a thought bubble that his attempt at showing interest has failed.
punchline: Dilbert's supposedly friendly question is really an insult, and he is surprised when Alice's furious reaction shows it isn't working as polite interest.
summary: A coworker's clumsy attempt at friendly curiosity about a grumpy colleague earns only a murderous stare.

title: Hot Flash Coworker Placed By Thermostat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone meet our new team member, Flashy.

transcript.speaker: Flashy
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Suddenly so hot!!! Burning!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Flashy will be in the cubicle by the thermostat.

transcript.speaker: Flashy
transcript.text: C-c-c-cold!

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss introduces a new team member nicknamed Flashy to the meeting. Flashy suddenly erupts in a burning hot flash, then shivers with cold in the next moment. The Boss decides to seat Flashy in the cubicle by the thermostat.
punchline: Flashy swings between sweltering and freezing, and the Boss's solution of seating Flashy next to the thermostat shows a typical managerial mix of well-meaning accommodation and cluelessness.
summary: A newcomer who swings abruptly between feeling scorched and frozen gets assigned a desk beside the office temperature control.

title: Scathing Letter Over Dongle Usage

transcript.speaker: Alice's coworker
transcript.text: I just fired off a scathing letter to a columnist for misusing the word "dongle."

transcript.speaker: Alice's coworker
transcript.text: I'm intoxicated with the feeling of verbal superiority. My sad life has meaning. I feel alive!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Columnist

transcript.speaker: Columnist
transcript.text: Dear Nutbag,

transcript.speaker: Columnist
transcript.text: Thanks for the input. Here's a link to a dictionary. I await your apology.

setting: Office break area, then the columnist's living room
situation: A woman holding a mug brags to Dilbert that she sent a harsh letter to a columnist for misusing the word "dongle," and says the feeling of superiority gives her sad life meaning. The final panel shows the columnist at home on his laptop, replying that she is the one who should consult a dictionary and apologize.
punchline: The pedantic complainer's smug victory is deflated when the columnist replies that she is actually the one who is wrong about the word, demanding an apology.
summary: A gloating nitpicker's gleeful complaint about a writer's word choice backfires when the writer fires back with a dictionary link.

file: 2005/2005-08-29_discount religin_tithing 5%_sin is in_no time with joiners.gif
title: Discount Religion With Unwanted Followers

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I decided to start a discount religion.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The tithing would only be 5% and I'd let people sin as much as they wanted.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The only problem is that I don't want to spend time with anyone who would join that sort of religion.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, with both in bed
situation: Ratbert sits up in bed next to Dilbert, who is reading a red book. Ratbert pitches the idea of a budget religion with a low 5% tithe and permissive rules about sinning. He then realizes the flaw: he would not want to associate with the kind of people who would join it.
punchline: A religion that lets people sin freely for cheap would only attract people Ratbert wouldn't want to spend time with, so the business plan defeats itself.
summary: A small lab-rat dreams up a bargain faith with lax rules, then realizes its congregation would be insufferable.

title: Catbert Fires Distrustful Employees

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The employee satisfaction survey says they don't trust management.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't worry. I'll find out who feels that way and fire them during the next retrenchment.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Purr? Who said purr?

setting: Office desk of the Boss, then an employee's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, reports to the Boss that an employee satisfaction survey shows staff don't trust management. He cheerfully promises to identify the people who answered that way and fire them in the next round of layoffs. In the last panel an employee at his computer is puzzled as Catbert crouches nearby, purring.
punchline: The survey is not meant to improve morale but to identify and fire anyone honest enough to say they distrust management, which proves their point and makes the answers unsafe to give.
summary: A sinister HR cat treats an honest staff survey as a hit list for the next round of layoffs.

file: 2005/2005-01-19_gay boss_nelson_male_no bomus_train to be boss_support family_gay_dating rugby team.gif
title: Bonus Goes to Man Supporting Family

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, this is your new supervisor, Nelson. You'll be training him to be your boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There won't be any bonuses this year because I gave it all to Nelson. He's a man, so he needs to support a family.

transcript.speaker: Nelson
transcript.text: I'm gay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um...civil union and adoption, right?

transcript.speaker: Nelson
transcript.text: I'm dating a rugby team.

situation: The Boss introduces Nelson as Tina's new supervisor, whom she must train to become her own boss. He then announces that the entire bonus pool is going to Nelson because a man needs to support a family. Nelson reveals he is gay, and when the Boss scrambles to justify the decision with civil union and adoption, Nelson replies he's dating a rugby team.
punchline: The Boss's sexist justification for giving Nelson the bonus collapses when Nelson says he's gay, and his attempt to rescue it by imagining a family is topped by Nelson's claim to be dating an entire rugby team, which is far from a family to support.
summary: A manager hands all the bonus money to a new hire on the sexist assumption that men must support families, only to be undercut by the man's unexpectedly unconventional love life.

title: Boss Criticizes Telling Others to Work Harder

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I asked you to help Alice on her project but all you did was tell her to work harder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't just tell someone to work harder and expect it to happen!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aren't you doing that right now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shut up and go work harder.

situation: The Boss scolds Wally for merely telling Alice to work harder when he was asked to actually help her with her project. He declares that simply telling someone to work harder doesn't produce results. Wally points out that the Boss is doing exactly that to him, and the Boss responds by ordering Wally to work harder.
punchline: The Boss is blind to his own hypocrisy, condemning an ineffective management tactic while using the very same tactic on Wally.
summary: A manager lectures an employee for giving useless exhortations, then responds to the obvious hypocrisy by issuing the same exhortation himself.
keywords: do as i say not as i do

title: Good News: Promotion Denied

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have good news about the promotion you wanted: You didn't get it!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How could you possibly call that good news?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't like positivity.

setting: Alice's cubicle and a nearby office
situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Alice that she was passed over for the promotion she wanted and calls it good news. Alice, furious, shouts at him asking how that could be good news. In the last panel the Boss, standing next to Catbert on a desk, deadpans that 'they' don't like positivity.
punchline: The Boss's absurd framing of a rejection as 'good news' is revealed as a deliberate, sarcastic jab at a company culture that punishes anyone who is positive.
summary: A manager spins a denied promotion as a bright spot, then admits the organization simply dislikes optimism.

title: Thief Who Checked the Weather

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, this year you did the work of four people and made over $10 million for the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But according to our web monitoring software, you used company resources to look at a weather web site.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thief.

setting: Boss's office, across a desk during a performance review
situation: The Boss meets with Alice for her review and praises her for doing the work of four people and earning over $10 million for the company. He then reveals that the web monitoring software caught her visiting a weather website on company time. He calls her a thief, while Alice glares angrily.
punchline: Management ignores an employee's enormous contribution and fixates on a trivial misuse of company resources, accusing her of theft for checking the weather.
summary: A manager lavishes praise on a hugely productive employee and then brands her a criminal over a quick look at a forecast.

file: 2005/2005-04-28_technical glitch_humble_condescending engineer_teach you to ask_drinking beer_study english_sorry.gif
title: Humbling Apology to Condescending Engineer

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh no. It's a technical glitch that I don't know how to fix.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaa! Now I must humble myself to some condescending engineer and ask for help!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: And how did I teach you to ask?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm sorry that I spent my college years drinking beer and studying English literature.

situation: Alice discovers a technical glitch on her computer that she cannot fix. She dreads having to humble herself before a condescending engineer to get help. When she asks, the engineer makes her recite a degrading apology for her non-technical college education.
punchline: The engineer's condescension is so extreme that asking for tech help requires apologizing for having studied English literature instead of engineering.
summary: A frustrated employee must grovel to a smug engineer for computer help and is forced to apologize for her humanities degree.

title: Diamond Time Machine Targets One Buyer

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: We've narrowed our target market to this guy.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: He's the only one rich enough and stupid enough to buy our high-end product.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: Our diamond-encrusted time machine will take you one hour into the future in only sixty minutes!

setting: Conference room during a marketing presentation
situation: A marketing presenter shows a photo of a single man holding a drink and says he is their entire target market. He explains this man is the only person rich and foolish enough to buy their high-end product. The product is then revealed as a diamond-encrusted time machine that merely takes you one hour into the future in sixty minutes.
punchline: The time machine does nothing more than what passing time already does for free, so only a rich fool would pay for it.
summary: A presenter pitches an absurdly overpriced gadget that delivers something everyone gets anyway, aimed at one gullible millionaire.

file: 2005/2005-03-26_hating software_integration project_hate it_simply mentioned_pros and cons_balanced anaysis_hatred.gif
title: Balanced Analysis Mistaken for Hatred

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's this I hear about you hating the software integration project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't hate it. I simply mentioned both the pros and the cons. People are so conditioned to take sides that a balanced analysis looks to them like hatred.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can you hate it so much??!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is one of those days when it's hard to be me.

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert over a rumor that he hates the software integration project. Dilbert explains that he only listed both the pros and cons, and that people mistake a balanced analysis for hatred. The Boss ignores the explanation and angrily asks how Dilbert can hate it so much.
punchline: Dilbert's calm, reasoned explanation is completely ignored by a boss who has already decided he is an opponent, proving Dilbert's point that balanced thinking gets treated as hostility.
summary: A boss hears that an engineer opposes a project, but when the engineer clarifies that he was merely even-handed, the boss only hears more hatred.

title: Alice's Dumpster Status Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, what's the status of your project?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The astonishing incompetence of others caused me to jump through a window and land in a dumpster.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So then, no issues?

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks Alice for a status update on her project. Alice, covered in garbage with trash in her wild hair, explains that her colleagues' incompetence drove her to leap through a window into a dumpster. The Boss responds by asking whether that means there are no issues.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he treats a woman who has literally jumped into a dumpster out of frustration as reporting a problem-free project.
summary: A garbage-covered Alice describes a desperate window leap, and her clueless manager takes it as a sign that everything is fine.

file: 2005/2005-06-15_paying for consulting_no recommendations_feel secure_shaping strategies_hate you_feel good.gif
title: Consultant Sells Reassurance, Not Recommendations

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I keep paying you for consulting, but you never make any recommendations.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm what you call a "feel good."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My job is to make you feel secure in the knowledge that someone brilliant is shaping your strategies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is weird; I hate you, but at the same time I feel good.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss complains that he keeps paying Dogbert for consulting yet never gets any recommendations. Dogbert explains that his role is simply to make the Boss feel secure that a brilliant mind is guiding his strategy. The Boss admits he resents Dogbert but feels good anyway, and Dogbert accepts thanks.
punchline: The consultant's real product is comforting reassurance rather than advice, and the Boss is so soothed that he doesn't mind paying for nothing.
summary: A consultant admits he is paid merely to make a manager feel confident, and the manager is oddly content with that arrangement.

file: 2005/2005-05-06_evil director_campiagn_employee happiness_forbidden fruit_no dating emplyees_date each other.gif
title: Banning Office Romance Makes It Tempting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: As part of my ongoing campaign against employee happiness...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Employees are not allowed to date each other.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now you're forbidden fruit... yummy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stay back, rule-breaker.

setting: Conference room during an HR meeting
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces to a conference table of employees that dating between coworkers is now prohibited. The new rule instantly backfires: Alice looks at Dilbert and says the ban makes him a tempting 'forbidden fruit'. Dilbert nervously tells her to keep her distance.
punchline: Catbert's rule meant to make employees unhappy ironically makes coworkers more attractive to each other, and Dilbert is the one now being pursued.
summary: An evil HR cat bans workplace dating, only to have the prohibition make a colleague suddenly eager to pursue Dilbert.

title: Boss's Car Call Causes Crash

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Rrring!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now what?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hi. It's your boss.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh no. I hear traffic. Where are you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my car.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa! It's a car call. He's using me to entertain himself while he's sitting in traffic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's everything?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll lose an hour of my life if I don't get him off the phone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Nice weather today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do me a favor and look in your briefcase to see if my latest report is there.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And turn down your radio so I can hear you... and check your calendar on your PDA.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Crash!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm going to hell.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's car
situation: The Boss calls Alice from his car while stuck in traffic, just to chat. Alice tries to get him off the phone with small talk, but he keeps piling on distracting requests, such as checking his report, turning down the radio and checking a PDA calendar. While driving and juggling all this, he crashes his car.
punchline: Alice wanted to avoid the call, but the Boss's distracting requests caused a car crash, leaving her to feel guilty and say she's going to hell.
summary: A bored commuting manager phones an employee to kill time, then wrecks his car while multitasking on her demands.

file: 2005/2005-04-04_nick name_illusion of competence_the wizard_info guru_punch more_break room_coffee.gif
title: Nickname to Fake Competence

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need a nickname to create the illusion of competence.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was thinking along the lines of "The Wizard" or "Info-Guru."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never wanted to punch you more than at this very moment.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: A balding coworker in glasses and a green shirt approaches Dilbert at the coffee machine and announces he needs a nickname to appear competent. He suggests impressive-sounding titles like "The Wizard" or "Info-Guru." Dilbert, holding the coffee pot, tells him he has never wanted to punch him more.
punchline: The coworker openly admits he wants a fancy nickname to fake expertise, which is so brazen and obnoxious that it pushes Dilbert to the edge of violence.
summary: A colleague shamelessly shops for a grandiose title to disguise his lack of skill, and the listener's patience nearly snaps.

title: Squashing the Reasonable Man

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company Lawyer

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: This contract would be subject to a "reasonable man" interpretation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where is this guy? I'll squash him like a bug!

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Okay, moving on...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's you! I knew it!

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: The company lawyer explains that a contract would be interpreted according to the legal standard of a "reasonable man." The Boss misunderstands this as a specific person and angrily vows to squash him. The lawyer silently continues, and the Boss then wrongly accuses the lawyer of being the man.
punchline: The Boss takes the legal term "reasonable man" literally as a person to attack, and then accuses the lawyer, which is a baffling conclusion.
summary: A manager mistakes a legal standard for an actual enemy and ends up blaming the lawyer who is explaining it.

title: Framing the Boss for Deletion

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: La-la-la-la-la...oops.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I inadvertently erased our entire customer database and all of the backups.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How can I explain this to our pointy-haired boss?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Grab your laptop and follow me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's only a prototype, so whatever you do, don't touch anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Touch touch touch

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! You erased the customer database!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All of the backups, too, you stupid, stupid #*@!*!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I should have stopped before #*@!*!

setting: Office cubicles and a conference room
situation: Asok accidentally erases the company's customer database and all its backups, and asks how to explain it to the boss. Wally has him bring a laptop to the boss and tells the boss not to touch anything, then loudly accuses the boss of erasing the database as soon as he touches the laptop. Asok ends up with a metal bowl on his head.
punchline: Wally cleverly frames the boss for Asok's mistake by telling him not to touch anything, knowing he will, and the boss takes the blame.
summary: A junior employee destroys critical data, so a cynical coworker tricks the boss into taking the fall.

title: Engineering Degree Meets Newsletter Duty

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm the editor of the department newsletter. That makes you my cub reporter.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Cub reporter??? I have an engineering degree from the India Institute of Technology — the most challenging university on the planet.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That'll come in handy during the copying phase. We get some fierce paper jams.

situation: Alice, the editor of the department newsletter, tells Asok he is now her cub reporter. Asok indignantly protests that he holds an engineering degree from the most challenging university on the planet. Alice calmly replies that his degree will be useful for fixing paper jams when copying the newsletter.
punchline: Alice dismisses Asok's elite engineering credentials by finding a use for them only in the menial task of clearing photocopier jams.
summary: A proud young engineer is drafted into newsletter duty and learns his prestigious degree qualifies him mainly to unjam the copier.

file: 2005/2005-06-12_tuesday off_kids tonsils_not suregon_rare blood type_donate blood_moral supprt_real winner_immoral and sick_cold on tuesday.gif
title: Tonsils Day Off Request Backfires

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I need Tuesday off because my son is having his tonsils removed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Since when do you know how to remove tonsils?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Um... I won't be performing the surgery myself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a rare blood type that you need to donate?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: No. Actually, I was planning on sitting in the waiting room to give him moral support.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So your kid is immoral and sick? He sounds like a real winner.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What I mean is that I plan to have a cold on Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I can see where your kid gets it from.

situation: An employee asks his boss for Tuesday off to be with his son, who is having his tonsils removed. The boss responds with absurd, willfully obtuse questions and then twists the phrase 'moral support' into an insult against the child. The frustrated employee backpedals and says he'll just call in sick with a cold, which the boss also insults.
punchline: The boss deliberately misreads 'moral support' as meaning the kid is immoral, and ends by insulting the employee's family no matter what he says, showing that any time-off request is met with hostility.
summary: A father's simple request to accompany his child to surgery gets deliberately twisted by a hostile boss into insults until the father gives up and resorts to faking illness.

title: Business Trip Caused Civil War

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My business trip to Elbonia was a big success.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If anyone tells you that I caused a civil war that plunged their society into darkness, it's a lie.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Did you loot me anything?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't know your size.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss proudly reports that his business trip to Elbonia was a success, then preemptively denies rumors that he caused a civil war there. A colleague, Ted, asks whether the Boss looted him a souvenir, and the Boss replies that he didn't know the colleague's size.
punchline: The Boss's flippant answer implicitly admits that he took part in the looting during the civil war he caused, only regretting that he didn't bring back a gift in the right size.
summary: A manager brushes off accusations of triggering a foreign civil war, then accidentally confirms the looting when asked about a souvenir.

title: Drugging Coworkers Backfires in Meeting

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: All of your problems are caused by emotionally unstable coworkers.

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: Try prescribing meds from the Internet to fix their defects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. That one was the wrong choice. Let's try something else.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Grrrr!

setting: Office break room, then a conference room
situation: A ghost in the break room tells Dilbert his problems come from emotionally unstable coworkers and advises him to fix them with medication ordered from the Internet. Dilbert follows the advice, apparently by secretly dosing his colleagues. In a meeting, the Boss is growling and snarling, and Dilbert admits that was the wrong drug and says he'll try a different one.
punchline: Dilbert treats his coworkers like malfunctioning products, secretly dosing them with unvetted Internet drugs, and merely shrugs and tries another drug when the Boss starts growling.
summary: After a ghost suggests chemically repairing his unstable colleagues, Dilbert experiments on them and casually moves on to a new attempt when the first goes badly.

title: Bribing Elbonians With Fake Nuclear Plans

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Elbonians won't do business with my company unless we bribe them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Offer to give them plans for building a nuclear weapon. Then give them plans to build microwave ovens instead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would that work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why do you think our garage is full of Persian rugs?

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dilbert explains that a foreign client, the Elbonians, demands a bribe before doing business with his company. Dogbert suggests a bait-and-switch: promise nuclear weapon plans, then hand over microwave oven plans. When Dilbert doubts it would work, Dogbert points to his own garage full of Persian rugs as proof.
punchline: Dogbert reveals he has already run this scam on other countries, and the garage full of Persian rugs is the loot, showing he is a successful con artist.
summary: Dogbert advises a bribery-by-deception scheme and backs up its effectiveness by hinting at a garage stuffed with ill-gotten rugs.

title: Boss Misplaces Quality Estimates

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, where are the quality estimates that I asked you for an hour ago?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's between your left arm and your stout torso, about elbow-high.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stupid elbow.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss angrily demands the quality estimates he requested from Alice an hour earlier. Alice points out that he is already holding the papers under his arm. Back at his desk, the Boss blames his elbow rather than himself.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless and unwilling to take responsibility that he blames his own elbow for hiding the document he was carrying the whole time.
summary: A manager chews out an employee for missing paperwork that he turns out to be carrying himself, then pins the blame on a body part.

title: Eagles Can't Type Status Reports

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, the status report that you e-mailed me is blank.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because eagles can't type.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The motivational poster in the break room says I should be like an eagle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The point of that poster is that your spirit should soar like an eagle while you continue to do mundane work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wouldn't I die if my spirit left my body to go soar?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're confusing your spirit with your soul.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: While your spirit is soaring, your soul should remain trapped in your body, slowly decaying while you create your status report.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Would it change anything if I got a poster that says, "You want it when?!!"

situation: The Boss complains that Wally's emailed status report was blank. Wally blames a motivational eagle poster, claiming eagles can't type, and the Boss explains the poster's intended meaning in increasingly grim terms. Wally finishes by suggesting a more honest poster.
punchline: The Boss's explanation of the motivational poster reveals it as a cynical call to endure soul-crushing drudgery, so Wally proposes a poster that captures the real, deadline-driven management attitude.
summary: A slacker employee uses a motivational poster as an excuse for a blank report and gets an unintentionally bleak lecture on spirits and souls in return.

file: 2005/2005-03-12_dont worry_high crime area_experts assure you_gange members_exhautsed_beat up.gif
title: Reassurance About Relocating to Crime Area

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't worry that the company is moving to a high-crime area.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My experts assure me that you'll have a 90% chance of survival every time you walk outside.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That estimate depends on the assumption that the gang members become exhausted from beating you up.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, addresses employees at a meeting and tries to reassure them about the company relocating to a high-crime neighborhood. He cites his experts' 90% survival odds for each trip outside. He then admits the estimate only holds if gang members tire themselves out beating people up.
punchline: The supposedly comforting survival statistic rests on the grim assumption that attackers will simply get tired, revealing how little HR actually cares about employee safety.
summary: A malicious HR cat offers a cheerful safety statistic for the new dangerous office location, then undercuts it with a darkly absurd caveat.

title: Merged CEOs Claim Married Couple Bond

transcript.speaker: CEO at podium
transcript.text: After the merger, we'll be sharing the job of CEO.

transcript.speaker: CEO at podium
transcript.text: We get along great, just like an old married couple. Ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: CEO at podium
transcript.text: He's the wife.

setting: Company auditorium during a merger announcement
situation: At a podium, one executive announces that after the merger he and another executive will share the job of CEO. He jokes that they get along like an old married couple while employees watch from the audience. He then whispers an aside, adding that the other man is the wife.
punchline: The executive's quip about being an old married couple turns into a barbed aside that casts his co-CEO as the 'wife', revealing his dominance and condescension, which hints that the shared leadership is not really equal.
summary: A merging company's co-CEOs present a united front, but one quietly undercuts his partner with a jab about marital roles.

file: 2005/2005-06-17_batch of tiger meat_project_chanllenging_delight stockholders_not challenging_less motivated.gif
title: Rejecting Projects Too Unchallenging for Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm ready for a new batch of tiger meat. Grrr!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I want a project that will challenge my abilities, bring glory to the company and delight our stockholders!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How about this one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nope. Not challenging enough. I'll give it to one of the less motivated employees.

situation: An employee, holding a coffee mug, announces he is hungry for a demanding new project that will bring glory to the company and please stockholders. Having made his speech, he proposes a project, but the boss turns it down as not challenging enough and says he'll hand it to a less motivated employee instead.
punchline: The boss's reasoning is backwards: because the project is too easy for the eager worker, it gets given to the unmotivated ones, so eagerness is no reward.
summary: A pumped-up employee begs for an ambitious assignment, but his boss rejects the offered work as too simple for him and passes it to the slackers.

title: Red Tag Compromise for Second Computer

transcript.speaker: Auditor
transcript.text: Having two computers is a violation of the company's 5S rules of standardized workspace.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need two computers to test my software. There's no way to do my job with one.

transcript.speaker: Auditor
transcript.text: I have a compromise solution. Put this little red tag on one of them and tell me later if anything bad happens.

situation: A workplace auditor visits Dilbert's cubicle and cites him for having two computers, which violates the company's 5S standardized workspace rules. Dilbert explains that he needs two machines to test his software. The auditor offers a 'compromise' of sticking a red tag on one computer and asking him to report later if anything bad happens.
punchline: The auditor's so-called compromise changes nothing practical, since a red tag is a meaningless gesture that lets the bureaucracy feel its rule was honored while Dilbert keeps both computers.
summary: A rule-enforcing inspector settles a dispute over extra equipment with a token sticker that solves nothing.

title: Dogbert Recommends a Vampire CEO

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Executive Search Firm

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to hire a big name CEO to get some buzz.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You want someone with a reputation for toughness, who knows how to get the most out of people.

transcript.speaker: Vampire CEO
transcript.text: Come back later. I'm still getting the most out of this one.

setting: Conference room at Dogbert's Executive Search Firm, then a dungeon-like castle
situation: Dogbert, acting as an executive recruiter, advises a pair of pointy-haired executives to hire a famous, tough CEO who gets the most out of people. In the last panel Dogbert's candidate turns out to be a caped vampire in a castle, who is currently draining the life from a victim and tells them to return later.
punchline: The tough CEO who gets 'the most out of people' is literally a vampire sucking the blood from his employee, mocking ruthless executives who exploit their workers.
summary: A headhunting dog's ideal hard-driving chief executive proves to be a bloodsucking creature of the night literally draining a victim.
keywords: get the most out of people

title: Hiring the Difficult Coworker Yourself

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an abusive, lying, back-stabbing, control freak.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But don't worry, because I'm sending you to a class on how to deal with difficult coworkers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it have been better to...

transcript.speaker: Difficult coworker
transcript.text: I've heard bad things about that guy.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and a coworker that he has hired an abusive, lying, back-stabbing control freak. Instead of fixing the hiring decision, he plans to send Dilbert to a class on dealing with difficult coworkers. Dilbert starts to ask whether it would have been better not to hire the person, but the new hire interrupts, pointing out that he has heard bad things about Dilbert.
punchline: The new hire, standing right there, is the difficult person and immediately starts badmouthing Dilbert, proving the Boss's mistake and showing that the 'solution' puts the burden on the wrong person.
summary: A manager knowingly brings in a toxic employee and expects an existing worker to take training to cope, only for the newcomer to start trashing that worker's reputation.

title: Base Tan Bet Ends in Pond

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I want to get a good base tan before I take my vacation.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That'll prevent me from getting a sunburn when I go to the beach.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think it's a myth that a base tan can protect you from sunburns.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You are so wrong! Let's make a bet. The loser has to jump into that freezing pond.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. I'll do a search on my wireless computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here you go: A base tan provides only a negligible SPF 4 protection.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm not jumping into that freezing pond.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Push

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You were already ignorant and contentious. I didn't want you to be a welcher too.

setting: Outdoor park with grass, trees and a pond
situation: Dilbert and a woman are walking outdoors when she claims a base tan will protect her from sunburn. Dilbert disagrees, and she proposes a bet that the loser jumps into a freezing pond. Dilbert looks up the facts on his wireless device and wins, but when she refuses to pay up, he pushes her into the pond.
punchline: Dilbert justifies shoving her into the pond by saying she was already ignorant and contentious and he didn't want her to be a welcher as well.
summary: After winning a bet over a sunburn myth, a man physically forces his sore-loser companion to honor the wager.

file: 2005/2005-02-28_meeting in elbonia_take a class_culture_accidentally offend_hello_gestures_2 meaning gestures.gif
title: Elbonian Gesture Cultural Training Class

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First, you'll need to take a class on their culture so you won't accidentally offend them.

transcript.text: This gesture either means "hello" or "I'd like to see your mittens on my bedroom floor, baby."

setting: Boss's office, then a cultural training classroom
situation: The Boss asks Wally to attend a meeting in Elbonia on his behalf and says he must first take a class on Elbonian culture to avoid giving offense. In the class, a robed instructor demonstrates a hand gesture while Wally and Dilbert sit at a table and listen.
punchline: The Elbonian gesture is so ambiguous that it could be a polite greeting or a crude come-on, which means the cultural training is useless for avoiding offense.
summary: A manager sends an employee to a foreign land after a cultural sensitivity course that reveals one innocent-looking gesture could be either a greeting or an inappropriate proposition.

title: Alice Kills Annoying Cubicle Cockroach

transcript.speaker: Cockroach
transcript.text: Good morning, Alice!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh, a cubicle cockroach.

transcript.speaker: Cockroach

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you have a flame thrower?

transcript.speaker: Cockroach
transcript.text: I can't complain; no one would listen!

situation: A human-sized cockroach in office attire cheerfully greets Alice and repeats a stale workplace joke while she tries to work. Alice privately resolves to kill it, then asks Dilbert if he has a flame thrower. The cockroach, now headless, cheerfully says he can't complain because no one would listen.
punchline: Alice destroys the annoying coworker-like cockroach, and even headless he keeps chatting, joking that he can't complain since nobody would listen, a jab at how ignored workers are.
summary: A chatty insect coworker with a corny joke gets decapitated by Alice, yet keeps up his cheerful banter.

file: 2005/2005-03-11_company relocating_high crime_tax reasons_ceo says_limo_parking garage_chain bike to whino_advice from ceo.gif
title: CEO's Dangerous Relocation Safety Advice

punchline: The CEO's safety advice only works for people wealthy enough to have limos, and his offhand suggestion for regular employees shows he doesn't care about their safety.
summary: A manager passes along an executive's out-of-touch comfort about moving the office somewhere dangerous, which only helps those who ride in limousines.

title: Doing Two Jobs, Expecting Bonus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't think it was possible, but for the past month I've done my own job plus Ted's, and done them well.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know that you're marveling at my accomplishment and wondering how you can reward me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I can fire Carl and make this idiot do his job too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll bet we're thinking of the same bonus amount!

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has been covering his own job and his coworker Ted's for a month, and hints that he deserves a reward. The Boss's thought bubble reveals he is considering firing another employee, Carl, and piling that work onto Dilbert as well. Dilbert, oblivious, says he bets they are thinking of the same bonus amount.
punchline: Dilbert expects a bonus for his extra effort, while the Boss is actually plotting to reward competence with even more unpaid work.
summary: An employee who has quietly doubled his workload angles for a payout, unaware his manager plans to dump a third person's duties on him instead.

title: Attorney Threatens Suit Over Time Machine

transcript.speaker: Attorney

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think you should consult with your client before being so belligerent.

situation: A lawyer warns Dogbert that he will sue if his client is hurt by Dogbert's untested time machine. Dogbert calmly suggests he consult his client first. In the last panel, Dogbert has raised himself on a scissor lift and is working the machine with a plunger while Dilbert and the Boss sit together in the capsule, so the client is the Boss.
punchline: The lawyer's client is the Boss, who is already sitting inside the untested time machine with Dilbert, so the threat comes too late and Dogbert is about to launch it anyway.
summary: A lawyer blusters about legal action against a dubious time machine, unaware that his own client is already strapped inside it.

title: Owl-Powered Monster Truck Sales Pitch

When Dilbert asks where the owls come from, the salesman explains that the engine noise stuns them so you can simply collect them from the ground.
punchline: The salesman's 'environmentally friendly' vehicle is a huge, noisy gas-guzzler that literally kills wildlife for fuel, absurdly contradicting the buyer's request.
summary: A car dealer sells a customer who wants an eco-friendly ride a colossal truck that runs on stunned owls.

title: Award Chair Replaces Stolen Chair

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: My dedication has been rewarded! This is the happiest moment of my life!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wow! It's lucky that I got a new chair on the same day that mine was stolen.

setting: Office meeting area and Asok's cubicle
situation: The Boss presents Asok with an award at a meeting, vaguely praising his work on 'whatever'. Asok is overjoyed to receive the prize, which turns out to be an office chair. Back in his cubicle, Asok remarks on the coincidence that he got a new chair on the very day his own chair was stolen.
punchline: The 'award' is just a chair, and Asok is so naive that he thinks its timing is lucky rather than realizing the Boss gave him a replacement for his stolen chair and called it a reward.
summary: A boss hands out a prize with no idea what it's for, and a gullible employee fails to notice it's merely a stand-in for the seat that was swiped from him.

title: Dilbert's Date Is the Crazy One

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: Do you think it's fair that you keep spitting on me just because you disagree with what I say?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: Why am I the one who always has to change to make other people happy?
