transcript.text: Because you're the crazy one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: Now you're all quiet. Why can't men learn to communicate?

setting: Outdoors on a walking path beside a hedge
situation: Dilbert walks outdoors with a woman on a date, both holding ice cream cones. She complains about his behavior and asks why she is always the one who has to change to keep others happy. Dilbert silently thinks that she is the crazy one, then she criticizes him for being quiet and says men can't communicate.
punchline: Dilbert's unspoken thought that she is the crazy one explains his silence, which she then blames on men's supposed inability to communicate, ironically proving she doesn't actually want honest communication.
summary: A woman scolds her quiet companion about communication while his unspoken thoughts reveal exactly why he stays silent.

title: Doctor Prescribes Monkey Brain Transplant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I keep forgetting where I put things.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: The problem is that you're stupid.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I recommend replacing your brain with a monkey brain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will that help?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: No, I just hate monkeys.

situation: The Boss, sitting half-dressed on an exam table, tells his doctor he keeps forgetting where he puts things. The doctor bluntly diagnoses him as stupid and recommends swapping his brain for a monkey's. When asked if that will help, the doctor admits it won't and that he simply dislikes monkeys.
punchline: The doctor's absurd treatment isn't medical at all; it is just a petty way of punishing a patient he considers stupid while indulging an unrelated grudge against monkeys.
summary: A forgetful patient gets an insulting diagnosis and a bizarre surgical recommendation that turns out to be motivated by sheer spite.

title: Asking Vendors for Freebies Politely

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The beta version looks great. Now ask if they'll toss in an archive option for no extra money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a great idea. Or... maybe I could save time by realizing that they aren't raging morons who enjoy working for free.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's all in the way you ask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll try yelling.

situation: The Boss reviews a vendor's beta software and tells Dilbert to ask the vendor to add an archive feature at no extra cost. Dilbert sarcastically points out that the vendor would never work for free. When the Boss insists it depends on how you ask, Dilbert says he'll try yelling.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests that yelling is the only way to get a vendor to work for free, mocking the Boss's belief that politeness or phrasing can extract free work.
summary: Told to wheedle extra software features out of a vendor without paying, Dilbert replies with sarcasm and agrees to shout his request.

file: 2005/2005-08-19_alleged dinosuar_beer can_best barbecue sauce_caught dinosaur_dental floss_pull tab_topper vs boss.gif
title: Topper Tops the Boss's Fish Story

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper vs. the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was the biggest fish ever caught in that lake!

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I once caught a dinosaur by using nothing but dental floss and a pull tab from a beer can.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to see this alleged dinosaur.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: Too late. I also make the world's best barbecue sauce.

situation: The Boss brags about the biggest fish ever caught in a lake, and his smug coworker Topper dismisses it as nothing. Topper claims he once caught a dinosaur using dental floss and a beer can pull tab. When the Boss asks to see the dinosaur, Topper says it's too late because he turned it into barbecue sauce.
punchline: Topper's absurd boast escalates beyond any possibility of proof, and he implies he cooked the dinosaur into barbecue sauce so there's no evidence to challenge his lie.
summary: A rival one-ups his boss's fishing tale with an impossible dinosaur story that conveniently left no evidence behind.

title: Dilbert Requests a BlackBerry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a BlackBerry so I can be in e-mail contact at all times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be able to do work all day and all night. My productivity will soar!

transcript.speaker: Unknown speaker
transcript.text: Trust me; it doesn't look good.

setting: The Boss's office, then a conference room meeting
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for a BlackBerry, promising he will work around the clock and boost productivity. In the last panel, a meeting is underway where Dilbert, the Boss and a coworker sit at the table while someone off to the side warns that using the device in this setting looks bad.
punchline: Having a BlackBerry makes you look rude and distracted in meetings, so the supposed productivity boost comes at a social cost, and it also means being on call all day and night.
summary: An employee pitches a handheld email device as a productivity miracle, only to be told it will make him look bad in meetings.

file: 2005/2005-02-01_furry log_nick name_cute names_creating hostile environment_squirrel infested stump.gif
title: Furry Log Versus Hostile Environment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, did you call the Director of Human Resources a "furry log"?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're promoting teamwork with a cute nickname or creating a hostile environment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which is it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's teamwork, you squirrel-infested stump.

situation: The Boss confronts Alice about calling the Director of Human Resources a "furry log" and admits he can't tell whether it is a friendly nickname or harassment. He asks her which it is. Alice insists it is teamwork while insulting him with a similar nature-themed name.
punchline: Alice claims her insult is just a cute teamwork nickname, then proves it is hostile by immediately insulting the Boss as a "squirrel-infested stump."
summary: A manager wonders whether an employee's odd nickname for an HR executive is friendly or abusive, and her answer settles nothing while insulting him too.

file: 2005/2005-08-03_my hat_can't see_perfect for job_reverse psychology_potentail jumpers.gif
title: Dogbert Negotiates With Jumper Victims

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I understand that you have an opening for a negotiator who deals with potential jumpers.

transcript.speaker: Police Chief
transcript.text: I can't see you because my hat is in the way, but you sound perfect for the job.

transcript.speaker: Police Chief
transcript.text: Your reverse psychology didn't work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What reverse psychology?

setting: A police chief's office, then a rooftop ledge
situation: Dogbert interviews with a police chief for a job as a negotiator who talks potential jumpers off ledges. The chief hires him without even seeing him over the brim of his hat. In the last panel the chief stands on the roof, and a pair of legs in the ground suggests someone jumped or was pushed off the ledge while Dogbert innocently denies using any reverse psychology.
punchline: Dogbert, a notoriously unscrupulous character, apparently used reverse psychology on a would-be jumper so that the person jumped, and he feigns innocence when confronted.
summary: A cynical dog gets hired to talk people off ledges, but his methods seem to push them over instead.

title: Stock Software Needs Atypical Testimonials

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm creating software that will help small investors pick stocks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It combines past trends that are not indicative of the future with the user's hubris and ignorance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now all I need are testimonials from people whose results are not typical!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So it works?

situation: Dogbert sits at a computer and tells Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, about his new stock-picking software for small investors. He cheerfully admits it just mixes unreliable past trends with the user's overconfidence and ignorance. He then says he only needs testimonials from people with atypical results, and Dilbert asks if it works.
punchline: Dogbert openly admits the software is worthless and that its marketing will rely on cherry-picked lucky outliers, mocking the 'results not typical' disclaimers of investment schemes.
summary: A scheming dog pitches a stock-picking program that is built on useless data and gullible users, planning to market it with hand-picked lucky success stories.

title: The Fastest Lawyer's Nine-Cent Bill

transcript.speaker: Homeless man
transcript.text: I was the world's fastest worker.

transcript.speaker: Homeless man
transcript.text: My big mistake was becoming a lawyer.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flashback

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Do you think I need an estate plan?

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Here's your will and here's my bill for 9 cents.

setting: A city sidewalk against a brick wall, then a flashback to a lawyer's office
situation: A disheveled, barefoot man in a tattered suit sits on the pavement beside a small orange creature and explains how he ended up homeless. In a flashback, he is a lawyer who answers a client's question about an estate plan by instantly handing over a finished will along with a bill for only nine cents.
punchline: He was so fast at his legal work that he billed for mere seconds of effort, charging nine cents instead of the hefty hourly fees lawyers normally collect, which ruined his career.
summary: A once-speedy attorney now living on the street blames his poverty on charging a pittance for his lightning-quick work.

title: Dogbert's Insulting Company FAQ

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert writes a F.A.Q. for the company web site

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Question 8: Why won't my file open when I'm eating toast?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Answer 8: That is the stupidest question ever! Do not have children!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I sure hope someone asks that question.

situation: Dogbert is writing a FAQ for the company web site and types out a ridiculous user question about files not opening while eating toast. He answers it with an insult and a recommendation that the asker not reproduce. Alone at his desk, he then thinks that he hopes someone actually asks the question.
punchline: Dogbert invents a silly question just so he can enjoy the chance to insult whoever might ask it, showing he writes the FAQ for his own amusement rather than to help users.
summary: A sarcastic dog composes a help page whose imaginary question exists only to let him belittle future readers.

title: World's Most Desperate Venture Capitalist

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vijay, the world's most desperate venture capitalist

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: Does anyone need a napkin to write on?

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: What are you thinking right now? Could it be a business plan?

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: Take my money!!! Take it!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's nice.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: During lunch, a venture capitalist named Vijay hovers over the table offering napkins and urging Dilbert and his coworkers to jot down business plans. When Dilbert merely chews his food, Vijay becomes frantic and starts forcing stacks of cash into his hands. A coworker at the table remarks that he is nice.
punchline: Venture capital is usually hard to get, but this investor is so desperate to fund any idea that he practically throws money at people, and the coworkers see it as a pleasant quirk.
summary: An overeager investor tries to shower a lunching engineer with cash before any idea has even been pitched.

title: Threatening Dilbert, Then Head-Sized Comeuppance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For a boss's pet, you're nice.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I see no reason to be unkind

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Buwhahaha! We're alone now, nerdling! Do my bidding or I will eat you alive!!!

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: They always forget to factor in your head size.

situation: Dilbert tells a woman, who is known as the boss's favorite, that she is surprisingly nice. She is polite until the boss is out of earshot, then turns monstrous and threatens to eat Dilbert alive unless he does her bidding. In the last panel she is stuck on top of Dilbert's head, apparently while trying to swallow him, and a bald coworker remarks that people always forget his head size.
punchline: The boss's pet's attempt to devour Dilbert fails because she can't fit his oversized head into her mouth, a running gag about Dilbert's big head.
summary: A seemingly sweet favorite of management reveals a menacing side when no one is watching, but her plan to swallow Dilbert is thwarted by his enormous head.

title: Cannibal Seeks Plump Seatmate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are there meals on this flight?

transcript.speaker: Airline Agent
transcript.text: Yes, if you're a cannibal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That is not funny. After this flight, I'm going to complain to your supervisor.

transcript.speaker: Cannibal
transcript.text: Can you put me next to the plump guy?

transcript.speaker: Airline Agent
transcript.text: Sure. He's in B8.

setting: Elbonia Airlines check-in counter at an airport
situation: The Boss asks an Elbonia Airlines agent whether meals are served on the flight and gets a sarcastic reply about cannibals. He threatens to complain to the agent's supervisor. A tribal cannibal then steps up and asks to be seated next to the plump guy, and the agent cheerfully gives him the seat number of the Boss.
punchline: The agent's cannibal joke turns out to be literally true when a cannibal asks to sit beside the plump passenger, and the agent hands over the Boss's seat, showing the airline treats passengers as food.
summary: A passenger who is offended by an airline agent's quip about in-flight meals watches in dismay as an actual cannibal asks to be seated next to him.

title: Overtime, Death, and Third Things

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know what two things are very similar?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unpaid overtime and death. They both deny me the pleasures of being alive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a good night kiss?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hey, you found a third thing!

setting: Outside a house at night, at the end of a date
situation: Dilbert stands with a woman at the end of an evening and complains that unpaid overtime and death are alike because both keep him from enjoying life. He then asks for a good night kiss. She retorts that he has just found a third thing that denies him the pleasures of being alive.
punchline: Dilbert's romantic request earns him a rejection disguised as agreement, since she implies that his company is as lifeless as death and unpaid overtime.
summary: A man grumbling about overworking and mortality on a date gets a sharp reply when he angles for an end-of-evening smooch.

title: Two CEOs, Double the Pay

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: After the merger, we'll have two CEOs sharing the top job.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A spokesperson explained "If our stockholders don't mind paying one CEO 450 times the average employee's salary. . .

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: . . . they shouldn't mind doing it twice."

situation: At a meeting table, the Pointy-Haired Boss reads from a paper announcing that two CEOs will share the top job after a merger. Captions quote a spokesperson who argues that stockholders already tolerate paying one CEO 450 times the average employee's salary, so paying two should be fine.
punchline: The company justifies doubling already outrageous executive pay by pointing out that shareholders have already accepted the absurdity once.
summary: A merger announcement is defended with the logic that overpaying one chief executive makes overpaying two perfectly acceptable.

title: Bonuses Before Worthless Receivables Surface

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only way to meet our sales target is by selling to customers who have bad credit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay. We'll get our bonuses before anyone realizes that the accounts receivables are worthless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key to getting bonuses is acting surprised later.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel unclean.

situation: Dilbert warns his boss that the sales target can only be reached by selling to customers with bad credit. The boss is unbothered, explaining that they will collect their bonuses before anyone discovers the receivables are worthless. He adds that they just need to act surprised later, leaving Dilbert feeling morally tainted.
punchline: The boss cheerfully treats fraudulent-looking sales as a bonus strategy, advising that feigned surprise is the way to avoid blame, while Dilbert is left feeling complicit.
summary: A manager plans to cash in on doomed sales and fake astonishment afterwards, to his employee's discomfort.

transcript.text: We want to maintain a smooth line-of-sight for aesthetic reasons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me see if I understand your point of view.

summary: An employee ridicules a petty decor rule by absurdly exaggerating its reasoning and then insulting the manager who enforces it.

She recognizes him as Carly, and he then rates her appearance with a number, as if he were a crude, leering stereotype of a man.
punchline: The salesman is the CEO of HP, and the strip implies he is Carly Fiorina, the real HP chief at the time, in a man's suit, so his number rating of the receptionist's looks mocks a stereotypical male boss. Meanwhile the receptionist's grand title is just an inflated name for her job.
summary: Two people reveal their supposedly grand hidden identities, and one of them turns out to be a famous executive who then awkwardly judges the other's looks.

title: Xeno's Doughnut Date Ruined

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Hurry.

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a date at a restaurant and makes a nerdy remark about people only taking half of the last doughnut, naming it after Zeno's paradox. His date reacts with growing despair and drinks her wine. The waiter, who overheard, offers to switch them to hard liquor, and the date urgently asks him to hurry.
punchline: Dilbert's pedantic math joke is so painfully dull that even the waiter sympathizes and his date desperately wants stronger alcohol to endure it.
summary: A man's geeky paradox joke on a date is so excruciating that the waiter offers hard liquor and his companion begs for it fast.

punchline: The speaker deflects blame onto whoever happens to be conveniently absent and unable to defend himself.
summary: A project leader waits for a colleague to step out of the room before pinning the blame for his failure on him.

title: Brain Surgery Without Anesthesia Coverage

transcript.text: That reminds me: Your insurance doesn't cover anesthesia.

The patient suspiciously asks how he can be sure Dogbert won't just eat the cauliflower and pretend the operation worked. Dogbert ignores the question and casually mentions the patient's insurance doesn't cover anesthesia.
punchline: Dogbert dodges the patient's fraud concern by revealing the operation will be performed while he is fully awake, since insurance won't pay for anesthesia.
summary: A con-artist doctor dog plans a ludicrous brain swap and then cheerfully reveals his patient will feel every moment of it.

transcript.text: Synergy

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thash sho bee-oo-tiful!!!

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert his business plan: an art gallery with a full bar that sells awful art at inflated prices. In the final panel, drunk patrons at the bar sit near a framed portrait and slur their praise, enthusiastically admiring it.
punchline: The bar and the terrible, overpriced art work together because intoxicated customers will gush over and buy anything, making the 'synergy' a scam.
summary: Dogbert's scheme pairs free-flowing alcohol with junk art so tipsy patrons will pay inflated prices and call it beautiful.

situation: Dogbert, running a tech support line, answers a caller's problem by telling him to reboot himself, then suggests cloning himself and putting the clone up for adoption. The puzzled caller listens on the phone while Dogbert escalates to insulting his parents' work.
punchline: Dogbert turns standard tech support jargon into a series of insults, implying the caller is a buggy, poorly built human product whose parents released him without proper testing.
summary: A tech support agent answers a user's trouble by treating the user as a faulty piece of software and mocking his upbringing in programmer terms.

title: Taking the Fifth Over Stolen Computers

transcript.text: Why did you leave your last job?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did they make you confess?

setting: Job interview in an office, across a desk
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and asks why he left his previous job. The candidate says he was accused of stealing four computers. When asked whether he was forced to confess, he replies that he took the fifth, which is ambiguous between the legal right and a fifth computer.
punchline: 'Taking the fifth' is a pun: the candidate means he stole a fifth computer, not that he invoked his right against self-incrimination, which in effect admits he was a thief.

title: Failing Eighty Percent of Wally

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his four staff members that company policy requires him to give failing reviews to 20% of his team. He calculates that this equals 80% of one person, then picks Wally and reads out a review that praises only Wally's calf muscles and ankles while condemning the rest of him.
punchline: The Boss takes a forced-ranking quota so literally that he fails a fraction of a person, dissecting Wally's body into passing and failing parts.
summary: Stuck with a mandatory quota of bad reviews, a manager does the math on his four employees and awards a body-part-by-body-part verdict to one unlucky worker.

title: Boss Cites Vendor Against Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to standardize the department on a new programming language.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With all due respect, that sort of decision should be made by someone who knows his mass from a black hole.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The vendor warned me that you couldn't be objective.

situation: The Boss announces he has chosen a new programming language to standardize the department on. Dilbert objects that the decision should be made by someone with technical knowledge, insulting the Boss's ignorance. The Boss dismisses the criticism by saying the vendor already warned him that Dilbert would be biased.
punchline: The Boss has been primed by the vendor to discount any technical objection as bias, so he can ignore expert advice and keep his uninformed decision.
summary: A manager picks a programming language without understanding it and waves off the engineer's protest by citing a sales pitch that pre-emptively labeled him biased.

file: 2005/2005-05-10_stress hump_no asignment_no compeer no freinds_resist_the hump.gif
title: New Employee Befriends Stress Hump

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new employee

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: No assignment... No computer... No friends to talk to...

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: It's just me and this huge stress hump.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Must... resist... urge... to name the hump... and talk to it.

transcript.speaker: Hump
transcript.text: Wazzup?

situation: A new employee sits alone in his cubicle with no assignment, no computer and no coworkers to talk to. He notices the stress lump on his own body and, growing desperate for company, struggles against the urge to name it and talk to it. The lump answers him anyway with a greeting.
punchline: The new employee's isolation and boredom are so extreme that he is on the verge of befriending his own stress hump, which then talks back, implying he is already losing his grip.
summary: Left with nothing to do and nobody to talk to, a lonely newcomer starts to hear his own body's stress bump greet him.

file: 2005/2005-11-10_underlings_anything useful_little people_deadly accident_vow_in office_listening to little people.gif
title: Boss Won't Hear From Underlings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, don't let the underlings of my underling come into my office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't learn anything useful by listening to the little people.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I renew my vow to lure you into a deadly accident!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! Whoa! Tell it to my underling.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to keep the underlings of his underling out of his office, claiming he can't learn anything useful from the little people. Carol, fed up with the condescension, renews her vow to lure him into a deadly accident. The Boss panics and tells her to take it up with his underling instead.
punchline: The Boss insists on ignoring everyone below him, so when Carol threatens him he reflexively applies the same rule and tries to send her to his underling, showing he is both arrogant and a coward.
summary: A snobbish manager shuts out lower-level staff until his assistant's murderous threat makes him pass the problem down the chain.

file: 2005/2005-01-24_stressful project_worst thing_pep talk_jumped window_imprint on window screen.gif
title: Pep Talk Ends in Window Disaster

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I hear that your project is stressful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes it helps if you ask yourself: What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd the pep talk go?

situation: A bald, glasses-wearing manager tells a visibly frazzled Alice that he's heard her project is stressful and suggests she ask herself what the worst thing that could happen is. In the last panel Dilbert asks how the pep talk went, and the manager stands beside a window with a human-shaped hole smashed through it, implying Alice has just jumped out.
punchline: The manager's advice to imagine the worst possible outcome backfires literally: Alice responds by hurling herself through the window, showing the pep talk made her feel worse, not better.
summary: A clueless supervisor's attempt to comfort a stressed employee leaves a person-shaped hole in the office window.

title: Cremated Liar Salsa Dances Bodiless

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Cremated Habitual Liar

transcript.speaker: The Cremated Habitual Liar
transcript.text: I'm learning to salsa dance in here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You are NOT salsa dancing! You have no body.

transcript.speaker: The Cremated Habitual Liar
transcript.text: Tell that to my dance instructor.

transcript.speaker: The Cremated Habitual Liar
transcript.text: Focus!

situation: A voice from an urn or bottle on Alice's desk, identified as the cremated habitual liar, claims to be learning salsa dancing inside it. Alice, sitting with her arms crossed, angrily points out that he has no body. He replies by invoking his dance instructor, then shouts 'Focus!' as if mid-lesson.
punchline: Even after being cremated, the habitual liar keeps lying, and doubles down on an impossible claim by inventing an imaginary dance instructor.
summary: A dead man's ashes in a bottle keep up their compulsive fibbing, insisting on dance lessons while an exasperated coworker calls the bluff.

title: Illegal Component Adds Flavor to Contract

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your bid to build our cell phone network is the lowest by far.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: But I'd feel more comfortable if it had an illegal component.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like a bribe? Or helping you build a nuclear weapon?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Yes, just something to add flavor.

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dilbert tells a bearded vendor in a tall dark hat that his bid to build the company's cell phone network is the lowest by far. The vendor says he would be more comfortable if the deal included something illegal. When Dilbert guesses a bribe or help building a nuclear weapon, the vendor cheerfully agrees and says it is just to add flavor.
punchline: The vendor treats serious crimes like bribery and nuclear weapons development as casual seasoning for a routine business contract.
summary: A cut-rate telecom contractor insists that a little criminal activity would make the deal feel more complete.

file: 2005/2005-12-13_dogberts_selfish cell phone_no number_can bother people_stop bothering me.gif
title: Dogbert's One-Way Cell Phone Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting Dogbert's Selfish Cell Phone Company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It has no phone number. You can call people and bother them when they're busy, but they can't do the same to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi Mom. Oh, nothing. I'm just walking someplace.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop bothering me!

setting: Dilbert's living room, then outdoors on a street
situation: Dogbert announces a new cell phone company whose phones have no number, so customers can call out and interrupt others but nobody can call them. Dilbert, now a customer, calls his mother while walking somewhere. The final panel suggests the service is meant to be inconsiderate.
punchline: The 'Stop bothering me!' burst in the last panel suggests that Dilbert is being rude to his mom, and that a phone service which lets you pester others while being unreachable yourself is built entirely for selfishness.
summary: Dogbert launches a phone service that lets subscribers interrupt everyone else while remaining impossible to reach, and Dilbert promptly uses it on his own mother.

file: 2005/2005-04-17_loopy_couldn't end story_vacation_cocnuts_rapped_round and hairy_coconut trees_brown_being chased_co worker.gif
title: Loopy's Endless Coconut Vacation Story

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Introducing Loopy, the woman who couldn't end a story

transcript.speaker: Loopy
transcript.text: Did I tell you about my vacation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Loopy
transcript.text: We learned about coconuts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trapped.

transcript.speaker: Loopy
transcript.text: Coconuts are round and hairy, and they grow on trees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must escape.

transcript.speaker: Loopy
transcript.text: Coconut trees are found in many countries.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must use my ejector seat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Foomp!

transcript.speaker: Loopy
transcript.text: They're brown.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! She has a pursuit chair!!!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Foomp!

transcript.speaker: Loopy
transcript.text: I took lots of pictures.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must...aim for traffic.

setting: Office cubicles, then outdoors over hills as the characters fly through the air
situation: Loopy, a new co-worker who can't end a story, corners Dilbert with a dull account of her vacation and coconuts. Dilbert escapes through the ceiling using an ejector seat built into his office chair. Loopy follows with her own ejector chair, and both parachute down while she keeps talking and Dilbert hopes to land in traffic.
punchline: Dilbert's extreme escape from a boring story fails because the talker has the same ejector-seat chair and pursues him mid-air, so he's reduced to hoping for a fatal landing in traffic.
summary: A coworker's tedious holiday chatter drives a man to eject from his chair, only for her to blast off after him still talking.

title: Catbert Scolds Alice's Desk Lunch

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Eating at your desk is like stealing from the company, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm working through my lunch hour, you furry log.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Furry log?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's a term of endearment.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, accuses Alice of stealing from the company because she eats at her desk. Alice, who is working through her lunch hour, insults him by calling him a furry log. When he questions the name, she calmly claims it is a term of endearment.
punchline: Alice responds to a bureaucratic accusation with an insult, then deadpans that it was affectionate, showing she has no fear of HR.
summary: An HR cat accuses a hard-working woman of theft for snacking at her desk, and she shrugs him off with a dismissive nickname.

title: Dilbert's Mixed Blessing Lunch Invitation

transcript.speaker: Female Coworker
transcript.text: All of my ex-boyfriends were sexy and handsome.

transcript.speaker: Female Coworker
transcript.text: I finally realized that dating sexy, handsome men isn't for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel a mixed blessing coming my way.

transcript.speaker: Female Coworker
transcript.text: What are you doing for lunch?

situation: A female coworker stands beside Dilbert's desk and tells him that all her exes were sexy and handsome, and that she has decided such men aren't right for her. Dilbert realizes where this is heading, and she then asks what he is doing for lunch.
punchline: She is implicitly inviting Dilbert to lunch because he is neither sexy nor handsome, which Dilbert recognizes as a backhanded compliment, a mixed blessing.
summary: A coworker swearing off good-looking men ends up inviting the plain-looking Dilbert out, an offer that is flattering and insulting at once.

file: 2005/2005-11-23_ted snadwhich_left in breakroom_marked ted_lost weight_anger_red faced.gif
title: The Ted Sandwich Bait-and-Switch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be right back. I'm going to grab a Ted sandwich before the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The food people always leave one sandwich in the break room fridge labeled Ted. It tastes like ham.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're looking good, Ted. Have you lost weight?

setting: Office cubicle area and conference room
situation: The Boss tells Alice he is going to eat the sandwich the catering staff always leave in the fridge labeled with Ted's name. In the meeting room, an angry Ted sits next to the Boss, who is eating his sandwich, while Dilbert innocently compliments Ted on looking like he has lost weight.
punchline: The Boss has been stealing Ted's labeled lunch, so Ted is going hungry and losing weight, and Dilbert's compliment unwittingly points out the result of the theft.
summary: A manager helps himself to a coworker's labeled fridge sandwich, and the hungry, fuming coworker is then complimented on his slimmer figure.

title: One Birthday Party, Already Over

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: In order to improve office efficiency, all birthdays will be celebrated on the same day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mean one celebration per year, or just once and then we're done forever?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Just once.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, at least I'll feel special once. What day is the celebration?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yesterday.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces at a meeting that all employee birthdays will be consolidated into a single celebration to boost efficiency. Dilbert asks whether this is yearly or a one-time event, and Catbert confirms it is a one-off. When Dilbert asks when it will be held, Catbert reveals it already happened.
punchline: The one-time birthday celebration was held yesterday, so employees never even got to enjoy the single party that replaced all their birthdays.
summary: An HR villain scraps every individual birthday in favor of one company party that turns out to have already come and gone.

title: Stress Hump Explodes After Denial

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Could I have a few days off to see if my stress hump goes away?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stress is all in your mind. I should fire you and your hump right now for even asking!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just because he said no?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It was the way he said it.

setting: The Boss's office, then the hallway
situation: An employee with a visible stress hump on his back asks the boss for a few days off to see if it goes away. The boss refuses, dismisses stress as imaginary and threatens to fire him and his hump. Afterward Dilbert asks if the denial caused the reaction, and the employee's stress hump has ballooned into a huge cloud-like growth.
punchline: The boss's hostile reaction made the employee's stress hump grow enormous, showing that stress is very real and that managers make it worse.
summary: A worker's physical stress deformity swells to enormous size after his boss scoffs at his request for time off.

title: Sourpuss Coughs Up Hairball Objection

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does anyone have an issue with the plan as I've outlined it?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Kah! Kah! Kah!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm with Sourpuss.

situation: Dilbert presents a plan to his colleagues at a meeting and asks if anyone objects. Sourpuss, the cat, retches violently over the table, apparently coughing up a hairball onto the papers. Alice, rather than criticizing the plan directly, says she agrees with the cat's reaction.
punchline: Alice sides with the cat's retching as the response to the plan, implying the plan is so bad it makes you sick.
summary: A cat's violent gagging at a proposal gets endorsed by a coworker as the most fitting review.

file: 2005/2005-01-01_evil director_himan resources_downsized_free dvd_live off land_shoplifting_running fast.gif
title: Catbert's Downsizing Survival DVD

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, assures a meeting that laid-off employees need not worry because they will receive a free DVD on living off the land. In the last panel, a laid-off man sits in an armchair at home watching the DVD on an old TV, taking notes as it advises that shoplifting success depends on running very fast.
punchline: The 'live off the land' DVD from HR turns out to be a guide to petty crime, showing how little help downsized employees really get.
summary: Human resources offers laid-off workers a survival video that turns out to be a shoplifting tutorial.

file: 2005/2005-04-20_doctors offcie_exam room_toxikill_drug comapny_totally hot_side effects_what eaten_doctor_thinking of date_drug rep_hot_payoff_kick back_medical.gif

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: The drug company's rep is totally hot and she said she'd take me to lunch if I sell enough of this stuff.

transcript.text: Will there be any side effects?

transcript.speaker: Doctor

situation: Dilbert is at a checkup, and the doctor tells him he is healthy but still needs to be prescribed a drug called Toxikill. The doctor explains that an attractive drug company rep promised him lunch if he sells enough of the drug. Dilbert asks about side effects, and the doctor answers in terms of his own lunch.
punchline: The doctor misunderstands the side-effects question as being about his own meal, showing that his only concern is the perk he gets for prescribing, not the patient's health.
summary: A physician admits he's pushing an unneeded medication on a healthy patient just to earn a lunch date with a pharmaceutical saleswoman.

title: Negotiator Wants Feedback After Shooting

transcript.text: I'll leave an evaluation form. Please let us know how we're doing!

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: Done deal.

setting: Outdoors beside a red police car, facing a building wall
situation: Dogbert, acting as a police negotiator, uses a megaphone from atop a police car to tell a suspect to surrender. When the suspect emerges, a police officer opens fire. Afterward Dogbert cheerfully announces he will leave an evaluation form for the suspect to rate the service.
punchline: The negotiator treats a violent police shootout like a customer service interaction, asking the person who was just shot at to fill out a satisfaction survey.
summary: A canine hostage negotiator blithely asks for service feedback after the cops gun down the suspect he was supposed to talk out.

title: Catbert Renames HR With Evil Laugh

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I might change my department's name.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: To "Workplace Services." Bu-wha-ha-ha-ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When things don't sound evil enough on their own, I like to toss in a bu-wha-ha-ha-ha.

setting: Catbert's office in the human resources department
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells an employee seated in front of his desk that he might rename his department. He announces the bland new name "Workplace Services" and bursts into an evil laugh. He then explains that he adds the laugh whenever something doesn't sound evil enough by itself.
punchline: The new name is so bland and harmless-sounding that Catbert has to add an evil laugh to keep it sounding sinister, which exposes how corporate euphemisms disguise unpleasant HR practices.
summary: A malevolent feline HR chief plans a friendlier department title and compensates for its blandness with a villainous cackle.

file: 2005/2005-01-02_weekly wally report_worthless iput_harmful advice_ignored email_priorities_my budget estimates_any success_format.gif
title: Wally's Report Full of Failures

transcript.text: The weekly Wally report is bristling with tales of success.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I gave worthless input to marketing because they weren't specific about what they wanted.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I missed Alice's project meeting because she never confirmed the location.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I gave harmful advice to the sales team because they rushed me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I ignored my e-mail for a week because you said to focus on priorities.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I didn't submit my budget estimates because Asok never told me what format to use.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can you call any of that success??!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, I'd compare it to my written objectives, but you never gave me any.

situation: The Boss praises Wally's weekly report for being full of success stories. Wally then reads out a series of failures and non-contributions, each blamed on someone else's lack of clarity or direction. When the Boss objects that these aren't successes, Wally says he can't measure against objectives because the Boss never gave him any.
punchline: Wally turns the tables by redefining laziness as success, since without written objectives the Boss has no basis for calling anything a failure.
summary: A slacker employee reports his do-nothing week as a triumph and neatly pins every shortfall on others, including the manager who set no goals.

title: Arguing With Made-Up Definitions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: From now on, all of my arguments will be based on definitions that are not in any dictionary.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, I could argue that you're a fascist because you're wearing pajamas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm only wearing the top.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Man, I wish I didn't know that.

situation: Dogbert stands on Dilbert's bed and announces that all his future arguments will rely on definitions found in no dictionary. He demonstrates by calling Dilbert a fascist for wearing pajamas. Dilbert responds by clarifying that he is only wearing the pajama top, which gives Dogbert more information than he wanted.
punchline: Dilbert literally defends himself against a nonsense accusation by revealing he's wearing no pajama bottoms, an embarrassing overshare that makes Dogbert regret engaging.
summary: Dogbert accuses a bedridden Dilbert of something absurd using invented terminology, and Dilbert's literal-minded rebuttal reveals far too much.

title: Cable Company Abusive Service Windows

transcript.speaker: Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I enjoy giving people abusive service windows.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Well, if you can't be home from March to October, then say goodbye to Regis and Kelly!

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, then a cable company service desk
situation: Ratbert announces he is quitting to work for the cable company, explaining that he enjoys giving customers abusive service windows. In the final panel he is at a phone desk wearing a headset, threatening a customer that if they can't be home from March to October for the installation, they'll lose their TV service.
punchline: Cable companies are mocked for giving customers absurdly long appointment windows, and Ratbert's job fits that exactly: a window stretching from March to October, with a threat to cut off daytime TV shows as the penalty.
summary: A small lab animal takes a call-center job at the cable company because he relishes forcing customers to wait around for months-long installation slots.

title: Boss's Calendar Always Open, Never Available

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need five minutes on the Pointy-Haired Boss's calendar.

transcript.speaker: Boss's Assistant
transcript.text: No can do.

transcript.speaker: Boss's Assistant
transcript.text: If I give you an appointment, I'll just have to cancel it later when something more important comes up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's he doing now?

transcript.speaker: Boss's Assistant
transcript.text: Combing his knuckles.

setting: Office cubicle area outside the boss's office
situation: Dilbert asks the Pointy-Haired Boss's assistant for a five-minute slot on the boss's calendar. She refuses, explaining that she would only have to cancel it later when something more important comes up. When Dilbert asks what the boss is doing right now, she says he is combing his knuckles.
punchline: The boss's calendar is guarded as if his time is precious, yet at this very moment he is doing something utterly trivial, so nothing 'more important' is actually going on.
summary: A gatekeeping assistant denies an employee a meeting slot with the boss, then reveals the boss is currently busy with a ridiculous grooming habit.

title: Ideal Candidate Thrives on Neglect

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you work well without supervision?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Yes! I thrive on vague objectives and a complete lack of recognition for my contribution!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you handle criticism?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'm not too proud to say it excites me!

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate across a desk. He asks whether the candidate can work without supervision and handle criticism. The candidate enthusiastically claims to love vague goals, no recognition, and criticism, telling the boss exactly what he wants to hear.
punchline: The candidate cheerfully embraces terrible working conditions as if they were perks, revealing that interviewees must pretend to enjoy being neglected and criticized to get hired.
summary: A job seeker eagerly pretends that poor management, zero appreciation and constant criticism are exactly what he's looking for in a position.

file: 2005/2005-05-05_share cubicle_date you_incredible time together_if it didn't work.gif

transcript.text: ...Always reminded of our incredible time together.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where's the bad?!! Where's the bad?!

situation: A female coworker stands behind Dilbert at his desk, hands on his shoulders, and says she would date him if they didn't share a cubicle. She explains that a breakup would mean seeing each other every day. When she describes this as being constantly reminded of their incredible time together, Dilbert frantically asks where the downside is.
punchline: The coworker presents the post-breakup scenario as a drawback, but she describes it so positively that Dilbert can't see any downside and desperately wants her to reconsider.
summary: A woman gives a flirty reason not to date her cubicle mate, but her argument backfires when it sounds like a perk to him.

file: 2005/2005-05-17_dilbert.com_owls for fuel_new suv_good idea_start breeding owls.gif
title: SUV Fueled By Owls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new SUV uses owls for fuel. It seemed like a good idea but now I can't find enough owls.

transcript.speaker: Alice

Alice deadpans that he will have to breed his own owls, and he agrees that was his plan. The final panel replaces the ending with a notice that the conclusion was deemed offensive and can only be seen on the Dilbert website.

summary: A manager's owl-burning car runs short of fuel, and the strip itself refuses to reveal how his breeding plan turns out.

title: Wally Swaps Boss's Chapstick With Glue

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tastes different.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I lost a good glue stick, but I gained a few hours of quiet.

situation: The Boss wanders into Wally's cubicle, finds what he thinks is his chapstick and applies it. Thinking it tastes different, he doesn't realize it's actually a glue stick. Later Wally tells Dilbert, over coffee, that sacrificing a glue stick was worth it for the peace and quiet.
punchline: Wally deliberately let the Boss put glue on his lips so his mouth would be stuck shut, trading a glue stick for hours of silence from the chatty Boss.
summary: A boss mistakes a glue stick for his lip balm, and a smug coworker happily accepts the loss in exchange for blissful silence.

title: Dogbert's Anger Management Whapping Demonstration

transcript.text: My goal is to transform you from angry nuts into...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Angry nuts who have paid me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need a volunteer for our first demonstration. You, come here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Put your head about here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now try to control your anger while I do this...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whap whap whap whap whap whap

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: A seminar room where Dogbert stands on a stool addressing a group of angry employees
situation: Dogbert runs an anger management seminar for a group of furious employees and admits his real goal is to make them angry nuts who have paid him. He picks a volunteer, has her bend over, and repeatedly whacks her with an implement while telling her to control her anger. She ends up seething and enraged, and Dogbert blames her lack of sleep.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately provokes the volunteer with physical abuse, then blames her rage on poor sleep rather than on his own whacking.
summary: A scheming dog charges angry people for a seminar, then beats a volunteer and dismisses her fury as tiredness.

file: 2005/2005-07-07_do something_let you know_spitting on forehead_whats worng.gif
title: Cursing and Spitting as Feedback

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When you do something that I don't like, I'll let you know by cursing and then spitting on your forehead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could just tell me what I did wrong.

situation: Alice walks beside Dilbert and announces that her way of expressing displeasure will be to curse at him and spit on his forehead. Dilbert suggests she could simply explain what he did wrong. Alice responds by cursing, showing she is already annoyed.
punchline: Dilbert's reasonable suggestion is exactly the kind of thing that triggers Alice's cursing, so her announced feedback method is immediately put to use.
summary: A colleague lays out her unpleasant method of showing irritation, and a polite suggestion for a calmer alternative promptly earns her scorn.
keywords: tell me what i did wrong

title: Kids Trained to Use Defibrillator

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Milt, you have a wife and kids. How do you find time to do everything you need to do?

transcript.speaker: Milt
transcript.text: I had to give up a few things, such as exercising and eating healthy food.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Milt
transcript.text: Nah. The kids are trained to use the defibrillator.

situation: Dilbert asks his coworker Milt how he manages to fit everything into his life while raising a family. Milt explains he gave up exercising and eating healthy food to save time. When Dilbert says that sounds dangerous, Milt calmly replies that his kids are trained to use a defibrillator.
punchline: Milt has sacrificed his health so thoroughly to save time that he expects heart failure, and has casually prepared his children to revive him.
summary: A busy father trades away his health for extra hours and has even taught his children to restart his heart when it fails.

file: 2005/2005-03-16_set a conference call_secretary's job_carol_ask question_set up appointmet.gif
title: Asok Questions Secretary's Duties Reversal

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Asok, your Pointy-haired Boss wants you to set up a conference call with all the division managers.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Um... wouldn't that be his secretary's job?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And aren't you his secretary?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hey, I know. Why don't you try to get an appointment with him so you can ask that question?

situation: Carol, the Boss's secretary, tells Asok that the boss wants him to arrange a conference call with all the division managers. Asok objects that this should be the secretary's job and points out that she is the secretary. Carol sarcastically tells him to book an appointment with the boss to raise that question.
punchline: Carol knows that getting an appointment with the boss goes through her, so she sarcastically dares Asok to challenge the arrangement through the very person he is complaining about.
summary: A secretary hands off her own scheduling duty to a junior engineer and shuts down his protest by sending him through her own gatekeeping.

title: Rude Or Useless: Dilbert Chooses

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, Dilbert, can you update the yield numbers for our discontinued chips?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, if I have to choose between being rude and doing something useless...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Consider my crazy glare.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I'll start being useless.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to update yield numbers for a product line that has already been discontinued. Dilbert hints that he would rather be rude than do pointless work, so the coworker responds with an intimidating glare. Dilbert gives in and agrees to do the useless task.
punchline: Dilbert's willingness to be rude is overridden by a coworker's menacing glare, so he ends up doing the pointless work after all.
summary: A man asked to compile figures for a product that no longer exists is bullied into the task by a scary stare.

title: Sourpuss Mocks Dilbert's Pointless Work

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sourpuss

transcript.speaker: Sourpuss
transcript.text: Whatever you're doing there looks like a complete waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Sourpuss
transcript.text: If you beat your head against the wall, that doesn't make it a drum.

transcript.speaker: Sourpuss
transcript.text: People say the glass is half full. But they don't say of what.

situation: Sourpuss, a gloomy, sarcastic coworker, stands behind Dilbert as he works at his computer. He delivers a string of bleak, cynical remarks, first calling Dilbert's work a waste of time, then mocking his effort with a drum analogy, then deflating the optimistic glass-half-full saying. Dilbert keeps typing without responding.
punchline: Sourpuss undermines optimism and effort with pessimistic non-sequiturs, pointing out that a half-full glass could be full of anything unpleasant.
summary: A relentlessly negative coworker hovers over a busy colleague and dismantles both his efforts and a famous optimistic saying.

title: Comparing Raises Ends in Screaming

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please don't discuss your raise with co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What-ever.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's see how the losers and morons did.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You only got 6%? I got 8%.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: 9%. Why do you ask?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: 7.5%. Anything less would be humiliating.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, let me see... I think it was...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Brace for impact.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: GAAA!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has she yet learned why it is a bad idea to discuss her raise with co-workers?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sounds like it.

setting: Office cubicles and the boss's office
situation: The boss asks Alice not to discuss her raise with co-workers, and she brushes him off. She then goes around the office telling people she got 8% and asking what they got, only to find that Dilbert's neighbours all got more than she did. When Wally reveals he got 8.5%, Alice screams in frustration while Dilbert and Asok listen from afar.
punchline: Alice ignored the advice against comparing raises and ended up learning that her coworkers, including the ones she called losers and morons, all got bigger raises than she did.
summary: A smug employee brags about her pay bump to everyone, then discovers she got the smallest increase in the office and howls in anguish.

title: Alice Rages Over Dongle Misuse

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! This writer misused the technical term "dongle." That idiot!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm e-mailing this loser to tell him I plan to boycott the newspaper!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Die, loser, die!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll come back later.

situation: Alice reads a newspaper and becomes furious that the writer misused the technical term "dongle." She angrily types an email threatening to boycott the paper while shouting at her screen. The Boss, who had come to her cubicle, quietly decides to leave and return later.
punchline: Alice's disproportionate rage over a minor technical terminology error is so alarming that even her boss retreats from her cubicle.
summary: An engineer's fury at a journalist's sloppy jargon escalates into a keyboard-pounding tirade that sends her manager scurrying away.

file: 2005/2005-03-04_america_arrogance_elbonians_end of time_fight you_fix problems_what we do.gif
title: Elbonians Resist Arrogant American Fixer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: American Consultant
transcript.text: I'm from America and I'm here to fix all of your problems.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Your arrogance is offensive. We will form an armed resistance and fight you to the end of time!

transcript.speaker: American Consultant
transcript.text: Um... why?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: It's just something we do.

situation: An American visitor sits across a table from several tall-hatted Elbonians and announces that he has come to fix all of their problems. The Elbonians declare his arrogance offensive and vow to fight him with an armed resistance until the end of time. When he asks why, they shrug it off as simply something they do.
punchline: The Elbonians' eternal armed resistance is a reflex rather than a reasoned response, mocking both the condescending outsider and the endless cycle of conflict that follows foreign 'help'.
summary: A confident foreigner offers to solve a country's problems and is promised eternal armed opposition for no particular reason.

file: 2005/2005-07-10_wally reflctor_bad people_make you work_offer no resistance_order made_requires work. they blow it off_no work necessary.gif
tags: requires work. they blow it off
title: Wally Teaches the Work Reflector

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Asok, the move that I am about to teach you is called the "Wally Reflector."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Throughout the day, bad people will try to make you do work for them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At first, offer no resistance, as if you actually plan to do the work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then ask the offender to do a little bit of work himself.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Allow me to demonstrate.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, I need you to design a database for all of our product features and services.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Glad to do it!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All I need from you is a comprehensive list of the data fields you need included.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh... wow. I'm really busy. I'll have to get back to you on that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I'll never see that idiot again.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You inspire me, in a creepy kind of way.

situation: Wally explains to Asok a technique for dodging unwanted work, then demonstrates it when a coworker asks him to design a database. Wally cheerfully agrees but asks the requester to supply a comprehensive list of data fields, and the coworker backs off, claiming to be too busy.
punchline: Wally avoids work by feigning enthusiasm and then demanding a small amount of effort from the requester, who never follows up, leaving Asok both impressed and slightly disturbed.
summary: A lazy veteran shows a young colleague how to make people abandon their work requests simply by asking them to do a bit of the prep themselves.

file: 2005/2005-03-02_no landing strips_jump out of plane_airplane_mud_cushion_fall_flap arms.gif
title: Landing in Elbonia Without Runways

transcript.speaker: Travel agent
transcript.text: Elbonia has no landing strips, so you'll have to jump out of the plane.

transcript.speaker: Travel agent
transcript.text: Try to flap your arms and aim for a plump Elbonian to cushion your fall.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Dang.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Airplane.

setting: Airline or travel counter, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: A balding customer in a green sweater is told by an Elbonian airline agent that Elbonia has no landing strips, so passengers must jump from the plane. The agent advises flapping arms and aiming for a plump Elbonian to break the fall. In the last panel, two Elbonians sit stuck in the mud, one grumbling that it hurt while the other calmly says the word for what just landed.
punchline: The Elbonians in the mud have evidently been landed on by plummeting passengers so often that they respond with weary resignation, and one simply names the airplane overhead.
summary: Travelers to a primitive country are told to parachute out and use locals as human landing cushions, which the muddy locals endure with deadpan weariness.

file: 2005/2005-12-28_new guy_project staus report_random pharse_generatormmeail_listens_when he's talking.gif
title: Random Phrase Generator Status Reports

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice

situation: The Boss asks Alice to train the new employee on writing project status reports. Alice cheerfully explains, right in front of the Boss, that nobody writes real reports because he never reads them, so everyone just uses a random phrase generator. When the new guy points out she said this in front of the Boss, she replies that the Boss only listens when he is talking.
punchline: Alice can openly admit the status reports are fake because the Boss never pays attention to anyone but himself.
summary: A trainee learns that the team's required reports are gibberish, and the oblivious manager standing right there never notices the confession.

file: 2005/2005-10-25_specter of unpaid overtime_guide you_shadowy region_neither life_or death_apparition_ghost.gif
title: Specter of Unpaid Overtime Visits

transcript.speaker: Specter

transcript.speaker: Specter
transcript.text: I will guide you to the shadowy region that is neither life nor death. It is existence without meaning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where is this awful place?

transcript.speaker: Specter
transcript.text: Right here. And if any sticky notes fall on the floor, I'll rake 'em up.

situation: A hooded specter in a yellow raincoat holding a rake appears beside Dilbert as he works at his computer. It announces that it will lead him to a shadowy region between life and death. Dilbert asks where this awful place is, and the specter reveals it is his own cubicle, where it will also tidy up fallen sticky notes.
punchline: The dreaded afterlife-like limbo of meaningless existence is simply Dilbert's ordinary workplace, implying that working unpaid overtime is indistinguishable from purgatory.
summary: A ghostly visitor promises to escort a worker to a dreary netherworld, only to reveal that the destination is the very desk he is already sitting at.

title: Cubicle Sharing With Attractive Coworker

transcript.text: But then I remembered the importance of teamwork.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he must share his cubicle because the company is short on space. Dilbert angrily vows to take the fight to the board of directors. When the Boss introduces the new cubicle mate, an attractive woman named Lola, Dilbert instantly reverses his position and praises teamwork.
punchline: Dilbert's principled outrage evaporates the moment he sees his new cubicle mate is an attractive woman, and he hypocritically claims to value teamwork.
summary: A furious employee's protest against cramped quarters vanishes as soon as his new roommate turns out to be an attractive woman.

file: 2005/2005-10-02_negative commentray_blog_fire_freedom of speech_our founding fathers_spitting on graves_not good work_final paycheck.gif
title: Freedom of Speech Gets Ted Fired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, you've been saying negative things about the company in your personal blog. We have to fire you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I have freedom of speech. It's my constitutional right to say whatever I want.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: If you fire me for my opinions, you'll be spitting on the graves of our founding fathers.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'll get the best lawyer that money can buy, and fight you all the way to the Supreme Court!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only way you can legally fire me is if my work isn't good.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Ooh.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I probably said too much here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your work isn't good. Here's your final paycheck.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Stupid founding fathers.

situation: The boss tells Ted he is being fired for criticizing the company on his personal blog. Ted defiantly invokes free speech, the founding fathers and a Supreme Court fight, then accidentally announces that the only legal way to fire him is for poor work. The boss immediately declares Ted's work not good and hands him his final paycheck.
punchline: Ted talks himself out of a job by blurting out the one legal loophole that lets the company fire him, then blames the founding fathers for his own mistake.
summary: A blogger's grand constitutional defense collapses when he carelessly hands his employer the exact excuse needed to terminate him.

file: 2005/2005-06-11_projects budget_ten percent_no thinking_picke dnumber_cutting hours worked_36 hours_affect result.gif
title: Ten Percent Cut, Ten Percent Less Work

transcript.text: Ten percent??

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anything can be cut by ten percent without affecting the result.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cool! I'm cutting back to 36 hours per week!

situation: The Boss informs Dilbert that his project's budget must be cut by ten percent. Dilbert objects that ten percent is an arbitrary round number chosen without thought. When the Boss insists anything can be cut by ten percent without affecting results, Dilbert applies the same logic to his own work and reduces his workweek to 36 hours.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's claim that a ten percent cut won't change the result against him by cutting his own hours by ten percent.
summary: When told to slash his budget by an arbitrary tenth, Dilbert cheerfully applies the same reasoning to his own workweek.

title: Boss Hires Porpoise as Lawyer

The Boss explains that porpoises save humans by ramming sharks with their snouts. Afterward, Dilbert and Wally find the company lawyer lying unconscious on the floor with a snout wound, implying the porpoise attacked him as a shark.
punchline: The porpoise treated the company lawyer as a shark and attacked him, a jab at lawyers being sharks and at the Boss's absurd hiring logic.
summary: A manager's odd new hire turns out to have an instinctive grudge against the legal department.

file: 2005/2005-01-20_tina trains_new boss_uniformed decions_sociopathic ego maniac_like to fidget.gif
title: Tina Trains Her New Boss

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You'll usually stand like this.

situation: Tina, a programmer, is showing her new boss the ropes. She explains that she does the real work from her chair while his role is to make uninformed decisions, act like a sociopathic egomaniac, and stand in a particular pose. The boss eagerly adds that he also likes to fidget and harrumph.
punchline: Tina's blunt job description of management as useless, arrogant meddling is so accurate that the boss cheerfully accepts it and adds his own habits to the list.
summary: A sharp-tongued engineer briefs her new supervisor on what managers actually do, and he agrees with enthusiasm.

title: Threatening a Vendor Who Won't Deliver

transcript.text: How about if I say we'll never buy from you again?

transcript.text: I'd say you're not exactly buying from us now.

setting: The Boss's office and a meeting with the vendor's sales rep
situation: Dilbert reports to The Boss that the vendor can't deliver parts for three months. The Boss says the vendor must have promised them to a customer who threatened harder, so Dilbert tries threatening the vendor rep by saying the company will never buy from them again. The rep points out that the company isn't buying anything at the moment anyway.
punchline: Dilbert's threat to stop buying is empty because the vendor isn't actually selling to him now, so he has no leverage at all.
summary: Following his boss's advice to get tough with a supplier, an employee discovers his threat carries no weight because the supplier is already not delivering.

title: Internet Pills Are Totally Safe

situation: During a meeting, Dilbert tells Wally he looks bloated and lethargic, then hands him a bottle of pills and 'prescribes' them. He reassures Wally of their safety by explaining he bought them online, while Alice looks on unimpressed.
punchline: Dilbert's claim that the pills are safe because he bought them on the Internet is the opposite of reassuring, mocking the dubious online drug trade and naive trust in anything found online.
summary: A coworker playing amateur doctor offers pills to a sluggish colleague and cites an online purchase as proof of their safety.

file: 2005/2005-06-30_board meeting_dipping employees_varnish_voted to fire you_100 million_1 million year.gif

summary: A boss who believes his identity has been stolen is dismayed to learn that his own underwear now counts as a stranger's.

setting: Office desk with a computer, then a red car outside
situation: Two FBI agents in suits and sunglasses confront Dogbert at his computer, accusing him of being the source of all internet spam. Dogbert claims to be the Director of the FBI and fires them both on the spot. The agents drive away, deciding the rumor that the director dresses up as other mammals must be true.
punchline: Dogbert escapes accountability by absurdly claiming to be the FBI Director, and the agents are so credulous they take it as confirmation of an odd rumor about their boss rather than questioning that he is a dog.
summary: Accused by federal agents of sending spam, a dog at a computer simply declares himself their boss and dismisses them, and they leave convinced he is a costume-wearing eccentric.

title: Promotion Candidate Has Manager Voice

transcript.text: The other candidate has no qualifications except for his manager-sounding voice.

transcript.text: And he doesn't make that face.

situation: The Boss congratulates Alice, telling her she is one of two candidates for a promotion to management. He then admits the rival candidate's only qualification is sounding like a manager. As the Boss mentions Alice's face, she glares at him furiously with her hair puffed up.
punchline: The Boss praises Alice by saying her main advantage over an unqualified rival is that she doesn't make an angry face, which she is making at that very moment because of his insulting remarks.
summary: A boss tells Alice she is up for promotion against a man who merely sounds managerial, then unwittingly provokes the very scowl he says she lacks.

file: 2005/2005-02-11_addicted to email_endorphins spike_loneliness and despair_email to self.gif
title: Dilbert's Email Addiction and Loneliness

transcript.text: I'm addicted to e-mail. My endorphins spike when I get a message.
