transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't talk about that.

situation: Dilbert sits up in bed with a device in his hands, confessing to Dogbert that he is addicted to e-mail and feels despair when his inbox is empty. Dogbert suggests he try sending e-mail to himself. Dilbert curtly shuts the topic down, implying he already does this.
punchline: Dogbert's obvious fix for an empty inbox is something Dilbert has clearly already tried and is ashamed of, revealing how deep his addiction runs.
summary: A lonely man confesses his need for incoming messages, and his dog's suggestion hits an embarrassing truth he refuses to discuss.

title: Circular Morality Explained By Garbage Man

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is it unethical for humans to clone themselves?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Morality is based on accepted norms. And accepted norms are based on morality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's self causing?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Ironi- cally, yes.

situation: Dilbert asks a garbage man why human cloning is considered unethical. The garbage man gives a circular answer, saying morality is based on accepted norms and norms are based on morality. Dilbert points out it is self-causing, and a second garbage man pops out of the trash can to agree.
punchline: The circular explanation of morality is literally self-causing, as a duplicate of the garbage man appears from the trash can, implying he is a clone himself.
summary: A philosophical answer about the circular nature of ethics is undercut when a duplicate of the answerer emerges from the garbage can.

file: 2005/2005-03-10_things that don't kill_great minds_think alike_spilt milk_different findings.gif
title: Inverted Proverbs Over Lunch

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed that the things that don't kill you make you weaker?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And great minds don't think alike. If they did, the patent office would only have about fifty inventions.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I started getting suspicious when I cried over spilt milk and the cashier took it off my bill.

setting: Office lunch table in the cafeteria or break room
situation: Wally eats lunch with Dilbert and Asok while delivering a series of cynical twists on familiar sayings. He argues that what doesn't kill you makes you weaker and that great minds don't think alike. He ends by describing how a cashier discounted his spilt milk. Dilbert and Asok sit and listen without reacting.
punchline: Wally's cynical rewrites of common proverbs end with the absurd claim that crying over spilt milk got him a discount, implying the old sayings were all wrong.
summary: A lazy coworker over lunch debunks several well-worn proverbs with his own sardonic observations and a spilled-drink anecdote.

title: Dinosaur Bodyguard Too Busy Snacking

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bob, my boss might be planning to kill me. Would you be my bodyguard?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I can't because I'm all busy eating a carrot stick.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about after you finish it?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: You mean nap time? Be serious!

situation: Dilbert asks Bob, a green dinosaur coworker, to act as his bodyguard because he fears his boss may want him dead. Bob says he can't because he is busy eating a carrot stick. When Dilbert suggests asking again after the snack, Bob replies that the time after that is nap time.
punchline: Bob treats a snack and a nap as more pressing than protecting a coworker from a possible murder, making him a hopelessly unreliable bodyguard.
summary: A worried employee seeks protection from a dim-witted dinosaur colleague whose busy schedule of snacking and napping leaves no room for guard duty.

title: Whacking the Employee Over Counteroffer

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have a job offer from another company, but I'll give you a chance to buy my loyalty.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I just sit back and let the loving begin.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And his opening offer is...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's right: Whack him in the parking lot.

situation: Wally tells his boss he has an outside job offer and gives the company a chance to win him back, then smugly sips coffee expecting to be showered with offers. The Boss quietly picks up the phone and, instead of making a counteroffer, orders a hit on Wally in the parking lot.
punchline: Wally expects to be courted with a better offer, but the boss responds to his loyalty ultimatum by ordering him murdered.
summary: An employee waving a rival job offer waits for a bidding war and instead gets a menacing phone call from his boss.

file: 2005/2005-02-27_deadline_upcoming_annual performance review_finish on time_agree to disagree_no raise_excuses_disrespect for workers_annual review_not paying_not fare wages.gif
title: Penalized For Predicted Lateness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project deadline is next month, and I can't imagine you finishing on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I dinged you on your annual performance review.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But...I will finish on time. I always finish on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, let's agree to disagree.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're basing my raise on what you imagine I won't do in the future!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Relax. If you do finish the project on time, I'll factor it into your next annual review.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well...okay. I guess it all averages out.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One year later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remember the project that I finished last year?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. But the new one looks like it will be late.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has marked him down on his annual review because he can't imagine Dilbert finishing his project on time. Dilbert protests that he always finishes on time, and the Boss promises to credit it in next year's review. A year later the Boss has forgotten the completed project and is already predicting the new one will be late.
punchline: The Boss punishes Dilbert for a failure he merely imagines, then forgets Dilbert's actual success, so the promised 'averaging out' never happens and Dilbert is penalized again.
summary: A manager docks an employee's review for a deadline he is sure will be missed, then conveniently forgets the on-time delivery that disproved him.

file: 2005/2005-10-28_specter_unpaid overtime_grim reaper_hit by rake_happened once_insulted wife.gif
title: Specter of Unpaid Overtime Rake

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I was visited by the specter of unpaid overtime. He hit me with his rake because he's trying to become a grim reaper.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hee hee!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I just realized that I only enjoy your stories when they involve you getting hit by a rake.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That only happened once.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to tell the gardener that you insulted his wife.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on and beside a green couch
situation: Dilbert, wearing a bandage around his head, tells Dogbert a story about being visited by the specter of unpaid overtime, who whacked him with a rake. Dogbert laughs and admits he only enjoys Dilbert's stories when Dilbert gets hit by a rake. When Dilbert protests it only happened once, Dogbert says he'll arrange for it to happen again by lying to the gardener.
punchline: Dogbert coldly plans to engineer more rake injuries for Dilbert by framing him to the gardener, showing he values his own amusement over Dilbert's safety.
summary: A bandaged Dilbert recounts a bizarre dream-like encounter, and his pet dog responds by plotting to get him hurt again for entertainment.

title: Cure for Difficult Coworkers: Cartooning

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to my seminar on dealing with difficult coworkers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Difficult coworkers generally fall into one of these groups.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The only way to deal with them is to quit your job and become a syndicated cartoonist.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks for coming.

setting: A seminar room with a flip chart and a small stool for the speaker
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool in front of a flip chart, opens a seminar on difficult coworkers. He shows a grid sorting them into lazy, mean, smart and crazy groups. His only advice is to quit your job and become a syndicated cartoonist, and he then thanks the audience and ends the seminar.
punchline: The seminar's only solution is to escape your coworkers by becoming a successful cartoonist, which is the author's own career path, making the advice useless to nearly everyone.
summary: A consultant's lecture on handling troublesome colleagues ends with a self-serving escape plan that few attendees could ever follow.

title: Cold Cure Causes Cold Symptoms

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I invented a cure for the common cold.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The possible side-effects are coughing, sore throat, runny nose, congestion and nausea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... it's a pill that makes you nauseous?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Only if you have a cold.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with both sitting in green armchairs
situation: Dogbert announces he has invented a cure for the common cold, then lists its side effects, which are just the symptoms of a cold plus nausea. Dilbert sums it up as a pill that makes you nauseous, and Dogbert says that only happens if you already have a cold.
punchline: The supposed cure's side effects are nearly identical to the cold's own symptoms, so the drug is essentially worthless, and Dogbert's dodge about only feeling nauseous when sick shows the absurdity of pharmaceutical side-effect disclaimers.
summary: A self-proclaimed cold remedy turns out to produce the very symptoms it claims to cure.

title: Wizard Versus Lizard Nickname Battle

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: From now on, my nickname will be "The Wizard." It speaks to my guru status.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think I'll call you "The Lizard." It speaks to your small brain and lack of ambition.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Please don't.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's see which one catches on quicker.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, announces that he wants everyone to call him "The Wizard" because of his supposed guru status. Alice, seated at her computer, responds by coining a insulting rival nickname for him, "The Lizard." She then proposes a race to see which nickname spreads through the office faster.
punchline: Alice turns Wally's self-flattering nickname attempt into a contest, knowing her insulting rhyme will stick faster than his boast.
summary: A coworker trying to give himself an impressive title is met with a rhyming insult from a colleague who bets hers will spread faster.

title: Free Internet Pills Backfire on Karl

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Karl, you're a habitual liar but these pills that I ordered over the Internet will cure you.

transcript.speaker: Karl
transcript.text: I've never lied in my life, but I can't resist free stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Are you alive?

transcript.speaker: Karl
transcript.text: Never felt better!

situation: Dilbert offers his coworker Karl, a habitual liar, a bottle of pills he bought online, promising they will cure the lying. Karl claims he has never lied but takes the pills anyway because they are free. In the last panel Karl has been reduced to a disembodied head with a lightbulb-like appearance, and Dilbert nervously asks if he is alive.
punchline: The mail-order pills cured Karl's lying in the worst way, leaving him barely alive while he cheerfully insists he has never felt better, showing his lying persists or the pills are deadly.
summary: A man tricks a fibbing coworker into swallowing dubious online pills that leave him in a bizarre and alarming state.

title: Absurd Password Rules Announced

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will no longer have access to code on any server but your own.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is it my imagination, or are all of our rules designed for the sole purpose of being huge inconveniences?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And starting today, all passwords must contain letters, numbers, doodles, sign language and squirrel noises.

situation: The Boss announces a new restriction limiting engineers to code on their own servers only. Alice sarcastically asks whether all the company's rules exist just to cause inconvenience. The Boss responds by announcing an even more ridiculous password policy.
punchline: Instead of denying Alice's accusation, the Boss confirms it by adding an absurd password requirement that includes doodles, sign language and squirrel noises.
summary: A manager piles on another pointless security rule, and when an employee complains about needless hassle, he answers with an even sillier one.

title: Employee Rationalizer Fixes Disgruntled Worker

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ed, you seem disgruntled.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You need 30 minutes in the Employee Rationalizer.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: I... I... don't mind bad management because... the commute is easy.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Better.

setting: Office, Catbert's desk and the Employee Rationalizer machine
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, notices that an employee named Ed looks disgruntled and orders him into the Employee Rationalizer. Ed ends up strapped into a chair with a metal helmet wired to a machine while Catbert operates the controls. Afterward Ed cheerfully justifies putting up with bad management.
punchline: The machine brainwashes unhappy employees into inventing flimsy excuses to tolerate bad management, such as an easy commute, so HR solves morale problems by rewiring workers instead of fixing the management.
summary: A malevolent HR cat zaps a grumpy employee's brain with a helmet machine until he cheerfully makes peace with his terrible bosses.

title: Wally's Coffee-Dangling Marathon Hat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I want you to represent our company in the corporate marathon.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Um... I can't run 26 miles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, you can. I've designed a special hat to help you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What the...?

setting: The Boss's office, then the starting line of a corporate marathon
situation: The Boss orders Wally to represent the company in a corporate marathon. Wally protests that he can't run 26 miles, and the Boss insists he can thanks to a special hat he designed. At the starting line, Wally wears a hat with a pole holding a coffee mug dangling in front of his face, like a carrot on a stick.
punchline: The Boss's special hat is just a coffee mug dangled on a stick in front of Wally, banking on Wally's love of coffee to drive him forward like a donkey chasing a carrot.
summary: A manager sends his lazy employee into a marathon wearing a hat that dangles a coffee mug in front of him as motivation.

file: 2005/2005-05-24_evil director_human resources_help balancing_personal life_no love_sound sunhealthy_pill crybaby_business.gif

Catbert recommends a book designed to destroy his hope of ever having a personal life so he can work more. When Dilbert objects that this sounds unhealthy, Catbert dismisses him and tells him to take a pill.
punchline: Instead of helping with work-life balance, the evil HR director solves the problem by eliminating the employee's personal life and then mocks him for complaining.
summary: Seeking better balance, an employee is handed a bleak book by his malicious HR chief that kills any hope of a life outside the office.
keywords: no one will ever love you

file: 2005/2005-02-17_last election_incredibly close_smart well inofrmed_intelligence factor_no right to complain.gif
title: Voting Is Absurd, Says Wally

transcript.text: The last election was incredibly close. That's why it's so important to vote.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Smart, well-informed people were evenly divided. Therefore, logically, that proves that intelligence is not a factor, so voting is absurd.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you have no right to complain about the result.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure I do.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss urges everyone to vote because the last election was so close. Wally argues that since smart, informed people split evenly, intelligence doesn't matter and voting is pointless. The Boss says that means Wally has no right to complain, and Wally confidently insists he does.
punchline: Wally dismisses voting with twisted logic but still holds firmly to his entitlement to complain about the outcome.
summary: A manager's civic pep talk about voting is met with a lazy employee's tortured reasoning for skipping it, while he still keeps his right to gripe.

file: 2005/2005-05-23_medical procedure_attractive to opposite sex_remove body part_sounds painful.gif
title: Full Body Parts Replacement for Attractiveness

transcript.text: There's a medical procedure that will make you more attractive to the opposite sex.

transcript.text: The doctors would remove every part of your body and replace them with the parts from an attractive guy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It sounds painful.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not if you do it all at once.

setting: Outdoors behind a stone wall on a grassy hillside
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert about a medical procedure that would make him attractive to the opposite sex by replacing every part of his body with parts from an attractive man. Dilbert objects that it sounds painful, and Dogbert assures him it wouldn't be if done all at once.
punchline: Dogbert's reassurance that the procedure isn't painful 'if you do it all at once' is absurd logic, since replacing your entire body would effectively mean killing Dilbert.
summary: Dogbert pitches a total body swap as a dating strategy and brushes off Dilbert's concern about pain with twisted logic.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert and delivers an assignment made up of acronyms and nonsense verbs that mean nothing. He then announces that he has no time to answer questions, leaving Dilbert with no way to clarify what he is meant to do.
punchline: The Boss gives an incomprehensible instruction and pre-emptively refuses to clarify it, setting Dilbert up to fail.
summary: A manager hands his employee a jargon-stuffed task that makes no sense and then declares he is too busy to explain it.

title: Time Machine Product Weight Loss Pitch

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: If our new product takes you sixty minutes into the future in one hour. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that the same as doing nothing at all?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: It also makes you lose weight if you stay in it long enough. . . while not eating.

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: Dilbert raises his hand in a meeting and asks a question about the company's new product, which supposedly carries you into the future at the normal rate of one hour per hour. When he points out that this is the same as doing nothing, the presenter answers with a ridiculous added benefit instead of a real defense.
punchline: The presenter has no real answer, so he touts a trivial side effect, losing weight by not eating, as if it were a feature of the product.
summary: A pitch for a useless gadget unravels when an engineer points out it does nothing, and the presenter responds with a absurd bonus claim.

title: Dogbert's Volcano Bungee Advice

transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Tell me again why I'd want to bungee jump into an active volcano?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because you can!

setting: A conference room during a consulting session, then the CEO's office
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells a boardroom that their CEO is the worst performer in the Fortune 500. His recommended solution is to push the CEO toward a career as a reckless adventurer. The CEO is then shown skeptically asking why he should bungee jump into an active volcano.
punchline: Dogbert's consulting advice is to get the incompetent CEO killed, and his only justification, 'because you can,' is a flimsy pretext for a fatal stunt.
summary: A consultant dog responds to a failing chief executive by steering him toward a deadly thrill-seeking hobby.

title: Free Samples for Celebrity Lookalikes

transcript.text: And you would be?

characters: Man in blue suit (Donald Trump lookalike)
setting: Outdoor walkway and bridge, then a sample-giveaway table
situation: Dilbert complains that his boss gives him no resources for a marketing campaign. Dogbert suggests handing out free samples to people who look like celebrities. Dilbert tries it and a man with an elaborate comb-over, accompanied by a woman in a red dress, announces he is Donald Trump and demands free stuff.
punchline: Celebrity lookalikes will claim to be the real thing and happily demand freebies, so the cheap marketing plan just hands free goods to wealthy-seeming freeloaders.
summary: With no budget for promotion, Dilbert follows Dogbert's advice to hand out free samples to celebrity lookalikes and promptly meets a pushy fake Trump.

title: Succession Plan Makes Boss Nervous

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You have to have a leadership succession plan.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There's a freeze on hiring, so you'll need to pick someone from your staff.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: So, if something horrible happened to you, I'd get a promotion?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This was a bad idea.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss he must have a leadership succession plan. Because hiring is frozen, the successor must come from his own staff. When the Boss sits down with an employee, she cheerfully notes she would get promoted if something horrible happened to him, and he realizes the idea was a mistake.
punchline: Picking a successor makes the Boss realize that his chosen replacement benefits directly from his misfortune, which makes him feel threatened.
summary: Forced by HR to name a successor from his own staff, a boss discovers that his heir apparent has a rather cheerful stake in his downfall.

title: Carol Cancels Boss's Work-Creating Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, why don't I have any meetings today?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Your meetings create work for me, so I canceled them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I could drop in on some people.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Harpoon.

setting: Office cubicle area, at Carol's desk
situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol why his calendar is empty. She flatly explains that she canceled his meetings because they generate extra work for her. When the Boss then suggests dropping in on people unannounced, Carol silently thinks of harpooning him and picks up a harpoon.
punchline: Carol has stopped his meetings to protect herself from extra work, and when the Boss threatens to pester coworkers in person instead, she reaches for a harpoon to deal with him.
summary: A secretary quietly wipes her boss's schedule clear to spare herself the hassle, then contemplates violence when he proposes bothering others instead.

title: Electrocuted Ratbert Becomes Executive Candidate

transcript.text: Dogbert's Executive Search Firm

transcript.text: Ratbert, would you like to be the CEO of a major corporation?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That had always been my dream... until I found this extension cord to gnaw on. Now I'm committed to seeing it through.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He's a risk-taker who won't stop until he achieves his goal.

setting: Dogbert's executive search firm office, then a boardroom
situation: Dogbert runs an executive search firm and asks Ratbert if he wants to be a CEO. Ratbert says he now only cares about gnawing an extension cord plugged into the wall. Dogbert then presents the electrified, frizzy-haired Ratbert to a board of directors, pitching his reckless obsession as a leadership strength.
punchline: Dogbert spins Ratbert's dangerous, mindless fixation on chewing a live electrical cord as admirable executive traits like risk-taking and single-minded determination.
summary: A search-firm dog pitches a shocked, frizzled rat to a corporate board as a bold, relentless leader because he keeps chewing a live power cord.

transcript.text: The New Guy

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We have a strong culture of teamwork here.

transcript.text: While you're doing those easy tasks, I'll be off doing assignments of unimaginable difficulty.

summary: A smooth-talking coworker offloads his workload onto the new hire under the banner of teamwork, until Dogbert exposes the scam.

title: Compliance Theater Makes Work Easier

transcript.text: My accomplishments this month include complying with our ISO 9000, Sarbanes-Oxley and SEI-5 policies.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And if you make a new policy, I will comply with it so fast it will make your head spin!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or is pretending to work getting easier?

situation: Wally sits at a meeting table with the Boss and Dilbert and proudly lists his monthly accomplishments, which consist entirely of complying with company policies. He then eagerly promises to comply instantly with any future policy. Afterward, walking down the hall with coffee, he muses to Dilbert that pretending to work seems to be getting easier.
punchline: Wally's only accomplishment is following bureaucratic compliance policies, which he realizes has made looking busy effortless, implying that such policies reward the appearance of work rather than real work.
summary: A lazy employee brags about obeying every corporate rule and then reflects that faking productivity has become suspiciously simple.

title: Candidate Admits Needing Supervision

transcript.text: Can you work well without supervision?

transcript.text: I think we're done here.

setting: Interview room with a conference table
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and asks whether he can work well without supervision. The candidate candidly answers that he needs constant supervision to stop him from stealing and harassing people. The Boss ends the interview, and the candidate politely asks if he can show himself out.
punchline: The candidate answers the standard interview question with shocking honesty, then asks to leave unsupervised, which is exactly the thing he said he shouldn't be trusted to do.
summary: A job applicant frankly confesses his criminal tendencies when asked about working independently, then requests to walk out alone.

title: Insulting Coworker Brings Job Satisfaction

transcript.text: We're having a problem with rats in the office.

transcript.text: You might want to upgrade your level of hygiene from "rat bait" to "unwashed."

transcript.text: I think I just felt my first tingle of job satisfaction!

punchline: Carol's job is so miserable that the only thing that has ever made her feel satisfied at work is insulting a coworker's poor hygiene.
summary: A sour employee turns a pest report into a personal insult and finds it the most rewarding moment of her working life.

title: Joke About Holding Up Wall

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are you doing? Holding up the wall?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Zing! That was a good one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you met the new structural engineer?

situation: The Boss spots a coworker leaning against a wall holding a coffee mug and quips that he's holding up the wall. The Boss privately congratulates himself on the joke and walks off. The wall then collapses, with the coworker's legs sticking out from under the rubble, as Dilbert introduces the new structural engineer.
punchline: The wall really was load-bearing on the coworker, and the new structural engineer has apparently built something that collapses, making the boss's lame joke a literal fact.
summary: A manager's smug wisecrack about a leaning coworker turns grimly literal when the wall comes down, just as a new engineer is introduced.

file: 2005/2005-01-03_new director_first impressions_office in lobby_nearest growler_directions_information booth_directs.gif
title: Director of First Impressions Receptionist Trick

transcript.speaker: Carol

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Why is my office in the lobby?

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Can you direct me to the nearest growler?

setting: Office cubicle area, then the company lobby
situation: The Boss promotes his assistant Carol to a grand-sounding title, Director of First Impressions pro tem, and she is thrilled by the promotion. In the last panel she is sitting at a desk in the lobby, where a visitor asks her for directions to the nearest growler, a place to get beer.
punchline: The impressive director title is really just a receptionist job, and Carol is now stuck giving directions to visitors.
summary: A fancy new job title turns out to be a disguise for relocating an employee to the front desk to greet and direct visitors.

title: Boss's Smaller Raise Is Bigger

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't feel bad if you only got a 3% raise; I only got 2% myself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can we feel bad that 2% of your pay is bigger than 3% of our pay?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't get all mathy on me.

situation: At a conference table, the Boss tries to console employees about their 3% raises by saying he only got 2%. Alice points out that 2% of his much larger salary is a bigger amount than 3% of theirs. The Boss dismisses her by complaining that she is getting too mathematical.
punchline: The Boss's claim of sacrifice falls apart under basic arithmetic, and instead of answering, he just objects to her using math.
summary: A manager claims solidarity over a smaller percentage raise until an employee points out the numbers favor him, and he waves off the logic.

title: Delusions of Effective PowerPoint Slides

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This PowerPoint slide could change our entire company strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The rest of the industry would have to copy us, and that could change the entire world!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone has been having delusions of effectiveness.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert works on a PowerPoint slide at his computer and daydreams that it will transform his company's strategy and then the whole industry and world. In the last panel the Boss sits across the desk, holding Dilbert's slide, and dismisses the idea by remarking that someone has been having delusions of effectiveness.
punchline: The Boss sarcastically treats Dilbert's belief that his work could matter as a delusion, implying that no one's effort at this company is ever effective.
summary: A hopeful engineer imagines his slide deck reshaping the world until his manager shoots down the notion with a dry putdown.

file: 2005/2005-12-11_billion dollar line_design_ecstatic_massive design flaws_press release_proper incenives_stock options_underwater.gif
title: Rushed Design, Blame the CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told our CEO that the design would be done in a month. He's ecstatic!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be good except that I told you it won't be done for six months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, I guess you'll have to tell him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's too late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He already issued a press release. You'll have to finish the design in a month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only way to do it in a month is to accept massive design flaws that will destroy a billion dollar line of business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay. My stock options are so underwater that it won't make any difference.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll just blame all of the problems on the Chinese company that manufactures our products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ultimately, it's the CEO's fault for failing to give me proper incentives.

situation: The Boss reveals he promised the CEO a design in one month when Dilbert had said it would take six, and the CEO has already announced it publicly. Dilbert warns that a one-month schedule means major design flaws that could ruin a billion dollar business. The Boss shrugs it off because his stock options are worthless and plans to shift blame to the overseas manufacturer and the CEO.
punchline: The Boss is willing to wreck a billion dollar product line because his underwater stock options remove any personal stake, and he'll blame everyone but himself, including the CEO for not giving him proper incentives.
summary: After overpromising a six-month project as a one-month job, a boss happily accepts disaster, since his worthless stock options mean he has nothing to lose and plenty of others to blame.

title: Taking a Refund on Baby Shower

transcript.text: I'm collecting money for Ted's baby shower.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My taxes already subsidize his other brats. I'm taking a refund.

transcript.speaker: Carol

transcript.speaker: Wally

situation: Carol approaches Wally at his desk, holding an envelope to collect money for Ted's baby shower. Wally declares that his taxes already subsidize Ted's other children and reaches into the envelope to take a refund. When Carol protests that she just added a five-dollar bill, Wally coolly dismisses it.
punchline: Wally treats a voluntary office gift collection like a tax system and pockets the cash, blaming Carol's 'poor fiscal planning' for her loss.
summary: A coworker passing the hat for a colleague's baby shower gets her own contribution taken by a cheapskate who claims he's owed a refund.

title: Inspirational Conference Room Names Cause Chaos

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The trouble started when you insisted on giving inspirational names to the conference rooms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I scheduled a project meeting for the "Quality" room and no one knew where to go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some people ended up in the "Teamwork" room while others went to the "Excellence" room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By the time we sorted it all out, someone else was scheduled to use our conference room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then it took three weeks to schedule another meeting when everyone could make it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But half of the team went to the "Action" room and sat there while we waited for them in the "Good Planning" room.

transcript.speaker: Man at door
transcript.text: I thought this was the budget meeting.

situation: Dilbert explains to the group, including the Boss, how the Boss's idea of giving inspirational names to conference rooms led to confusion. People went to the wrong rooms, meetings were bumped, and rescheduling took weeks. A man then walks in at the end, having expected a different meeting.
punchline: After Dilbert's lengthy account of the room-name fiasco, the arriving attendee shows the chaos is ongoing: he has come to the wrong meeting entirely, believing it was the budget meeting.
summary: A long-winded post-mortem of a conference room naming scheme gone wrong ends with yet another person who wandered into the wrong meeting.

title: Job Applicant: Half Hominid, Half Oyster

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: I'm halfway between hominid and oyster. Someday I hope my light-sensitive blob will become an eye!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think we can use you.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: Oh, man, you're giving me a serious pearl.

setting: Job interview at a conference table in an office
situation: The Boss interviews a strange job candidate with a tail whose resume claims he is an intermediate species. The candidate explains he is halfway between hominid and oyster and hopes his light-sensitive blob will evolve into an eye. The Boss rejects him, and the candidate responds with an oyster-themed pun.
punchline: Being rejected, the half-oyster applicant says the boss is giving him a 'serious pearl', a pun on the oyster's irritant-turned-pearl in place of 'a serious pearl' of wisdom or a hard time.
summary: A hiring manager turns down a candidate who is part human and part oyster, and the rejected applicant reacts with a shellfish pun.

file: 2005/2005-04-10_regular goals_stretch goals_sacrifice health_personal life_criminal conduct_bonus_salaries below budget_ultra stretchy_employee rights_taken advantage_cheat employee.gif
title: Stretch Goals Require Criminal Conduct

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: Manager

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: The stretch goals require all of that plus some sort of criminal conduct.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm guessing that your boss gave you the regular goals, and you came up with the stretch goals on your own.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That way, when I achieve the regular goals, you'll get a raise but I'll get none because I missed the stretch goals.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then you'll get a bonus for keeping salaries below budget.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Maybe we should talk about the ultra-stretchy goals later.

setting: Manager's office, a desk during a performance goal review
situation: A manager hands Alice her annual goals, split into regular goals and stretch goals. He cheerfully explains that the regular goals cost her health and personal life while the stretch goals also require criminal conduct. Alice deduces that he invented the stretch goals himself so she will miss them, leaving him with a bonus for holding salaries down.
punchline: The manager invents impossible stretch goals so employees can never earn raises, which lets him collect a bonus for underspending the salary budget, and he is only embarrassed that Alice saw through it.
summary: An employee works out that her boss's unattainable bonus targets are a scheme to pocket money meant for her raise.

file: 2005/2005-07-23_calculate expected value_pretend to be dead_cover ears.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert tries to explain to the Boss how to make a decision by calculating the expected value of each outcome. punchline: The Boss would rather feign death than sit through a mathematical explanation, and he is not even convincing at it, since he covers his ears.
summary: Faced with a lecture on decision math, a manager fakes his own demise to escape it.

title: Wally's Sandwich Job Interview

transcript.speaker: Narrator

punchline: Wally turns the classic interview question about weaknesses into a literal answer, naming his sandwich's cheese while also demonstrating his complete disregard for interview etiquette.
summary: A job candidate ignores his interviewer's objection, munches a sandwich through the session, and answers the weakness question with a food item.

title: Breakfast Guy Declines Massage Duty

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Five-star hotel

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mmm... a nice massage and then breakfast.

transcript.text: Well, I would "get rubbin," but I'm only the breakfast guy.

setting: Hotel room at a five-star hotel
situation: The Boss, in a bathrobe, phones room service to order breakfast and book a massage, then relaxes on the bed anticipating both. A waiter arrives carrying a pitcher of juice and finds the Boss sprawled face-down on the serving cart, apparently expecting the waiter to rub him down.
punchline: The Boss, assuming a five-star hotel would handle everything through one person, lies on the breakfast cart for a massage, but the waiter points out he only delivers breakfast, not massages.
summary: A pampered executive books room service and a rubdown, then ends up draped over the food cart when the server explains his job stops at breakfast.

file: 2005/2005-10-09_company values_question_action_results_twice as much_imagination_all over the map_soon and perfect.gif
title: Boss Demands Everything Soon and Perfectly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just do everything soon and perfectly!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or is he all over the map on this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I forget what we were talking about.

setting: Conference room during a company values presentation
situation: The Boss presents the company values, a bias for action and a passion for results, and asks the audience not to ask questions. punchline: Probing the vague company values exposes that management's real expectation is an impossible demand for everything to be fast and flawless.
summary: A manager's slogan-based values talk collapses into an absurd, contradictory demand when an employee asks a few simple questions.

title: Director of First Impressions Snaps

transcript.text: Beat it, you walrus!

situation: A receptionist sits at her desk thinking that her fancy title, Director of First Impressions, is just a disguise for a plain receptionist job. She suddenly screams out her realization, then angrily snaps at a man in a suit who has approached her desk. The man, taken aback by her hostility, decides to send an e-mail instead.
punchline: The receptionist's inflated job title can't mask the reality of her job, and when she snaps at a visitor, she proves she is a terrible first impression.
summary: A receptionist who realizes her grand title is just window dressing erupts at a visitor, who retreats to email.

title: Delivery Man Insults Receptionist Unintentionally

situation: A delivery man arrives with a package and finds a woman sitting at the reception desk. She explains she is not the receptionist, and he cheerfully agrees, saying companies hire attractive people for that job. He then says he will wait for the real receptionist to return.
punchline: The delivery man's agreement that she is not the receptionist doubles as an insult about her looks, while he openly admits he is eager to ogle the real receptionist.
summary: A courier cheerfully confirms a woman is no receptionist by implying she is not good-looking enough for the job, then plans to wait for the real one.

title: Grimace To Prove You're Working

transcript.text: Could you grimace so I know you're working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Here you go.

situation: The Boss complains to Wally that he has watched him for half an hour and seen no work. Wally explains he is waiting for his program to compile while mentally designing the next module. The Boss asks him to grimace so he can tell he is working, and Wally obligingly makes a strained face.
punchline: The Boss judges productivity by visible effort rather than results, so Wally simply fakes a pained expression to satisfy him.
summary: A manager who can't see any output asks his employee to pull a pained face as proof that thinking is happening.

situation: The Boss struggles with a bad cell phone connection in the hallway, and an engineer offers to help by telling him to go up on the roof to test reception. The Boss is locked out on the roof with a dead phone and no way down, so he jumps toward a garbage bin in the alley. Below, the engineer and a colleague watch him fall, with the engineer remarking it will teach him to keep his battery charged.
punchline: The engineer deliberately tricked the clueless Boss into getting stranded on the roof, and calmly frames his fall as a lesson about charging his phone battery.
summary: A technician sends his gullible superior onto a locked rooftop under the guise of troubleshooting, leaving him to leap to safety.

title: Cubicle Cockroach Gets Reassigned

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Cockroach
transcript.text: Erk!!!

situation: A cockroach-like employee in a shirt and tie gloats in front of the Boss's desk that nothing can remove him from his cubicle. The Boss calmly announces he is being moved to a special project. The cockroach, suddenly alarmed, shuffles away.
punchline: The supposedly unremovable employee is defeated by a simple management reassignment to a 'special project', showing that a boss can dislodge anyone by changing their assignment.
summary: A smug entrenched worker boasting that he can never be dislodged is undone when his manager simply transfers him elsewhere.

situation: Dilbert reports to The Boss that the company's total sales to Elbonia amount to a single software package, and concludes that Elbonians must be pirating software on a massive scale. summary: A sales report from a poor mud-dwelling country is interpreted as proof of rampant piracy, while the locals can barely afford a toy for their pig.

transcript.text: This is surprisingly motivational.

situation: Dilbert warns the Boss that Elbonian hackers are trying to steal the company's source code. punchline: The new hire is instantly physically deformed by workplace stress on his very first day, and the boss dismisses it as something everyone just gets used to.
summary: A keen newcomer seeking direction is brushed off by a distracted manager and promptly develops a stress-bent spine.

summary: A hard-working employee learns that the new strategist hired to replace her workload has produced nothing except lowering her own rank.

file: 2005/2005-01-07_new strategy_sales stink_cutting costs_lose hope_working great_higher margins.gif

file: 2005/2005-12-21_charging time_projects_no work_wind_existence of your wind_farting around.gif
