punchline: Wally's wind analogy for invisible work backfires when the Boss points out that people complain about his wind, which implies flatulence, so Wally's own metaphor condemns him.
summary: A slacker's clever excuse that unseen work is like the wind gets turned against him when his manager mentions complaints about his wind.

file: 2005/2005-12-15_venture capitalist_most desparate_vc business_idea worth funding_crooked teeth.gif
title: Desperate Venture Capitalist Stalks Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: I'm Vijay, the world's most desperate venture capitalist.

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: The VC business is more competitive than ever. I'm going to stalk you until you come up with an idea worth funding.

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: No pressure, but all of my kids have crooked teeth.

situation: A venture capitalist named Vijay stands over Dilbert at his desk and announces that he is desperate for deals. He says he will stalk Dilbert until Dilbert comes up with a fundable idea. In the last panel he hovers right behind Dilbert's chair and adds a guilt-inducing remark about his children.
punchline: Vijay pretends to apply no pressure while actually guilt-tripping Dilbert by implying his kids' unaffordable orthodontic bills depend on Dilbert inventing something fundable.
summary: A cash-strapped investor hovers over an engineer's shoulder, demanding a brilliant idea and hinting that his children's dental problems rest on it.

file: 2005/2005-08-25_moving along until_coding language changed_methodlogy_endless stairway_sea submairne_mc escher_morale_add features.gif
title: Escher Timeline Meets Extra Features

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The project was moving along well until management changed our coding language and methodology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now our timeline is represented by this M.C. Escher print of an endless stairway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This deep-sea submarine is looking for our morale.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would this be a bad time to add a few features?

setting: Conference room during a project status presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a project status report to his boss and another manager, using a sock-puppet-style pointer. He explains that management's change of coding language and methodology has wrecked the schedule and morale. The boss responds by asking whether it's a bad time to add more features.
punchline: After hearing that the project's timeline is endless and morale is at rock bottom, the clueless boss still asks to pile on more features.
summary: A presenter describes a derailed project with an impossible schedule and crushed spirits, only for his manager to request additional work.

file: 2005/2005-10-10_our annual report_positive spin_poor results_stock plummenting_can't afford us.gif
title: Spinning Poor Results Into Annual Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, I want you to write our annual report.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: How should I explain our poor results?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just give it a positive spin.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: If you have to ask why our stock keeps plummeting, you can't afford us.

setting: The Boss's office, then Tina's desk
situation: The Boss tells Tina, the technical writer, to write the company's annual report. When she asks how to handle the company's poor results, he tells her to put a positive spin on it. Tina then writes the report, spinning the bad news as an exclusive club that only elite investors can afford to belong to.
punchline: Tina's spin turns the plummeting stock into a luxury exclusivity pitch, implying that anyone who questions why it keeps falling simply isn't wealthy enough to be an investor.
summary: Told to dress up dismal corporate performance, a technical writer drafts a snooty line that makes a collapsing share price sound like an exclusive privilege.

title: Brain Transplant Salad Dressing Joke

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd your brain transplant work out?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Great. Ask me anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What Roman general was famous for crossing the Rubicon River?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Caesar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. That's right.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Phew! I'm glad I didn't go with Dijon vinaigrette.

setting: Office, with Dilbert holding a coffee mug
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker with a bandaged head how his brain transplant went. To test it, Dilbert quizzes him on Roman history and the coworker answers correctly. The coworker then reveals he was relieved that he hadn't received a brain from a salad dressing.
punchline: The coworker's relief at not getting a Dijon vinaigrette brain plays on 'Caesar' being both the Roman general and a salad dressing, implying his answer could have been influenced by the brain he received.
summary: A man recovering from a brain swap aces a history question, then jokes that he is glad his new brain wasn't a salad dressing.

title: Wally's Useless Help for Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I want you to go help Alice on her project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you tried working harder? Sometimes that works.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope she doesn't become dependent on my help.

situation: The Boss orders Wally to go help Alice with her project. Wally walks over to Alice's desk, holding his coffee mug, and offers only the advice to try working harder. He then muses that he hopes she won't become dependent on his help.
punchline: Wally's 'help' is a worthless platitude, yet he smugly worries that Alice will come to rely on it.
summary: Sent to assist a coworker, a lazy employee offers one lazy suggestion and then frets that she'll lean on him too much.

title: Pension Rescue Plan: Workplace Hazards

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Management is pleased to announce that it has a plan to make your pension fund solvent.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In unrelated news, the guidelines for workplace safety have been relaxed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO reminds you that smoking is cool.

setting: Conference room meeting, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss reads from a paper at a meeting, announcing that management has a plan to make the employee pension fund solvent. A caption then notes, supposedly unrelated, that workplace safety guidelines have been relaxed. The Boss then adds that the CEO says smoking is cool.
punchline: Management's plan to fix the pension fund is to loosen safety rules and encourage smoking so employees die before they can collect their pensions.
summary: A pension shortfall gets solved by quietly making the workplace more deadly, with a wink that the two announcements are totally unconnected.

file: 2005/2005-08-14_evil wind blowing_dark soul_evil director_human resources_employee survey_over reacted_well being_business.gif
title: Satisfaction Survey Used to Cut Benefits

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I feel an evil wind blowing my way.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My soul is filling with darkness... Suddenly I am cold, oh, so cold.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hello-o-o, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! What are you doing here?!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's time for the annual employee satisfaction survey.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Perhaps I overreacted. I don't see how this could possibly be bad.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It is evident from these questions that you care about my wellbeing!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I love the part where they think I'm here to help.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purr purr

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two weeks later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're delighted with their benefits. It looks like we can save some money there.

setting: Office cubicle and a conference room
situation: Asok senses dread as Catbert, the evil HR director, shows up at his cubicle to hand out the annual employee satisfaction survey. Asok decides he overreacted and happily fills it out, believing the company cares about him. Two weeks later the Boss reads the results and concludes that employees are so pleased with their benefits that they can be cut.
punchline: The satisfaction survey was never meant to help employees; HR uses the glowing answers as an excuse to cut benefits and save money.
summary: A trusting engineer completes a staff questionnaire and learns too late that his cheerful answers will be used to justify slashing perks.

title: Company Strategy? What Strategy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does my project fit into our company's overall strategy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Beats me. I didn't even know we had a strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never ask a question if you don't want to hear the answer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's why I never say "How are you?"

setting: Office, at the Boss's desk and Dogbert's workstation
situation: Dilbert asks his boss how his project fits into the company's overall strategy. The boss admits he doesn't know and didn't even realize the company had a strategy. Dilbert then reflects that you shouldn't ask questions you don't want answered, and Dogbert says that's why he never asks 'How are you?'
punchline: The boss's answer reveals the company has no strategy, and Dogbert's quip about avoiding small talk shows he'd rather not hear honest answers, even to pleasantries.
summary: A worker seeking to understand how his work serves the business learns from his clueless manager that nobody ever defined a plan.

file: 2005/2005-12-17_desperate venture capitalist_math grades_first idea_mezzanine funding_cash bag_students_education.gif
title: Desperate Venture Capitalist Courts Schoolkids

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vijay, the world's most desperate venture capitalist

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: You two have good math grades.

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: If you grow up and marry and produce a little engineer baby, I want to invest in its first idea.

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: Please don't be too late!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Dude, we're already looking for mezzanine funding.

setting: Outdoors on a street, where two schoolchildren with backpacks stand
situation: A venture capitalist introduced as the world's most desperate approaches two schoolkids with good math grades while clutching a bag of money. He offers to fund the first idea of their hypothetical future engineer baby. The kids respond with a dismissive reply about already seeking later-stage funding, and Vijay anxiously hopes they won't be too late.
punchline: The venture capitalist is so desperate for the next big investment that he tries to lock in funding from children for a baby that doesn't exist yet, yet the kids casually talk about mezzanine financing as if they're already seasoned startup founders.
summary: An eager investor pitches a pair of math-whiz kids on bankrolling their future offspring's inventions, only to be brushed off by their startup jargon.

file: 2005/2005-10-29_happiness not realted_level of wealth_relative wealth_good job.gif
title: Happiness Is Relative: Cut His Pay

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Research has shown that happiness is not related to one's absolute level of wealth.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: What matters is one's relative wealth compared to other people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, if I do a good job, could you cut this guy's pay?

setting: Conference room around a meeting table
situation: At a meeting table, a bald man in glasses explains that research shows happiness depends on relative wealth rather than absolute wealth. Dilbert takes this to heart and asks the Boss to reward his good work not with a raise, but by cutting the pay of the man sitting next to him.
punchline: Dilbert cynically applies the relative-wealth finding by asking that a coworker's pay be reduced as his reward, since that would make him happier than a raise would.
summary: Told that happiness comes from earning more than others, an employee requests that a colleague's salary be slashed as payment for his own good performance.

title: Boss Punishes Employee for Initiative

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I have a great idea.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I was chatting with the Director of Marketing and we. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never discuss ideas with the Director of Marketing! Never!

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Erk!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You work for me! When you talk to other managers it undercuts my authority!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I accept ideas from another manager, it's just like he's my boss!

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Amazing! Did you know that your behavior is described on page 27 of the "Putrid Boss" book? It's the chapter on killing initiative and bullying!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's fascinating. Now let me show you something that isn't in the book.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like someone has been showing initiative.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Please shut up.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway
situation: A manager tells the Boss he has a great idea and mentions chatting with the Director of Marketing. The Boss explodes, insisting that talking to other managers undermines his authority. The manager cites a book describing this exact bullying behavior, and the Boss responds by beating him with a mallet.
punchline: Pointing out the Boss's bad behavior with a helpful book only earns the manager a literal hammering, proving that initiative gets punished.
summary: A boss who forbids his staff from sharing ideas with other departments reacts to criticism of his management style with a wooden mallet.

title: Save Your Question for the Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you come to a meeting at three?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to tell everyone that Project Acorn is canceled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You just told me. So I don't need to go, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You might have questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I don't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe someone at the meeting will ask a question that you didn't think of.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I attend every meeting in the world just in case someone asks a good question?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Save that one for the meeting.

situation: The Boss invites Dilbert to a meeting at three to announce that Project Acorn is canceled. Dilbert points out the Boss has just told him, so he has no reason to attend. The Boss insists he might have questions, and Dilbert argues that this logic would require attending every meeting in existence.
punchline: When Dilbert makes a sharp, rational point against needless meetings, the Boss fails to rebut it and simply tells him to raise it at the meeting, which still requires attending the meeting.
summary: A manager insists an employee attend a meeting to hear news he has already been given, and answers his logical objection by asking him to bring it up there.

title: Agile Means More Work, Fewer People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need three more programmers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Use agile programming methods.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Agile programming doesn't just mean doing more work with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Find me some words that DO mean that and ask again.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for three more programmers to handle the workload. The boss tells him to use agile programming methods instead. Dilbert objects that agile doesn't simply mean more work with fewer people, and the boss tells him to come back with words that do mean that.
punchline: The boss wants to use a legitimate methodology as a cover for understaffing, and responds to Dilbert's correct objection by asking him to redefine terms so the request can be refused.
summary: A manager denies a hiring request by invoking a software buzzword, then demands that the engineer supply language that makes the excuse fit.

title: Asok Blows Up Insulting Cowboy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tex, I'd like you to meet Asok, our intern.

transcript.speaker: Tex
transcript.text: Asok? What kind of name is that? Are you a taxi driver?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Um... no.

transcript.speaker: Tex
transcript.text: I've produced bigger things than you by eating fiber!

transcript.speaker: Tex
transcript.text: Do they have schools where you came from?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, Asok graduated from the Indian Institute of Technology. So if I were you, I wouldn't make him angry.

transcript.speaker: Tex
transcript.text: Why? What's he gonna do? Gnaw on my ankle?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Explode! Explode!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BOOM!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They taught you some good stuff.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Nah. You can't even get in unless you can do that.

situation: Dilbert introduces the intern Asok to Tex, a cowboy-hatted visitor, who responds with a string of racist and belittling insults about Asok's name and background. Dilbert warns Tex that Asok is an Indian Institute of Technology graduate, but Tex mocks him anyway. Asok silently concentrates, Tex's body explodes, and only his skeleton in a smoking shirt remains.
punchline: Asok's elite IIT education apparently includes the ability to make people explode with his mind, which he casually dismisses as a basic admission requirement.
summary: A bigoted blowhard keeps insulting a young engineer until the engineer's prestigious schooling pays off in a very literal blast.

title: VP's Experience Is Shampoo, Astrology

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new VP of Marketing has twenty years of experience in an unrelated industry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But he assured me that technology is the same as shampoo.

transcript.speaker: Astrologer
transcript.text: I predict smooth sailing.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Technology? I thought you said astrology.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces to colleagues at a meeting table that the new VP of Marketing has twenty years of experience in an unrelated industry, but claims technology is the same as shampoo. The new VP, who also has pointy hair, confidently predicts smooth sailing, and a bald colleague realizes the VP thinks they are in astrology, not technology.
punchline: The new VP is so unqualified that he doesn't even know which industry he has joined, mistaking technology for astrology, which undermines his confident prediction of smooth sailing.
summary: A newly hired marketing executive with experience in a totally different field confidently reassures the team, only to reveal he misunderstood what industry the company is in.

title: Pet Employee Gets Hawaii Assignment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry that I might give all of the good projects to my pet employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Petricia, I'd like you to evaluate cutting-edge technologies in Hawaii.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now, who's left to wax my back?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss reassures his team that he won't just hand all the good projects to his favorite employee. He then immediately assigns Petricia, his pet employee, a trip to Hawaii to evaluate cutting-edge technologies. With her gone, he asks who is left to wax his back.
punchline: The Boss denies favoritism while blatantly practicing it, then reveals that his pet employee's real job is personal grooming services, which he must now find someone else to perform.
summary: A manager claims he plays no favorites, instantly sends his protegee on a lavish island trip, and then wonders who will handle his personal grooming.

file: 2005/2005-03-25_you're ugly_or rumor is ugly_bad news_ugly rumor.gif
title: Ugly Rumor Or Ugly Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm the victim of an ugly rumor at work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you saying that the rumor is ugly or that the rumor is that you're ugly?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm saying the rumor itself is ugly.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, then I have more bad news for you.

situation: Dilbert comes home with his briefcase and tells Dogbert, who is lounging on the couch, that he is the victim of an ugly rumor at work. Dogbert asks whether the rumor is ugly or whether the rumor is that Dilbert himself is ugly. Dilbert clarifies that the rumor is ugly, and Dogbert replies that he has more bad news.
punchline: Dogbert's reply implies that Dilbert really is ugly, so the ambiguity he raised was not just wordplay but a polite way of delivering an insult.
summary: A man complains about a nasty workplace rumor, and his dog's pedantic question turns into a deadpan insult about his looks.

title: Promotion Blocked, Outsider Hired Instead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to promote you, but the lowest salary band for the next level is 20% higher than your current pay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Raises are capped at 5%, so there's no way to give you the promotion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I plan to hire someone from the outside that you can train to be your supervisor.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss tells Alice he would like to promote her, but the next salary band starts 20% above her pay and raises are capped at 5%. Rather than fix the policy, he announces he will hire an outsider at the higher salary. Alice will have to train that person to become her own supervisor.
punchline: Company pay rules make it impossible to promote a deserving employee, yet an outside hire can get the higher salary, so she must train her own boss.
summary: A manager explains that rigid pay rules block his employee's promotion and then proposes bringing in a stranger for her to groom as her superior.

title: Boss Faxes Strategy Instead of Shredding

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, shred this.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The shredder is right behind you, next to the fax.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if I do it wrong?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Only a complete moron could do it wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... I think I might have just faxed our strategy someplace.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And that's why you never see a water fountain in a men's restroom.

situation: The Boss hands Carol a document to shred, and she tells him the shredder is right behind him next to the fax machine. He worries about doing it wrong, and she assures him only a complete moron could. He then admits he has faxed the company's strategy somewhere instead of shredding it.
punchline: Carol's deadpan remark implies that the Boss is exactly the kind of moron who can't be trusted with simple tasks, comparing him to the reason there are no water fountains in men's restrooms, meaning men can't be trusted to keep things sanitary.
summary: A manager told he'd have to be an idiot to misuse the shredder promptly sends his confidential plans out by fax instead.

title: Boss Dismisses Resource Complaint With Nonsense

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have enough resources to do my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Isn't that like saying, "How now, brown cow"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You think things can't get worse. But they can.

situation: Dilbert stands in front of his boss's desk and explains that he lacks the resources to do his job. The Boss, reading a newspaper, replies with a meaningless comparison to 'How now, brown cow'. Dilbert walks away thinking that things can always get worse.
punchline: The boss answers a legitimate complaint with a nonsensical non-sequitur, proving that management cannot even comprehend the problem, let alone fix it.
summary: An employee asks for more resources and gets a baffling, irrelevant remark from a boss who barely looks up from his paper.

title: New Guy Befriends the Lazy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new employee

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Maybe if I make a friend at work it will reduce my stress hump.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: I must choose carefully because I will be judged by the people I choose to associate with.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Hi. I'm the new guy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The lazy people have found each other.

situation: A new employee thinks about making a friend at work to reduce his stress, and worries that his choice of associates will reflect on him. He peeks around a cubicle wall and introduces himself to Wally, who is idle at his desk. The Boss watches from behind and remarks that the lazy people have found each other.
punchline: The new guy's careful choice of friend backfires because he picks the laziest person in the office, and the Boss immediately judges him by that association.
summary: A newcomer carefully picks a workplace friend, only to land on the office slacker while his boss looks on disapprovingly.

file: 2005/2005-08-18_topper versus alice_secret government_sleep deprived_slept since febraury_punch_rip head_vulgar.gif
title: Sleep Deprivation One-Upmanship Gets Violent

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper versus Alice

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't get much sleep last night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm part of a secret government test on sleep deprivation. I haven't slept since February.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I so want to punch you right now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's nothing. I'll rip off my own head and make me eat it.

situation: Alice, holding a coffee mug, complains that she didn't sleep much the night before. A coworker immediately tries to top her by claiming he is in a secret government sleep deprivation test and hasn't slept since February. When Alice says she wants to punch him, he tops that too with an absurd threat against himself.
punchline: The coworker compulsively one-ups every complaint, even Alice's threat of violence, escalating to a ridiculous self-inflicted threat.
summary: A colleague who can't resist outdoing every grievance trumps a tired coworker's complaint, then even her urge to hit him.

title: Harpoon Returns at Review Time

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It's a harpoon. I see a lot of this.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It's caused by a combination of doughnut-eating and agitating a secretary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you remove it?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Yes, but it will just come back at annual review time.

situation: The Boss lies on an exam table with a large harpoon sticking out of his back. The doctor calmly says he sees this often and explains it comes from eating doughnuts and annoying a secretary. When the Boss asks if it can be removed, the doctor says yes but it will return at annual review time.
punchline: Employees metaphorically harpoon the boss when they get the chance, and annual reviews are the moment staff get to stab him back, so the harpoon is inevitable.
summary: A physician matter-of-factly diagnoses a harpoon lodged in the boss's back and warns that it will be replaced whenever employee evaluations come around.

file: 2005/2005-05-04_date co owrker_anything has pulse_bed judgement_restraining orders.gif
title: Dogbert's Low Standards for Dating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I date a coworker?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should date anything that has a pulse, bad judgement and no restraining orders against you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But she has to be hot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Settle for "still warm."

setting: Outdoors on a grassy path and beside a stone wall
situation: Dilbert walks outside with Dogbert and asks whether he should date a coworker. Dogbert advises him to date anyone with a pulse, poor judgement and no restraining orders against him. When Dilbert insists she must be hot, Dogbert tells him to settle for a woman who is merely still warm.
punchline: Dogbert's advice lowers Dilbert's dating standards so far that being alive, or barely so, counts as a qualification, and "still warm" darkly implies a corpse.
summary: Dilbert asks about workplace romance and his dog responds by cheerfully setting the bar for a partner absurdly, morbidly low.

title: Bonus for Selling to Insolvent Customer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I got a bonus for selling stuff to a customer who probably can't pay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does your soda taste any less delicious?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Congratulations; you're a sociopath.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It feels kinda good.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on a blue couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with a soda and tells Dogbert he got a bonus for selling to a customer who likely cannot pay. Dogbert asks whether his soda tastes any less delicious, and Dilbert says no. Dogbert declares him a sociopath, and Dilbert admits it feels kind of good.
punchline: Dilbert feels no guilt about profiting from a questionable sale, which Dogbert says is the mark of a sociopath, and Dilbert cheerfully agrees it feels good.
summary: After pocketing a reward for a dubious sale, a man calmly discovers his conscience has nothing to say about it.

file: 2005/2005-11-19_gullible world magazine_engineering_before and after_picture_before picture pose_sexy.gif
title: Engineering Makes You Sexier Photo

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: May I take your picture for a feature story in "Gullible World" magazine?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a story about how engineering makes you sexier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gosh, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Perfect. Now all I need is someone to pose for the "after" picture.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert, holding a camera, asks Dilbert to be photographed for a magazine story and says it is about how engineering makes you sexier. Dilbert flattered agrees and is photographed as the 'before' subject. Dogbert then says he just needs someone to pose for the 'after' picture, while a shirtless, flexing Dilbert looks on.
punchline: Dogbert's magazine story is a before-and-after pitch where Dilbert, the engineer, is the 'before' picture, implying engineering makes you less sexy, and the flattered Dilbert is too gullible to notice the insult.
summary: A flattered engineer lets his dog snap a photo for a magazine piece, only to learn he has been cast as the unattractive half of a comparison.

file: 2005/2005-07-12_don't sit by popel_full flight_suitcase_overhead comaprtment_bin_scotch over.gif
title: Stowed in the Overhead Bin

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your seat is next to mine, but I don't like to sit by people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a full flight, so I don't see how I could... Oh dear...

transcript.speaker: Man in overhead bin
transcript.text: No, I will not "scooch over."

situation: A boss tells the passenger assigned to the seat beside him that he dislikes sitting near people. Noticing the flight is full, he glances at the overhead bin, and in the last panel the passenger has been stuffed into the bin on top of luggage. He refuses to scoot over while another traveler loads a suitcase.
punchline: The boss's antisocial preference is so selfish that he effectively evicts his seatmate to the overhead luggage compartment, and the squashed passenger still defiantly refuses to make room.
summary: A boss who hates sitting near others solves the problem of a full plane by relegating his seatmate to the luggage rack.

file: 2005/2005-07-21_elbonia bid_nuclear war head_plans_internet_few things modified_ginat toaster_enriched bread_technology.gif
title: Nuclear Warhead Plans Become Toaster

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't worry. I got the plans off the Internet and I modified a few things.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Now all we need is some highly enriched bread.

setting: Conference room, then an Elbonian mud-filled workshop
situation: The Boss admits he promised Elbonia plans for a nuclear warhead in order to win a bid. Dilbert reassures him that he downloaded plans from the Internet and altered a few things. In the last panel, Elbonians standing in mud next to a giant toaster say all they need now is highly enriched bread.
punchline: Dilbert's modified plans produce a giant toaster instead of a nuclear weapon, so the Elbonians need 'enriched bread' rather than enriched uranium.
summary: Dilbert quietly sabotages a dangerous contract promise by tweaking online weapon blueprints so that they describe a kitchen appliance.

title: Pyramids Research Derails Design Review

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's my design plan. Are there any questions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It reminds me of Egyptian hieroglyphics. Are you sure they didn't patent it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I don't think that's likely.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But there's still some risk?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: First of all, I didn't use hieroglyphics. Secondly, the ancient Egyptians didn't have microchips. Thirdly, they didn't have patent laws.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh yeah? Then how did they build the pyramids?

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: Good point.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do some research on that question and get back to us next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next on the agenda: Why do our projects take so long?

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: What?

setting: Conference room during a design review meeting
situation: Dilbert presents his design plan and The Boss worries it resembles Egyptian hieroglyphics that might be patented. Dilbert rebuts the idea logically, but The Boss counters by asking how the pyramids got built and assigns Dilbert to research that irrelevant question. The Boss then asks why their projects take so long.
punchline: The Boss sends Dilbert off on a pointless research tangent and then, without any self-awareness, asks why projects take so long.
summary: A manager's far-fetched worry about ancient patents sends an engineer off on useless research, right before the manager wonders why work is always late.
keywords: why do projects take so long

title: Consultant Doubles Fees With Outsourcing Threat

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I found a way to double my management consulting fees.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend outsourcing your job to India.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll double your fee if you never say that again.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Wag!

setting: Dilbert's kitchen table, then the Boss's office
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert over coffee that he has found a way to double his management consulting fees. He then tells the Boss that he recommends outsourcing the Boss's own job to India. The frightened Boss offers to pay double if Dogbert never says that again, and Dogbert wags his tail.
punchline: Dogbert makes money by threatening to outsource his client's job, and the Boss pays double just to keep him from repeating the recommendation.
summary: A scheming consultant dog discovers that scaring a manager with the prospect of overseas replacement is the most profitable advice he can give.

title: Weather Report as Veiled Reference

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hi. I'm calling to check the references of your ex-employee named Ted.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We have a company policy against giving references. But I'd be happy to discuss the weather with you.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The clouds are moving lazily across the sky, and everyone thinks they're stupid.

setting: Two office desks with telephones, one at the caller's company and one in Catbert's HR office
situation: A woman phones a company to check the references of a former employee named Ted. Catbert, the HR director, says company policy forbids giving references but offers to discuss the weather instead. He then describes the clouds in terms that obviously stand in for Ted.
punchline: Catbert dodges the no-references policy by using a weather metaphor to deliver a scathing review, calling Ted lazy and stupid without technically breaking the rule.
summary: A policy that bans job references is neatly sidestepped when a sly HR cat gives a damning verdict on a former worker through a remark about clouds.

file: 2005/2005-08-30_company policy_least expensive flight_17 connecting flights_elbonain prison_dressed as a ballerina_desecrate monument.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much would I have to desecrate a national monument to get one night in jail?

setting: Office cubicle, then an Elbonian landscape
situation: A travel agent tells the Boss she booked the cheapest flight, as company policy requires. The itinerary has 17 connecting flights and a mandatory night in an Elbonian prison dressed as a ballerina. In the final panel the Boss, wearing a tutu and carrying a bag, stands in Elbonia between two guards and asks what it would take to be jailed instead.

summary: A rigidly cost-cutting travel booking sends an employee on an absurd journey that leaves him begging for an ordinary jail cell.

title: Slight Promotion, Shaved Cubicle Walls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I decided to give you a slight promotion!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gasp! A slight promotion!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The pay will be the same but you can make your cubicle slightly larger by shaving the ragged fabric on the inside walls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your new title is spelled just like the old one but it's pronounced totally differently.

situation: The Boss announces to Asok that he is getting a slight promotion. The reward turns out to be no pay increase, just permission to enlarge his cubicle by shaving the fabric off the inside walls, plus a new title that is spelled the same as the old one but pronounced differently. In the last panel Asok is dancing with joy and music notes while The Boss looks on.
punchline: The promotion is entirely meaningless, yet Asok is delighted by the trivial perks, while the title change is a cheap non-change that costs the company nothing.
summary: A manager rewards a young employee with a hollow promotion consisting of a barely bigger cubicle and a title that only sounds different.

title: Automation Praised As Laziness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I show you something that I'm proud of?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I automated a task that used to take me three hours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, well, well. Isn't that just like you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Resourceful?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you just turn my brilliant accomplishment into a character flaw?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Complainer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's just forget the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Quitter.

situation: Dilbert proudly shows the Boss that he automated a task that used to take him three hours. The Boss twists the achievement into a negative trait, calling him lazy when Dilbert hopes for 'resourceful'. Each time Dilbert reacts, the Boss slaps another negative label on him, ending with 'Quitter'.
punchline: No matter what Dilbert does or says, the Boss reframes it as a character flaw, so a genuine accomplishment earns only criticism.
summary: A proud engineer's time-saving innovation is met by a manager who answers every reaction with a fresh insult.

title: VP Steals Credit, Gets Corrected

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: V.P. of Engineering

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I had the idea of saving money by combining our four databases.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Excuse me. That was Alice's idea. You said it was impossible, so she did it on her own time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carry on. I'll jump in if I notice any more errors.

setting: Conference room during a meeting with the V.P. of Engineering
situation: At a meeting, the pointy-haired Boss takes credit for the idea of saving money by combining four databases. Asok interrupts to point out that it was actually Alice's idea, and that the Boss had called it impossible. The Boss, annoyed, brushes off the correction and invites Asok to continue presenting.
punchline: The Boss, caught claiming credit for an idea he had dismissed as impossible, deflects by pretending the correction was merely him noticing an error, rather than admitting he was wrong.
summary: A manager passes off a successful employee's project as his own until a junior colleague exposes the lie.

title: Seatmate Cannibal Is Predictably Annoying

transcript.speaker: Businessman

transcript.text: These guys are all the same. I know what's going to happen next.

transcript.speaker: Cannibal
transcript.text: My hairy skull isn't touching you.

transcript.speaker: Businessman
transcript.text: Right on schedule.

situation: A bald businessman reading a fishing magazine sits on a plane next to a cannibal in a grass skirt with a bone in his hair, holding a skull. The businessman complains in his thoughts that the cannibal is predictable, then the cannibal waves the skull and childishly taunts that it isn't touching him.
punchline: The seatmate's annoying behavior is not cannibalism but the schoolyard 'I'm not touching you' taunt, which the businessman wearily predicted.
summary: A weary airline passenger expects the worst from his cannibal neighbor, who instead pesters him with a childish teasing game using a skull.

title: Hit Man Endless Cycle Is Free

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The trouble with hiring a hit man is that you have to have him killed to cover your tracks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you need a hit man to hit the guy who killed the hit man. It's an endless cycle!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But ultimately, it's all free, right?

setting: Office, with Catbert seated in a green armchair
situation: Catbert, sitting in an armchair, explains the downside of hiring a hit man: you must have him killed to cover your tracks. The Boss realizes this creates an endless chain of killings, then hopefully asks whether it all ends up costing nothing.
punchline: The Boss ignores the grim moral and logistical absurdity of endless murders and fixates only on the hope that the whole scheme is somehow free, reflecting his cheapness and indifference to ethics.
summary: A cat explains the logistics of murder-for-hire to a manager who only cares whether the grisly scheme comes without a price tag.

file: 2005/2005-10-15_return frisbee_doesn't fly_software cd_total idiot_users manual_poorly written.gif

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk

transcript.text: In my defense, the user's manual was poorly written.

transcript.speaker: Pig
transcript.text: Plus you're a total idiot.

situation: A hooded, bearded customer with a pig companion tries to return a software CD at a store counter, claiming it is a Frisbee that doesn't fly right. The clerk points out it is a software CD and that only an idiot would mistake it for a Frisbee. The customer blames the poorly written user's manual, and the pig bluntly agrees the customer is an idiot.
punchline: The customer deflects blame onto the documentation for his own absurd mistake, and the pig undercuts the excuse by stating the obvious truth that he is a total idiot.
summary: A man tries to return a disc he mistook for a flying toy, blames the instructions, and his pig sidekick calls him out.

title: Blaming Wally For Project Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, after I left the meeting yesterday, did you blame me for the failure of the project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting a bad vibe from people today. That sort of rumor could stain my reputation and ruin my entire future.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How dare you accuse me...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, well. Look who's impeding Wally again.

situation: Dilbert confronts Wally, who sits at his desk holding a coffee mug, suspecting he was blamed for a failed project after Dilbert left a meeting. Dilbert worries that the rumor could ruin his reputation. Wally feigns offense at the accusation, and the Boss arrives and sides with Wally, accusing Dilbert of getting in Wally's way.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to protect his reputation backfires when the Boss assumes Dilbert is the problem, showing that the blame has already stuck and Wally's scapegoating worked.
summary: A worried engineer suspects a coworker pinned a project's failure on him, only to have his boss arrive and treat him as the obstacle.

file: 2005/2005-01-28_response to letter_apologize_admits error_starting war_mean spirit_hating minorities.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now do you apologize?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Plan B: I accuse him of hating minorities.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert that the newspaper columnist she harshly criticized for misusing the word "dongle" has replied with a link to a dictionary. She realizes she was wrong, and Dilbert asks if she will now apologize. Instead she decides to fall back on accusing the columnist of hating minorities.
punchline: Rather than admit her mistake and apologize, Alice escalates by making a baseless and nastier accusation against the person who proved her wrong.
summary: Caught being wrong in a public spat, Alice skips the apology and plans to smear her critic with an unrelated charge.

title: Ratbert CEO Renames Assistant

transcript.text: Ratbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Miss Pennington, have my driver fetch the limo.

transcript.speaker: Miss Pennington (on phone)
transcript.text: My name isn't Miss Pennington. It's Harold.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Um... and... I'll have it legally changed to Miss Pennington so you won't be wrong.

transcript.speaker: Miss Pennington (on phone)
transcript.text: Plus the surgery.

setting: Ratbert's CEO office, seated at a desk with a phone
situation: Ratbert, now a CEO, phones his assistant and calls her Miss Pennington, only to be told that the name is actually Harold. Rather than apologize, Ratbert offers to legally change Harold's name to Miss Pennington so that he won't have been wrong. Harold responds by adding that the surgery must be included too.
punchline: The powerful boss would rather force an employee to change their name than admit a mistake, and the employee escalates the absurd demand by adding gender-reassignment surgery.
summary: A newly minted executive refuses to admit he got his assistant's name wrong and offers to rewrite the assistant's identity instead, at a steep price.

title: Serial Returner Gets Organs Harvested

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'd like to return this scarf.

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: What's wrong with it?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It isn't um... scarfy enough.

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: I'll just run your card through the computer and...

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: Uh-oh... You're on our bad customer list. You've returned over a thousand items to this store.

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: In fact, you've purchased and returned this same scarf seventeen times.

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: Company policy says that I have to harvest your organs and sell them on eBay.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It was good while it lasted.

situation: An elderly woman tries to return a scarf, claiming it isn't 'scarfy' enough. When the clerk runs her card, the computer reveals she is on the bad customer list, having returned over a thousand items, including this same scarf seventeen times. The clerk explains that company policy requires him to harvest her organs and sell them on eBay, and she calmly accepts her fate.
punchline: A chronic returner's punishment under company policy is absurdly extreme (organ harvesting for eBay), and she resignedly accepts it as if it were a routine consequence.
summary: A shopper who habitually returns merchandise learns that the store's policy for such customers is to have their organs sold online, and she takes the news with weary acceptance.

file: 2005/2005-03-17_conference call_boss_15 people_availablity_august 6th_5 minutes_so far so good.gif
title: Scheduling Around Boss's Five-Minute Window

transcript.text: Only August sixth between 8:35 and 8:40.

transcript.speaker: Asok

setting: Asok's office cubicle, on the phone at his desk
situation: Asok, the intern, phones an executive's office to schedule a conference call involving the executive and 15 other people. When he asks for all available times in the next six months, he is told the executive is free only on one date for a five-minute window. Asok calmly responds as if the plan is still on track.
punchline: Asok's cheerful 'so far, so good' ignores that finding a time slot that works for 16 people in a single five-minute window is essentially impossible.
summary: An intern trying to book a big conference call learns the executive's entire availability for half a year is a five-minute gap and optimistically carries on.

situation: A bearded customer boasts about completing the Iditarod dogsled race. Topper, a compulsive one-upper, claims he did it while pretending to be one of the dogs. The customer is put off and says he won't buy from Topper's company, so Topper tries to top that too by threatening to burn his own company down.
punchline: Topper's need to outdo everyone is so compulsive that he sabotages the sale and even tries to one-up the customer's refusal by vowing to destroy his own company.
summary: A salesman who cannot stop topping every anecdote drives off a client and then tries to outdo the rejection itself with self-destruction.

title: Accounting Demands Originals, Gets Fax Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Accounting Department

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Monster
transcript.text: Just fax them.

situation: A green monster in the accounting department phones Alice to say her travel expenses can't be processed because she submitted copies of receipts instead of originals. punchline: Accounting insists on original receipts, then suggests faxing them, which would produce exactly the copies they just rejected.
summary: A bureaucrat's demand for paper originals collapses under its own illogical workaround when the same person recommends sending a fax.

file: 2005/2005-04-08_handpicked_team_no budget_laziness_least effirt_yvonne_hotness_power over men_manipulated by all_good meeting_business.gif

transcript.text: Wally, your laziness helps you accomplish the most work with the least effort. Yvonne, your hotness gives you the power to make men do what you want for nothing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, then Yvonne convinced me to do her work and Wally went on disability leave.

summary: A manager recruits two employees for their cheap talents, only to end up doing the work himself while one of them goes on leave.

title: Developing Coffee-Sipping Noises Instead of Software

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I couldn't buy the software I need to do my job because of your freeze on expenses.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And our I.S. policy says I can't use the freeware version that is readily available.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I used the week to develop some new coffee-sipping noises.

situation: Wally sits at a meeting table holding a coffee mug and explains to the Boss why he got no work done. Management froze expenses so he couldn't buy the software he needs, and IT policy forbids him from using the free alternative. With no way to do his job, he spent the week perfecting his coffee-sipping noises.
punchline: Wally turns two contradictory corporate policies into a justification for doing absolutely nothing productive, presenting his slacking as the only logical outcome.
summary: Blocked by both a spending freeze and a ban on free alternatives, an employee reports that his week's output was a repertoire of beverage slurping sounds.

title: Core Values Missing Hygiene

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our core values are service, integrity, respect, teamwork, responsibility, trust, diversity, value, honesty, fun, passion, fairness and excellence.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How should we deal with the inherent conflicts? I mean, what if I want to be irresponsible in a fun and passionate way?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to do all of them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I notice that hygiene didn't make the list.

situation: The Boss reads out a very long list of corporate core values to the team at a meeting. Wally asks how to handle values that conflict, such as being irresponsible in a fun way, and the Boss says all of them must be followed. Wally then points out that hygiene is missing from the list.
punchline: Wally's dig that hygiene isn't among the values suggests he is dodging bathing, while also mocking how bloated and contradictory corporate value lists are.
summary: A manager recites an endless list of company ideals, and a slacker employee exploits the contradictions before noting that cleanliness was left off.

title: Hiring Someone To Do Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to hire someone to do all of the unpleasant parts of my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That way I'll be free to concentrate on strategy.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Secondly, I'd like to hire someone to do strategy.

setting: Catbert's office, where the human resources director sits on a desk
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the HR director, that he wants to hire someone to take over the unpleasant parts of his job so he can focus on strategy. Catbert accepts this as reasonable. The Boss then adds a second request: hire someone to do the strategy as well.
punchline: The Boss delegates away every part of his job, even the one thing he claimed he wanted to keep, revealing he has no real function.
summary: A manager sets out to offload his drudgery onto a new hire, then promptly offloads the supposedly important remainder too.
