transcript.text: While we're gone, you'll need to answer everyone's phone.

setting: Office cubicle area, at Carol's desk
situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol that he is taking the whole staff to a five-star restaurant for lunch. He describes the food and wine in glowing, almost sensual terms. Then he reveals that Carol is not coming and must stay behind to cover everyone's phones.
punchline: The Boss builds up the amazing lunch as a treat for the entire staff, then reveals that Carol is excluded and will be stuck answering phones, making his 'entire staff' claim a cruel bait-and-switch.
summary: A manager raves about an extravagant team lunch to his assistant before casually assigning her to stay behind and work the phones.

file: 2005/2005-01-16_certified massage therapist_clicking_every week_few minutes_lengthy questionarie_one hand_pen pal_used pen.gif
title: Massage Therapist Substitutes Ballpoint Pen

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Certified massage therapist

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist
transcript.text: Fill out this lengthy medical questionnaire.

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist (thought)
transcript.text: That'll save me a few minutes of touching him.

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist (thought)
transcript.text: I wonder if he'd know if I only used one hand.

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist (thought)
transcript.text: Actually, how would he even know if it's a hand?

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist (thought)
transcript.text: Maybe I have an object in here that feels like a hand.

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist (thought)
transcript.text: This ballpoint pen will work.

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist
transcript.text: I'm finding some tension here.

transcript.speaker: Massage Therapist
transcript.text: Okay, it's gone now.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She says I should come back every week until my muscles stop clicking.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sounds like you found a pen pal.

situation: A massage therapist hands Dilbert a long medical questionnaire to fill out, then plots to cut corners by using only one hand, and then a ballpoint pen, in place of her hands. Dilbert lies face down, unaware, and later reports that his muscles are clicking and that she wants him back weekly.
punchline: The therapist is secretly massaging Dilbert with a clicking ballpoint pen, and Dogbert's 'pen pal' quip points out what Dilbert fails to realize.
summary: A lazy masseuse swaps her hands for a clicking pen while her unsuspecting client lies face down, and Dogbert hints at the deception.

title: Cubicle Sharing Lap Seating Fantasy

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I hope you don't mind that I'll be sharing your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Umm...I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: There's only one chair. Do you mind if I sit on your lap?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Umm...I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't imagine how this could be better.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Which one of the Star Trek series did you like best?

situation: A new female coworker announces she will be sharing Dilbert's cubicle, then asks to sit on his lap because there is only one chair. Dilbert agrees, and as she sits on his lap typing on a laptop, he thinks the situation couldn't be better. She then chats with him about which Star Trek series he liked best.
punchline: Dilbert's dream scenario of an attractive woman on his lap is perfectly matched to his nerdy interests, as she cheerfully raises Star Trek, making it the ultimate geek fantasy.
summary: A friendly new officemate squeezes into a lonely engineer's cubicle and onto his lap, and the conversation turns to his favorite sci-fi franchise.

file: 2005/2005-10-23_evil director_fly on plane_guidelines_key employees_ceo_presdient_same flight_interns_run with sciccors_plastic bags_over heads.gif
title: Interns Are Expendable Flight Guidelines

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I have new guidelines on who can fly on the same plane.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We can't risk losing too many key employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The CEO and the President are not allowed to be on the same flight.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No more than three vice presidents may be on the same flight.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What are the guidelines for interns?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Infinite interns are allowed on the same flight. You are also allowed to run with scissors and put plastic bags over your heads.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How many interns are allowed per plastic bag?

setting: Conference room at a company meeting
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, presents new corporate travel guidelines limiting how many key executives can share a flight. When an employee asks about interns, Catbert says there is no limit and that they may run with scissors and wear plastic bags on their heads. The employee then asks how many interns can share one bag.
punchline: Interns are treated as completely disposable, so the only worry is how to fit more of them into each hazardous situation, with the employee's question showing he has absorbed this callous logic.
summary: Human resources protects its executives with careful flight rules while declaring that unlimited interns can be put in any danger without concern.

file: 2005/2005-08-06_comapny_sells defective prodcuts_karma_bed doodle_wandered_bad things_they deserve it.gif
title: Karma Justifies Selling Defective Products

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I feel guilty because my company sells defective products.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I believe in karma. That means I can do bad things to people all day long and I assume they deserve it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By the way, where are we?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think we wandered into a bad doodle.

setting: A strange, sketchy, surreal landscape with odd mushroom-like structures (a 'bad doodle')
situation: Dilbert confesses he feels guilty because his company sells defective products. Dogbert offers a twisted take on karma, claiming he can harm people all day because he assumes they deserve it. Dilbert then asks where they are, and Dogbert says they've wandered into a bad doodle.
punchline: Dogbert's self-serving karma logic assumes everyone he wrongs deserves it, and the strip ends with the meta-joke that they are standing in a poorly drawn, bad doodle.
summary: Dogbert twists the idea of karma into a blanket excuse for mistreating people, then the pair realize they have strayed into a crudely drawn, surreal scene.

title: CEO Dogbert's Absurd Intelligence Boost

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The best part about being CEO is that it made me smarter. Watch this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The capital of Japan is Mitsubishi.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's right! You're a genius!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yesterday I would have said nine.

setting: Conference room at a company meeting table
situation: Dogbert, now CEO, claims his new position has made him smarter and offers a demonstration. He states an absurd wrong answer, that the capital of Japan is Mitsubishi, and the Boss enthusiastically praises him as a genius. Dogbert then adds that the day before he would have given an even more nonsensical answer.
punchline: Executives are praised as brilliant no matter how wrong they are, and Dogbert's claimed 'improvement' is just a different flavor of nonsense, since yesterday he would have said 'nine'.
summary: A newly promoted CEO shows off his supposed boost in intelligence with a ridiculous answer that his flattering subordinates applaud anyway.

title: Documenting the Documented Process Process

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In order to avoid shoddy mistakes, everything we do from now on will be part of a documented process.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What documented process did you use to decide what documented process to use?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or is this one of those shoddy mistakes I keep hearing about?

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that everything will now follow a documented process in order to prevent shoddy mistakes. Wally, sitting next to Dilbert, asks what documented process the Boss used to choose that policy, then suggests the decision itself might be one of the shoddy mistakes.
punchline: The Boss's decision to mandate documented processes was itself made without any documented process, exposing the policy as the kind of shoddy mistake it was meant to prevent.
summary: A manager's sweeping new rule about documentation is undercut when an employee points out the rule was adopted without following any process at all.

file: 2005/2005-12-12_ran six miles_topper_hopped to work_broken leg_better_more better.gif
title: Topping a Coworker's Running Story

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I ran six miles even though I was sore.

transcript.speaker: Man in tie
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Man in tie
transcript.text: I broke my leg and hopped all the way to work this morning.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You hopped 40 miles on your one good leg?

transcript.speaker: Man in tie
transcript.text: On the broken one.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: At a meeting, a woman with big hair brags that she ran six miles despite being sore. A coworker brushes this off and claims he hopped all the way to work after breaking his leg. When she questions the distance, he escalates by saying he hopped on the broken leg.
punchline: The coworker compulsively one-ups every claim, even contradicting his own story with an absurd exaggeration just to win the contest of toughness.
summary: Two colleagues compete over who suffered more, and one keeps inflating his tale until it becomes impossible.

file: 2005/2005-06-19_right away_three weeks_deadline_soar with eagles_motivational poster_over weekend cell phone_sail boat.gif
title: Boss Parrots Motivational Poster Slogans

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This needs to be done right away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to the date, you've had this on your desk for three weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I'll have to work all weekend to finish it by the deadline!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes you have to soar with the eagles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! You're reading that from the motivational poster behind me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I have any questions about this, can I call you over the weekend?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My cell phone doesn't work when I'm on my sixty-foot, luxury sailboat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ay-yi-yi-yi!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, if you can't take the heat, get out of the ...uh... kitchen.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document he demands be done right away, but Dilbert notices it has sat on the Boss's desk for three weeks, forcing him to work all weekend. The Boss deflects with clichés read off a motivational poster, then reveals he will be unreachable on his luxury sailboat while Dilbert works.
punchline: The Boss's procrastination becomes Dilbert's weekend emergency, and he excuses it with hollow poster slogans while he himself goes sailing.
summary: A manager sits on a project for weeks, then dumps the rush on his employee and answers complaints with recycled platitudes before heading off on his yacht.

title: Easier to Moonlight Than Upgrade

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My computer is too slow. I need to upgrade it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a cost-benefit analysis including the cost of all alternatives, and vice president approval.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was easier to get a second job and pay for the upgrade myself.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a computer upgrade because his machine is too slow. The boss demands a cost-benefit analysis covering every alternative plus vice president approval. In the last panel Dilbert, now wearing a different uniform at home with Dogbert, explains he took a second job to pay for the upgrade himself.
punchline: The company's approval bureaucracy is so burdensome that working a second job to buy the equipment yourself is the easier path.
summary: Faced with absurd red tape to replace a sluggish computer, an engineer finds it simpler to moonlight and buy the upgrade with his own money.

title: Tech Support Demands 625 Fixes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello. My CrashInBox(tm) computer keeps freezing up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There are 25 possible fixes but they must be tried in every possible combination.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's 625 things I'd have to try with no guarantee that any of it will work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So you're saying you're lazy?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and Dogbert's tech support desk, connected by phone
situation: Dilbert phones tech support because his computer keeps freezing. Dogbert, working as the support agent, says there are 25 possible fixes that must be tried in every combination. When Dilbert points out that means 625 attempts with no guarantee of success, Dogbert accuses him of being lazy.
punchline: The tech support agent turns the customer's entirely reasonable objection to an absurd, unworkable procedure into an accusation of laziness, blaming the user for the support process's failings.
summary: A help-desk dog hands a caller an impossibly long troubleshooting routine and then blames him for balking at it.

file: 2005/2005-04-23_watch my shows_invite me over_cable_pulled_bug in salad.gif
title: Mom Only Calls for Cabling

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: While you're here, be a dear and run some Cat-5 to my walk-in closet so I can watch my shows when I'm in there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that you only invite me over when you need a cable pulled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I don't want to put a bug in your salad, but I will.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm glad we had this talk.

situation: Dilbert's mother, chopping vegetables for a salad, asks him to run network cable to her walk-in closet so she can watch TV there. Dilbert complains that she only invites him over when she needs a cable pulled. She responds with a threat to put a bug in his salad, and he cheerfully accepts the outcome of the conversation.
punchline: Dilbert's mother turns his complaint into a veiled threat of poisoning his food, a pun on 'bug' as an insect and as a software defect, and he meekly says he's glad they talked.
summary: A mother who treats her engineer son as free tech support threatens to contaminate his dinner when he calls her out on it.

file: 2005/2005-02-20_pre meeting_problems_fix them_budgets_deadlines_technical stuff_any questions_feel nauseated_great job_compliments.gif
title: Boss Coaches Dilbert Into Saying Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's have a pre-meeting before your meeting with our vice president.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't mention any problems because he might try to fix them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't say anything about budgets or deadlines because he might reduce them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leave out the technical stuff because it will only confuse him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That leaves me nothing to talk about.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perfect!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello... and in summary, are there any questions?

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Wow! That's the first presentation that hasn't made me feel nauseated or dizzy! Great job!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does success make me hate humanity?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They deserve it.

setting: Boss's office and a conference room
situation: The Boss holds a pre-meeting to coach Dilbert on what to leave out of his presentation to the vice president: problems, budgets, deadlines and technical details. Dilbert points out that leaves nothing to say, and the Boss approves. Dilbert delivers a blank presentation and the vice president praises it as the best he has seen.
punchline: A presentation with no content is rewarded as a triumph, showing that management values empty, comfortable talk over real information, and leaving Dilbert cynical about the people who deserve such disdain.
summary: After being told to omit everything meaningful from a presentation, Dilbert delivers an empty talk that the executive loves.

file: 2005/2005-03-27_work load_complaints_drowning in work_priorotize_fax_new guy set_faxing project_reading comics.gif
title: Carol Prioritizes Away Extra Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, the new manager hasn't hired an admin, so I said he could share you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What?!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm drowning in work, and you want to double my load???!!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's no big deal. Just prioritize your work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I need you to fax this.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: No can do.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My top priority is getting the new guy all set up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm...I guess that's fair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll send him over.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I can't order your business cards; I need to do a huge faxing project!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hee hee! Marmaduke is sitting on something again!

situation: The Boss tells Carol, his admin, that she must also support the new manager and then asks her to fax something. Carol takes his advice to prioritize literally, declaring that setting up the new guy is her top priority, which pushes the Boss's fax down the list. When the new manager comes by for business cards, she claims she's too busy with a huge faxing project, then secretly reads the comics.
punchline: Carol turns the Boss's advice to 'prioritize' into a way to avoid work, stalling everyone with made-up priorities while she reads the funny pages.
summary: An overloaded assistant uses her boss's own advice about prioritizing to dodge every task and enjoy the newspaper comics.

title: Wits, Computer, and Stolen Pencil

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might have no budget and no staff to help me on my project, but that doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because all I need are my wits and my computer.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My computer is too slow. I'm taking yours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My wits and...this pencil.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, isn't that my pencil?

situation: Dilbert boasts that he can complete his project despite having no budget and no staff, since he still has his wits and his computer. A coworker walks up, announces his own computer is too slow, and takes Dilbert's. Dilbert is left with only a pencil, which the coworker then claims is his.
punchline: Each time Dilbert names the one resource he still has, a coworker takes it away, until even his last pencil turns out to belong to someone else.
summary: A resource-starved engineer's optimistic list of what he still owns is whittled down by a scavenging colleague until nothing is left.

file: 2005/2005-07-05_dating pretty boys_look best_act best_more bread!_knows he can't do better.gif
title: Dating Dilbert: Lowering Her Standards

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I'm tired of dating pretty boys where I need to look and act my best all the time.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I want a guy who knows he can't do better than me, no matter what I look like.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: More bread!!!

setting: A restaurant table by a large window
situation: Dilbert sits quietly at a restaurant table across from his date while she explains that she is tired of dating good-looking men and wants someone who knows he can't do better than her. In the last panel she drops all pretense of manners, stuffs her face with bread and shouts for more, crumbs flying.
punchline: Having found a man who feels lucky to be with her, she immediately stops acting her best and behaves as badly as she likes, which shows exactly what she wanted in a partner.
summary: A woman on a date announces she wants a man too insecure to expect anything of her, then promptly gorges herself on bread like a barbarian.

file: 2005/2005-10-11_trends are positive_crushing debt_moronic management_aging product line.gif
title: Tina's Tiny-Font Annual Report Footnote

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tina writes the annual report.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: All trends are positive.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Footnote 5: Unless you consider our crushing debt, moronic management, and aging product line.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What font is this? It's so tiny.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Enron Beelzebub.

setting: Tina's office and the Boss's desk
situation: Tina writes the company's annual report, claiming all trends are positive, then buries a brutally honest footnote admitting the company's debt, bad management, and aging products. The Boss examines the report with a magnifying glass and asks what font was used because the text is so tiny. Tina answers with a font name that references the Enron scandal.
punchline: Tina hides the damning truth about the company in microscopic footnote text and jokes that the font is named after Enron, the infamous company known for deceptive accounting.
summary: A technical writer technically discloses her company's serious problems in a footnote so small her boss needs a magnifying glass to read it.

title: Dogbert's Hostile FAQ Question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired Mr. Dogbert to write the F.A.Q. for our web site.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key is to anticipate our customers' most likely questions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Question 1: Where does your CEO live? I need to know so I can throw your cruddy product through his biggest window.

setting: Conference room and Dogbert's computer desk
situation: The Boss explains at a meeting that he has hired Dogbert, as a consultant, to write the FAQ for the company website, stressing the need to anticipate customers' likely questions. Dogbert then types the first FAQ question, imagining an angry customer who wants the CEO's home address so he can hurl the bad product through the CEO's window.
punchline: Dogbert anticipates that the most likely customer question is an enraged demand for the CEO's address, which is a sarcastic admission that the company's product is terrible and customers are furious.
summary: A consultant dog tasked with predicting customer questions concludes that buyers of the shoddy product will mainly want to know where to vent their rage.

file: 2005/2005-12-02_hammerhead bob_start butting into private lives_sense annoyance.gif
title: Hammerhead Bob Learns ESP

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great. The only seat is next to Hammerhead Bob.

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: I'm learning ESP so I can start butting into people's private thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: I sense annoyance, yet there seems to be no cause.

situation: Dilbert enters a meeting room and silently grumbles that the only free seat is next to Hammerhead Bob, a hammer-headed coworker. After Dilbert sits down, Bob announces he is learning ESP so he can intrude on people's private thoughts. He then declares he senses Dilbert's annoyance but can't see any reason for it.
punchline: Bob claims psychic powers to read minds, yet fails to realize that he himself is the cause of Dilbert's annoyance.
summary: A man stuck beside an oblivious coworker is told that the coworker is developing mind-reading skills, which still can't identify the obvious source of his irritation.

title: Blaming Those Left Off Invite List

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to blame people who won't be in the room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the boss's assistant, for the list of invitees to a debriefing meeting. After she hands it over, he explains that he likes to blame people who won't be in the room. He then tells the Boss, who is standing there, that he is not on the list.
punchline: Dilbert is planning to pin the blame for the project's failure on the Boss, since being excluded from the debriefing means he can't defend himself.
summary: A man gathers the guest list for a post-mortem so he can steer the finger-pointing toward whoever has been left out, and the boss turns out to be that person.

title: Punching the New Guy's Hump

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The New Guy

punchline: Tina presented her violent act as a helpful remedy, but admits she had no real expertise and was just looking for an excuse to hit someone.
summary: A coworker claims she can cure a colleague's back lump, wallops him, and then confesses the cure was only a pretext for the punch.

title: Sponsoring the Steroid-Tainted Stadium

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: Our marketing plan was to find a sports stadium to brand with our company's name.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive

transcript.speaker: Baseball Fan
transcript.text: How do you feel about the new stadium name?

transcript.speaker: Muscular Baseball Player
transcript.text: Rage. Same as always.

setting: A conference room, then a baseball field
situation: In a meeting, a marketing executive explains that the company chose to put its name on a stadium. The team they picked was selected because its players are so juiced up on steroids that the company's own poor reputation looks good by comparison. On the field, a fan asks a hulking, over-muscled player how he feels about the new stadium name.
punchline: The company deliberately sponsored a steroid-riddled team so its bad reputation would look better, and the player's answer of 'rage' is a nod to steroid-induced roid rage.
summary: A firm with a bad image buys naming rights to a stadium full of doped-up athletes so it will look respectable next to them.

title: Arriving in Elbonia Headfirst

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate landing in Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whump!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi. I'm from America and I'm here to help.

setting: Muddy Elbonian village with mud huts
situation: A traveler falls headfirst through the sky with his suitcase and lands with a thud, plunging into the Elbonian mud. His head is buried and his legs stick up, yet he politely introduces himself as an American here to help while a pig watches nearby.
punchline: He delivers a cheerful, rehearsed aid-worker greeting while stuck upside down in mud, mocking the arrogance and ineptitude of outsiders who arrive to 'help' a foreign country.
summary: A foreign helper crash-lands in a mud pit yet still announces his good intentions to the locals.

title: Marathon Team Bad News

transcript.text: I have some good news and some bad news.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The good news is that the company is going to sponsor a corporate marathon team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The bad news is that one of you has to run 26 miles tomorrow.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss addresses his employees at a meeting, announcing good news and bad news. The good news is that the company will sponsor a corporate marathon team. The bad news is that one of the employees must run a full marathon tomorrow, and Dilbert, Wally and Alice listen warily.
punchline: The company's 'sponsorship' is just a perk for management's image, with the cost falling on an unprepared employee who must run 26 miles with no notice or training.
summary: A manager cheerfully announces a company-sponsored marathon team, then reveals that some unlucky staffer has to run the race the very next day.

file: 2005/2005-11-02_flashy_thermostat_turn up_boiling_build device_get heat_from your hot flash.gif
title: Flashy's Heat-Harvesting Device Trap

transcript.speaker: Coworker in parka
transcript.text: Flashy, do you mind if I turn up the thermostat a few degrees?

transcript.speaker: Flashy
transcript.text: Yes. It's boiling in here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in parka
transcript.text: Would you mind if we built a device that would redirect the radiant heat from your body?

transcript.speaker: Flashy
transcript.text: Okay, fine.

transcript.speaker: Flashy
transcript.text: I should have asked more questions.

situation: A coworker bundled in a parka asks Flashy, who is overheated from hot flashes, if he can raise the thermostat. When she refuses, he instead asks permission to build a device to redirect her body heat, and she casually agrees. In the last panel a large insulated heat-collecting duct hangs over her head and she realizes she should have asked more questions.
punchline: Flashy agreed to an alternative without asking what it involved, and ended up with a heat-harvesting contraption clamped over her head to warm her chilly coworker.
summary: A freezing office worker gets around a thermostat dispute by tricking his hot-flashing colleague into agreeing to a vaguely described heat-capturing gadget.

title: Stupidity-Blocking Headphones Are Just Headphones

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: This is a prototype of the product I've been developing for the past year.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I modified a pair of standard noise-cancellation headphones to recognize stupidity and block it before it reaches your ears.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Put these on and you'll enjoy the total bliss that comes from avoiding the chatter of idiots.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do they work?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said, do they work?!!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Does anyone have any questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those are ordinary headphones, aren't they?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: If you act like you can't hear, they're a prototype.

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: A bald engineer presents a prototype pair of headphones he claims were modified to detect and block stupidity. When Dilbert asks if they work, the engineer pretends not to hear, ignores further questions, and finally admits to Dilbert that they are ordinary headphones and he only pretends not to hear.
punchline: The 'stupidity-blocking' headphones are just ordinary headphones, and their only function is giving the wearer an excuse to ignore people by pretending not to hear them.
summary: An inventor unveils a year-long project that turns out to be plain headphones worn as a cover for ignoring everyone.

title: Hammerhead Bob Prescribes Herbal Remedy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hammerhead Bob

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: Hey, what are you talking about? I'm an expert on many topics.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Try to get this through your thick head: you are not welcome in our conversation.

transcript.speaker: Hammerhead Bob
transcript.text: Irritable, eh? Try cramp bark and dandelion root.

situation: Hammerhead Bob butts into a conversation between two women holding coffee mugs, claiming to be an expert on many topics. Alice bluntly tells him he is not welcome in the conversation. Bob ignores the insult and responds by diagnosing her as irritable and recommending herbal remedies.
punchline: Bob is so oblivious that he treats being told off as a symptom of irritability and offers unsolicited herbal medical advice, proving exactly why he isn't welcome.
summary: A self-proclaimed know-it-all barges into a chat, gets rebuked, and responds by prescribing herbs for the rebuker's bad mood.

title: Raises Based on Boss Day Gifts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a list of gifts I received on National Boss Day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sort them by dollar value and assign annual raises based on who gave the most.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Now I regret the Sculpture-O-Gum.

situation: The Boss hands an employee a list of gifts he received on National Boss Day. He instructs the employee to rank the givers by dollar value and assign annual raises according to who gave the most. The employee, thinking silently, regrets having given a cheap Sculpture-O-Gum gift.
punchline: The Boss openly turns a Boss Day gift into a bribery scheme for raises, leaving the employee regretting their cheap gift.
summary: A manager decides that pay raises should be proportional to the value of the presents his staff gave him, and one worker realizes their novelty gift was a costly mistake.

title: Dogbert Insults Boss as Life Coach

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm Dogbert, your life coach. I'm here because you're an unmotivated, drifting, unorganized dolt.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Life coach? I didn't ask for a life coach.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Which part of "unmotivated, drifting, unorganized dolt" is confusing you?

situation: Dogbert stands on the Boss's desk and announces he is the Boss's life coach, bluntly explaining that the Boss is an unmotivated, drifting, unorganized dolt. The Boss objects that he never requested a life coach. Dogbert responds by asking which part of his insulting description the Boss fails to understand.
punchline: Dogbert treats the Boss's lack of self-awareness as proof that he needs a life coach, using the insult itself as the justification for the unwanted service.
summary: An uninvited life coach justifies his visit by calling his client a hopeless dolt and then mocks him for not grasping the obvious.

title: Dogbert Fires Stores as CEO

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I keep getting bad service at stores.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do what I do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I say I'm the CEO of their company and then I fire them all.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't look like a CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Too sexy?

setting: Outdoors on a path through grassy hills
situation: Dilbert complains to Dogbert about poor service in stores. Dogbert explains his method: he claims to be the CEO of the store's company and fires all the employees. Dilbert points out that Dogbert doesn't look like a CEO, and Dogbert asks if he's too sexy.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd confidence deflects the obvious objection that a small dog hardly looks like a CEO by suggesting the real problem is that he's too attractive.
summary: A dog solves his service complaints by impersonating a top executive and dismissing the staff, then waves off doubts about his credibility with vanity.

title: Boss Hoards Paper for Free Trip

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A prestigious window-facing cubicle has just become available.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It'll be a perfect place to store all of the printer paper I bought so I could win a free trip from the paper vendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And maybe the sunlight will bleach out the visible wood chips.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss announces that a prestigious window-facing cubicle has opened up. He then reveals he wants to use it as storage for a huge stockpile of printer paper he bought. He did this to qualify for a free trip from the paper vendor, and he hopes sunlight will bleach the wood chips out of the cheap paper.
punchline: The Boss is wasting company money on excess low-quality paper just to earn himself a personal perk, and he's sacrificing a coveted cubicle to hide the evidence.
summary: A manager admits he overbought flawed paper to score a vendor's vacation prize and plans to stash it in a coveted office space.

file: 2005/2005-05-07_attorney_contact_cubicle opened_dividing up workspace_eyebrows_my client_prove_naked_got him for everything_legal.gif
title: Cubicle Roommate Divorce Settlement

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A cubicle vacancy opened up, so I'll be moving out of here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My attorney will contact you about dividing up our workspace property.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: Next, can you prove that you had both eyebrows before you met my client?

situation: Alice announces that she is moving to a newly vacant cubicle and says her attorney will contact Dilbert about dividing their shared workspace property. In the last panel her attorney arrives, carrying Dilbert's belongings, and Dilbert stands there stripped to nothing. The attorney asks him to prove he had both eyebrows before meeting Alice.
punchline: Sharing a cubicle is treated like a bitter divorce, with the lawyer taking everything Dilbert owns, even his clothes, and absurdly claiming credit for his eyebrows.
summary: A coworker leaving a shared cubicle treats the split like an ugly divorce, and her lawyer leaves her former cubicle-mate with nothing at all.

title: Dogbert Consults Very Slowly, Billing Hourly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mister Dogbert has agreed to consult for $400 per hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know it's expensive but you get what you pay for.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's get the ball rolling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My first question is: What process will you be using to arrive at your recommendations?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silence; Dogbert sits motionless while the Boss and a colleague wait.)

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Very...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Slow one.

situation: The Boss introduces Dogbert to a meeting as a consultant billing $400 per hour and asks what process he will use to reach his recommendations. Dogbert answers with an agonizingly slow, drawn-out pause between words, "A... very... slow one." The others wait patiently while the meter runs.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately drags out his answer word by word because he bills by the hour, literally making his process a slow one.
summary: A pricey consultant stretches a simple answer across several painfully slow panels, since every second of delay earns him more money.
keywords: you get what you pay for

file: 2005/2005-10-13_liberty_calculating_how eich_willing to date_happily married_four trillion dollars.gif
title: Alice Prices Dating Dilbert: Trillions

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I took the liberty of calculating how rich you'd have to be...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Before I'd be willing to date you. The number is four trillion dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're happily married.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's all factored in.

situation: Alice walks up to Dilbert, who is seated at his computer, holding a printed sheet. She announces she has calculated how wealthy he would need to be before she would date him, and the answer is four trillion dollars. Dilbert points out that she is happily married, and she replies that this has already been accounted for in the figure.
punchline: Alice's absurdly huge price tag already includes the obstacle of her happy marriage, which is a polite way of saying there is essentially no chance she would ever date Dilbert.
summary: A coworker presents a printed calculation showing the astronomical fortune it would take for her to consider dating a hapless engineer.

title: Dilbert Refuses to Defend Assumptions

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How can you think that the software integration project is a waste of time??!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But if history is my guide, you will abuse the next hour of my life by insisting that I defend your misunderstanding of what I think.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So why do you think it's a waste of time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I work while you hallucinate?

situation: Alice storms up to Dilbert's desk and angrily asks how he can think the software integration project is a waste of time. Dilbert, who never said that, calmly predicts she will waste an hour insisting he defend a view he doesn't hold. Alice ignores this and asks why he thinks it's a waste of time, and Dilbert goes on working while she rants.
punchline: Alice proves Dilbert's prediction right by immediately demanding he justify an opinion he never expressed, so he tells her to keep hallucinating while he gets on with his work.
summary: A furious coworker accuses Dilbert of an opinion he doesn't hold, and he sarcastically lets her argue with her own imagination while he keeps working.

file: 2005/2005-02-06_ceo visist_donuts_taste test_all donuts_dont panic_fix donuts_screaming_fresh and delicious.gif
title: Carol Tastes Every Doughnut

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I want to be certain that everything is perfect for the CEO's visit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Check the doughnuts to make sure that they're fresh and delicious.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Mmm...this one is okay.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: How can I be sure this isn't the one good doughnut in the batch.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll have to taste every one of them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol!!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Don't panic. I can fix this.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: This is odd: most of my doughnut is delicious, but one part tastes like gum.

setting: Office cubicles and a conference room
situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to check that the doughnuts for the CEO's visit are fresh and delicious. Carol, worried that one good doughnut might be a fluke, samples every one and eats the whole batch. The Boss screams her name when he finds the doughnuts gone, and Carol's quick fix is to serve the CEO a doughnut with gum in it.
punchline: Carol's literal-minded quality check ate all the doughnuts, and her desperate fix was a gum-filled replacement that the CEO bit into.
summary: A secretary told to inspect refreshments for a VIP visit overzealously devours them all, then covers the loss with a very bad substitute.

file: 2005/2005-08-28_new director_wist decision support_out source contracts_north elbonia_government reward.gif
title: Post-Decision Support Justifies Boss's Nuclear Outsourcing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My job could not be more meaningless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking at my new Director of Post-Decision Support!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: After I make a decision, your job is to figure out why it was the right one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Save those tears of joy for later. We've got work to do!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to outsource our nuclear contracts to North Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And in return, they'll give us food, if they ever figure out how to grow any.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I expect some fallout from this decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, it won't be long before there's a government reward for killing him.

situation: Dilbert thinks his job couldn't be more meaningless, then the Boss appoints him Director of Post-Decision Support, meaning he must invent justifications after the Boss has already decided. The Boss then announces he has outsourced the company's nuclear contracts to North Elbonia in exchange for food they may not be able to grow. Dilbert predicts fallout, then notes that a government reward for killing the Boss will soon exist.
punchline: Dilbert's job is to rationalize terrible decisions after the fact, and the best 'plus side' he can find for the Boss's reckless nuclear outsourcing is that someone will soon be rewarded for assassinating him.
summary: A new role of justifying decisions after they are made is quickly tested by an absurdly dangerous outsourcing choice.

title: Dogbert Cancels Guilt With Arrogance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever feel guilty for scamming innocent people out of their money?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I only scam the people who would do the same thing to me if they were smarter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So you use arrogance to cancel guilt?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a good system.

setting: A couch surrounded by bags of money, in Dogbert's lair
situation: Dilbert sits on a couch piled with money bags and asks Dogbert whether he feels guilty about scamming innocent people. Dogbert says no, explaining he only scams people who would do the same to him if they were smarter. Dilbert sums it up as using arrogance to cancel guilt, and Dogbert approves of the system.
punchline: Dogbert's self-justification rests entirely on assuming his victims are dumber than him, so his arrogance neatly erases any guilt.
summary: A sleek scammer dog explains that his moral clearance comes from believing his marks are less clever than he is.

title: Faking a Vanishing Time Machine

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your time machine is a fraud, but no one needs to know.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: With a few minor modifications, the user will vanish, and everyone will assume it worked.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is in case you don't completely vanish.

setting: A conference room, then the inventor's lab with the machine
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, tells a team that their time machine is a fraud but that no one needs to know. He proposes modifying it so the user disappears and everyone will assume it worked. In the last panel the machine has become a metal chamber with a toilet tank on top, and Dogbert stands by holding a plunger.
punchline: Dogbert's fake time travel works by flushing the user down a toilet, and the plunger is his backup in case the person gets stuck instead of vanishing.
summary: A consultant turns a bogus time machine into a disguised toilet that makes its occupant disappear, complete with a plunger for mishaps.

file: 2005/2005-03-15_fist of death_alice implicated_beat up men_high crime_area_office_picture_pyramid shaped hair.gif
title: Fist of Death Pyramid Hair

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because every one of them was beaten up in front of the building by a guy with pyramid-shaped hair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Police released this sketch. The guy likes to yell something about a "Fist of Death."

situation: The Boss tells Alice and Dilbert that senior management is relocating the office away from a high-crime area because every member of senior management was beaten up outside the building. He then shows a police sketch of the attacker, who has pyramid-shaped hair and yells about a "Fist of Death." The sketch resembles Alice, who sits at the table looking stunned.
punchline: The police sketch of the attacker looks like Alice, implying she is the one who has been beating up senior management with her "Fist of Death."
summary: A manager explains an office move prompted by assaults on executives, then unwittingly reveals a sketch of the culprit that looks just like a coworker.

file: 2005/2005-11-27_buiness stragey_list_past years_no afraid of change_deserve bonus_generous_good looking_rhetorical question.gif
title: Boss Answers Rhetorical Question Himself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold on.

transcript.text: I made a list of all of our strategies for the past five years.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You have to give him credit. The man knows how to answer a rhetorical question.

setting: Conference room during a strategy meeting
situation: The Boss begins to announce a new business strategy, but Dilbert interrupts with a list showing there have been seventeen strategies in five years. Dilbert asks what that tells them, and the Boss answers with a string of flattering conclusions about himself, including deserving a huge bonus.
punchline: Dilbert's rhetorical question was meant to expose constant strategy flip-flopping, but the Boss sincerely answers it with self-serving praise, spinning the criticism into a case for his own bonus.
summary: A manager turns an employee's pointed challenge about his endless strategy changes into a self-congratulating argument for more pay.

title: Manager Brags About Attending Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All you did this quarter is design one microchip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In comparison, I found the time to attend dozens of meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now do you see what it takes to be a manager?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sadly, yes.

situation: The Boss criticizes Dilbert for only designing one microchip all quarter, while boasting that he himself attended dozens of meetings. He asks Dilbert whether he now understands what management requires, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic 'Sadly, yes' shows he understands that management means wasting time in meetings rather than producing anything of value.
summary: A boss belittles an engineer's single finished chip by bragging about his own packed meeting calendar, unaware his employee finds this proves how unproductive management is.

file: 2005/2005-01-14_statistical analysis_efforts and rewards_sea of randomness_devoid of purpose_lactation.gif
title: Effort Unrelated to Rewards, Then Shopping

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I did a statistical analysis and found no correlation between my efforts and my rewards.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I felt adrift in a sea of randomness, desperate and absurd, devoid of purpose, lost.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And then I got paid and I purchased some unnecessary merchandise and now I feel fine.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Lactation can't be far behind.

situation: Asok stands in Wally's cubicle holding a sheet of paper and describes how his statistical analysis showed no link between his work and his pay. He says he felt lost and purposeless until payday, when buying unnecessary things made him feel fine. Wally, sitting at his desk with a coffee mug, replies deadpan with a remark about lactation.
punchline: Wally's non sequitur compares Asok's instant comfort from consumer spending to a conditioned physiological reflex, mocking how easily a paycheck and a purchase dispel an existential crisis.
summary: A young employee confesses that a paycheck and some pointless shopping cured his despair over a random reward system, and his coworker responds with a bizarre biological quip.

file: 2005/2005-05-08_audit_150 million_software system_scrap entire thing_worthless_norma software system_clever combo_tweak it_sell the zeros_few minutes.gif

summary: A consultant tells a boss his expensive software is useless because it contains only one of the two binary digits, then sells him the missing one.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, sees a résumé on a colleague's screen and asks if it's his. punchline: Ted deliberately prints ten copies of his résumé so the Boss will see it and know he's job hunting, while he claims it just shows he's not a people pleaser.
summary: A cubicle dweller lets his boss discover his job-hunting by mass-printing his résumé at the shared printer just as the boss approaches.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate

situation: Wally is interviewing a job candidate and describes a position with no salary, where the worker must pay the company $1,000 a month and work from home. summary: A job seeker meets a pay-to-work scheme with no salary and no company identity, and only asks about having his own home office.

title: Boss's Journal Yields Instant Growth

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant or advisor, hands the Boss a journal and advises him to record everything he does so he can find where he needs help. The Boss then writes entries that merely describe the act of writing in the journal, and he concludes that he has experienced personal growth.
punchline: The Boss's journal entries are empty self-referential repetition, yet he mistakes this pointless exercise for meaningful self-improvement.
summary: A self-help tip from Dogbert leaves the boss scribbling about his own scribbling and congratulating himself on his progress.

title: Dilbert Feels Disrespect Coming On

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert notices Wally making a strained, teeth-baring expression and asks about it. Wally explains he is rehearsing a grimace meant to signal he is too overworked to take on any more tasks. Dilbert points out that the face also looks like intestinal distress, and Wally cheerfully calls that a subplot.

summary: Wally rehearses a pained expression to look too busy for extra work, and it accidentally reads as stomach trouble.

title: Honest Post-Mortem Blames Absent Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And by "honest," I mean blaming people who aren't here.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Look! You're doing it again!

setting: Conference room during a project post-mortem meeting
situation: The Boss opens a project post-mortem by asking everyone to be honest about what went wrong. An employee takes this literally and bluntly blames the Boss's incompetent leadership for the team's failure. The Boss then redefines 'honest' as blaming people who are absent, and the employee points out that he is doing exactly that.
punchline: The Boss demands honesty but only wants blame directed at absent people, so he is hypocritically doing the very blaming he claims to want, and an employee calls him out on it.
summary: A manager invites candid feedback on a failed project, but when an employee faults his leadership he insists that real honesty means pinning blame on people who are not in the room.

transcript.text: Confused look... Huge invoice... This man is a victim of consult and blabbery.

setting: Office, then the Boss's office with investigators
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, rattles off a stream of meaningless business buzzwords to the Boss. In the last panel, a police officer and a coroner examine the Boss slumped in his chair with a magnifying glass, noting his confused look and huge invoice.
punchline: The Boss has been rendered senseless by Dogbert's jargon and bill, and the crime scene is treated like a murder by 'consult and blabbery' (a play on 'assault and battery').
summary: A consultant's torrent of buzzwords leaves a manager slumped and bewildered, and investigators diagnose him as a casualty of jargon and an enormous bill.

file: 2005/2005-03-31_liar_habitual liar_died_feel great_head is skull_attached to body_yoga.gif
title: Skeleton Insists He Feels Great

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Habitual Liar

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I thought you died.

transcript.speaker: Skeleton colleague
transcript.text: No, I feel great!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm sure you're dead. Your head is a skull.

transcript.speaker: Skeleton colleague
transcript.text: I cut back on carbs.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your head isn't even attached to your body.

transcript.speaker: Skeleton colleague
transcript.text: I take yoga.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: At a meeting, Alice confronts a colleague who is plainly a skeleton, saying she thought he had died. He insists he is fine and offers diet and exercise explanations for his skull head. Alice finally picks up his detached skull, yet he still claims he is alive and healthy.
punchline: The habitual liar keeps denying an obvious reality, giving absurd excuses like carb-cutting and yoga to explain being a dead skeleton.
summary: A coworker who is clearly a skeleton refuses to admit he's dead, blaming a low-carb diet and yoga for his skull and detached head.

file: 2005/2005-11-12_board meeting_outsourcing_ceo job_26 million_elbonian ceo_good guy_consulting contract.gif
title: Dogbert Outsources the CEO

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Board meeting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend outsourcing your CEO's job and saving the company $26 million per year.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For $4 per year you can hire an Elbonian CEO who is just as good as this guy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now do you understand why you should have renewed my consulting contract?

setting: Corporate boardroom during a board meeting
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, addresses the board and recommends outsourcing the CEO's job to save $26 million a year. He claims an Elbonian CEO costing $4 per year would be just as good as the current one. The CEO grows angrier as Dogbert reveals he is making the pitch because his own consulting contract was not renewed.
punchline: Dogbert is petty revenge-consulting, threatening the CEO's job as payback for not renewing his contract, while also implying the CEO adds little value.
summary: A spurned consultant gets even with the company by proposing that its pricey chief executive be replaced by a nearly free overseas substitute.

title: Hotel Movie Rental Horror

transcript.speaker: Desk Clerk
transcript.text: I hope you enjoyed your stay. I'll just check to see what movies you rented.

transcript.speaker: Desk Clerk
transcript.text: GAA!!! GAAA!!! GAAA!!! GAAA!!! GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Hotel Manager
transcript.text: And I recommend that we burn the furniture.

situation: The Boss is checking out of a hotel when the desk clerk looks up the movies he rented during his stay. The clerk reads the printout and screams in horror, then the manager and staff huddle together and recommend burning the furniture in the Boss's room.
punchline: The Boss's in-room movie rentals were so disturbing (implied adult films) that the hotel staff want to destroy everything he touched.
summary: A hotel clerk checking a guest's pay-per-view history reacts with such revulsion that the staff decide the room's furnishings must be incinerated.

title: Dinosaur Bob Eats Blackberry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bob, I bought you a BlackBerry so I can send you e-mail day or night.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Thank you! I always wanted one of these!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: De-e-elicious.

situation: Dilbert gives his pet dinosaur Bob a BlackBerry so he can email him around the clock. Bob gratefully accepts it, then in the last panel is shown thinking about how tasty it is, implying he has eaten the device.
punchline: Instead of a communication tool, the dinosaur treats the BlackBerry as a snack, so Dilbert's always-on email plan fails before it begins.
summary: A man hands his pet dinosaur a handheld email device, and the creature's idea of putting it to use turns out to be dinner.

title: Demanding Inspiration From Failed Motivator

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Once again you have failed to motivate me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't want to become like my coworkers, always plotting ways to sabotage your career.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now would be a good time for you to say something inspirational.

situation: At a meeting table, Wally tells The Boss he has failed to motivate him again. He then adds that he does not want to turn into his coworkers, who are always plotting to sabotage the boss's career. Wally then cues The Boss to deliver an inspirational line.
punchline: Wally implies he is the one coworker not scheming against the boss, yet it is only a thinly veiled threat, and he still expects the boss to inspire him on demand.
summary: A lazy employee faults his manager for failing to energize him while hinting that sabotage by others is the alternative, then asks for a pep talk.

title: Career Criminal Applies for Corporate Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your resume says you're a career criminal.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Yup.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... Why are you applying for a job here?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: I'm getting tendonitis in my pistol-whipping arm.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: I thought I'd try the slower paced life of white collar crime.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Security.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: How much can I expect to embezzle in my first year?

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Earl?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Lefty!

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Forget this job. Security is where the big money is.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Can you get me in?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should start locking my desk.

setting: The Boss's office during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews a job applicant whose resume lists a career in crime. The applicant explains he wants to switch to white collar crime and asks how much he can embezzle. When The Boss calls security, the guard turns out to be an old criminal buddy, and the two of them start discussing how security is the more lucrative route.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to protect the company fails because security is staffed by criminals too, leaving him to conclude that the only sensible response is to lock his own desk.
summary: A hiring manager's interview with a self-declared career criminal goes sideways when the security guard he summons turns out to be the applicant's old partner in crime.

file: 2005/2005-10-18_court ordered_email records_deleted_system mainentance_wink wink_flirting_in on it_scam.gif
title: Winking Lawyer Suggests Deleting Emails

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company Lawyer

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: The court ordered us to turn over all of our e-mail records.

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Gosh. I sure hope they don't get deleted during regularly scheduled system maintenance.

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Oh no. That would be bad! Wink! Wink!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good grief, man! How can you be flirting at a time like this?

situation: The company lawyer tells the Boss that a court has ordered the company to hand over all its e-mail records. He then hints, with exaggerated feigned concern, that the e-mails might get deleted during routine system maintenance, and winks to signal the real plan. The oblivious Boss mistakes the winking for flirting.
punchline: The lawyer is clumsily hinting at destroying evidence with a nudge-nudge wink, but the clueless Boss thinks he is being hit on.
summary: A lawyer broadly hints that subpoenaed messages could conveniently vanish, while his dim boss misreads his winks as a come-on.

file: 2005/2005-01-08_transformational change_feel different_nauseas felling_going to hurl_change feels like.gif
title: Transformational Change Makes Alice Queasy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our differentiating value-added strategy is transformational change.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How was that? Does anyone feel different?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My urge to hurl has increased a little bit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what change feels like.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company's strategy is 'transformational change' and then asks whether anyone feels different. Alice replies that her urge to vomit has grown slightly, and the Boss cheerfully tells her that this is exactly what change feels like. Dilbert sits beside them listening.
punchline: The Boss treats Alice's nausea at his buzzword-filled strategy as proof that the change is working, dismissing her disgust as the normal sensation of transformation.
summary: A manager spouts jargon about a new strategy, and when a coworker says it makes her sick, he insists that queasiness is simply what progress feels like.

file: 2005/2005-04-26_rated good_you're not good_company policy_fire anyone_hiring freeze_get paid.gif
title: Rated Good For Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I'm rating you "good" but not because you are.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Company policy says I have to fire anyone rated lower than good, and the hiring freeze means it would shrink my empire.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So you can get paid for doing nothing as long as you don't kill anyone.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't promise that.

setting: Boss's office, at a conference table during a performance review
situation: The Boss sits across a table from Wally during a performance review and explains that he is giving him a "good" rating even though Wally doesn't deserve it. Company policy requires firing anyone rated below good, and with a hiring freeze in place, losing Wally would shrink the Boss's department. He tells Wally he can keep collecting pay for doing nothing as long as he doesn't kill anyone.
punchline: Wally, the lazy employee, cannot promise he won't kill anyone, a dark joke implying he is both useless and possibly dangerous but protected by the Boss's self-interest.
summary: A manager inflates a slacker's review to protect his headcount, then sets one tiny condition that the slacker won't guarantee.

title: Boss Hires Office Sourpuss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meet our new sourpuss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard that every office has one. And we didn't, so I went out and got one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does anything ever sound like a bad idea to you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leadership is 90% optimism.

situation: The Boss introduces a scowling, cat-like new employee he deliberately hired as the office sourpuss, because he heard every office has one. Dilbert, seated at his computer, asks whether anything ever strikes the Boss as a bad idea, and the Boss responds with a leadership platitude about optimism.
punchline: The Boss's relentless optimism makes him blind to how absurd it is to hire someone just to fill the role of office sourpuss, and his cheerful platitude is no answer to Dilbert's pointed question.
summary: Hearing that offices usually have a grump, the boss recruits one on purpose and brushes off criticism with a motivational slogan.

file: 2005/2005-11-07_dance club_allow anyone_screen potential customers_dance moves_incorporated air guitar.gif
title: Ratbert's Impossibly Exclusive Dance Club

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I opened a dance club that's so exclusive I don't allow anyone in.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I personally screen every potential customer until I find a reason to exclude.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Have your dance moves ever incorporated the air guitar?

transcript.speaker: Man in red suit
transcript.text: Yes.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then the velvet-rope line outside Ratbert's dance club
situation: Ratbert tells Dilbert that he has opened a dance club so exclusive that nobody is admitted. In the last panel he stands on a stool at the velvet rope with a clipboard, interrogating a man in a red suit about whether his dance moves have ever included air guitar, while a woman waits behind him in line.
punchline: Ratbert's screening is a hunt for any excuse to reject people, and the man's honest 'Yes' to a trivial question will likely get him turned away, making the club's exclusivity absurd.
summary: A tiny doorman interrogates hopeful partygoers with ridiculous questions so he can turn every one of them away from his club.

title: Urgent Email Gets Deleted as Spam

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Subject: URGENT

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, give me your budget numbers as soon as possible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Technology is amazing. I type one message and within minutes I'll have my data.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: First order of business: delete all spam e-mail that has a subject of "URGENT".

situation: The Boss types an email marked URGENT asking Dilbert for his budget numbers and sits back, marveling at how quickly technology will deliver his data. In the final panel Dilbert, at his own computer, decides to start his work session by deleting all spam emails with the subject 'URGENT', which will include the Boss's message.
punchline: The Boss's urgent request will never be answered because Dilbert is about to delete it unread as spam, since spammers also label their junk 'URGENT'.
summary: A manager gleefully fires off a high-priority email demanding data, unaware his subordinate is about to purge every message with that exact label.

file: 2005/2005-04-13_worlds greatest intern_plagues_bought plague_less prominent placement_alice called it.gif
title: Alice Spots the Intern Plaque Scam

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Alice, you are looking at the newest member of "The World's Greatest Interns."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's a scam to convince gullible interns to buy overpriced wall plaques.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I'll be displaying you less prominently than we had discussed.

situation: An intern stands by Alice's cubicle and proudly announces he has been named one of 'The World's Greatest Interns.' Alice immediately identifies the award as a scam designed to sell overpriced wall plaques to gullible interns. The intern, now deflated, walks away holding his plaque and says he will hang it less prominently than planned.
punchline: Alice's blunt exposure of the award as a vanity-plaque racket instantly deflates the intern's pride, so he quietly demotes the plaque's place on his wall.
summary: A proud intern shows off his supposed honor until Alice reveals it's just a gimmick to sell him a plaque.

file: 2005/2005-06-29_losing empathy_ceo two days_decorating office_more important_healthcare_varnished desk.gif
title: Ratbert CEO Loses Empathy Fast

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I've only been CEO for two days and already I'm losing my empathy.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: For example, I'm pretty sure that decorating my office is more important than your healthcare.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Which reminds me: I plan to have you varnished and used as my desk.

setting: CEO's office, with the Boss sitting across the desk
situation: Ratbert, newly promoted to CEO, tells the Boss he is already losing his empathy after only two days in the job. He says that decorating his office matters more than the Boss's healthcare, then announces he plans to have the Boss varnished and used as a desk.
punchline: Power corrupts almost instantly: Ratbert's empathy vanishes so quickly that he casually plans to turn an employee into furniture.
summary: A freshly crowned rodent executive cheerfully admits that authority is already making him callous toward his staff, with absurd consequences for his subordinate.

title: Grim Reaper's Blunt Rake Problem

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Someday I hope to get into the grim reaping field.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: I don't mind working these unpaid overtime cases, but just once I'd like to see one of you guys die.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Hey, I just realized that my rake is very blunt.

situation: A figure in a yellow hooded robe carrying a rake stands beside Dilbert's cubicle and complains that he wants to enter the grim reaping field. He grumbles about working unpaid overtime cases while never getting to see anyone die. Then he realizes his rake is blunt, implying he has been failing to kill the overworked employees.
punchline: The would-be Grim Reaper's blunt tool is why the overworked, unpaid employees keep surviving, so they are doomed to keep working instead of dying.
summary: A frustrated, rake-wielding reaper wannabe lingers in a cubicle, wondering why no one ever dies, until he discovers his tool is dull.

file: 2005/2005-07-01_failed ceo_worth 100 million_all reverse_head in glass_successful engineer_kind of funny.gif
title: Dogbert Explains Why Irony Is Funny

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're a successful engineer and I'm a failed CEO. It's kind of funny that I'm worth $100 million and you're not.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's funny because it's all reverse of how it should be.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's funny because your head wouldn't normally fit inside a glass.

situation: Dogbert, perched on the arm of Dilbert's chair, points out the irony that he is a failed CEO worth $100 million while Dilbert is a successful engineer who is not rich. He then explains why the irony is funny, but in the last panel Dogbert is shown with his head stuck inside Dilbert's drinking glass, and his explanation shifts to the absurdity of that.
punchline: Dogbert's explanation of why his situation is funny gets muffled and absurd because his head is stuck in a glass, so the real joke becomes the physical gag rather than the ironic wealth gap.
summary: A wealthy but supposedly failed Dogbert lectures his friend on irony while quietly getting his head trapped in a drinking glass.

title: Cauliflower Brain Replacement Specialist

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I'm referring you to a specialist who can treat your absent-mindedness.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: His method is untested, but I think it's worth a chance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll replace my brain with a cauliflower?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're just like brains, but much cheaper.

setting: Doctor's office, then a specialist's examination room
situation: A doctor tells the Pointy-Haired Boss he is referring him to a specialist for absent-mindedness, warning that the specialist's method is untested. The specialist turns out to be Dogbert in a doctor's outfit with a stethoscope. The Boss, holding his own brain, asks if it will be replaced with a cauliflower.
punchline: Dogbert's cost-cutting brain replacement with a cheap vegetable implies the Boss barely needs a real brain, and his quackery is justified purely by price.
summary: A dubious specialist plans to swap a patient's brain for a cheaper vegetable substitute.

title: Smartsizing the Process Improvement Process

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I don't know how to say this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to lean up the process improvement process so I have to smartsize one resource.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Wow. Usually it's just a figure of speech when people say, "I don't know how to say this."

situation: The Boss sits across the table from Ted and says he doesn't know how to deliver bad news. He then announces, in tangled buzzwords, that he has to lay off one person to trim the process improvement process. Ted observes that the boss truly cannot say it plainly.
punchline: The boss's attempt to announce a layoff is so wrapped in corporate jargon that Ted notes he literally doesn't know how to say it, unlike the usual figure of speech.
summary: A manager fumbles through buzzword-laden language to tell an employee someone is being let go, proving he really can't say it directly.

file: 2005/2005-03-13_project caribou_new chip_prorc_muskrat project_project meerkat_names of projects_too similar.gif

punchline: The Boss makes sweeping decisions about nonexistent projects because of a muddled naming scheme, then blames everyone but himself for the mix-up.
summary: A manager who cannot tell animal-themed project codenames apart issues a batch of orders for projects that were never real, and shrugs off the blame.

file: 2005/2005-12-05_cross charging_freshly brewed coffee_tempting pasteries_time to project_meeting_wrong meeting_mis placed_business.gif
title: Meeting Crasher Charges Time Elsewhere
