transcript.text: Um... why are you here?

transcript.speaker: Bald man with glasses
transcript.text: Originally I was seduced by the smell of your freshly brewed coffee and tempting pastries.

transcript.speaker: Bald man with glasses
transcript.text: But now I'm all about cross-charging my time to your project.

situation: At a meeting, one attendee asks a bald man with glasses why he is there. He admits he only came for the coffee and pastries, but has since realized he can bill his time to the meeting's project instead of his own.
punchline: The uninvited attendee has found a way to turn free snacks into billable hours by cross-charging his time to someone else's project.
summary: A gatecrasher at a meeting confesses that he came for the snacks and stayed to bill his hours to a different budget.

title: Seventy Percent Chance of Ruin

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The project has a 70% chance of minor success and a 30% chance of corporate ruination.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like those odds. When can we start?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Start?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wish we had ten more projects like this one.

setting: Conference room during a project presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a chart to the Boss and a coworker showing the project has a 70% chance of only minor success and a 30% chance of destroying the company. The Boss cheerfully says he likes those odds and asks when they can start. Dilbert is stunned, and wishes the company had ten more projects like this one.
punchline: The Boss hears a 30% chance of corporate ruin as a good bet, so Dilbert sarcastically wishes for ten more such projects, since repeating that risk would almost certainly destroy the company.
summary: A manager happily green-lights a venture after being told it could wipe out the whole company, prompting a deadpan wish for many more like it.

file: 2005/2005-07-13_wake up call_^am_bellmen_head of bed_blind maids_pants_manager_five star hotel.gif

punchline: The Boss's ridiculous, entitled demands are so out of touch that the clerk can tell he is a manager, and he proudly confirms it.
summary: A pampered boss makes outlandish room-service requests and cheerfully admits that of course he is management.

file: 2005/2005-06-14_bill for consulting_past year_all in head_recommendation_status quo_everything right.gif

title: Expert in an Impossibly Narrow Field

He says the field is so narrow that it needs no knowledge at all. When Dilbert asks what the field is, Wally says there's no way to know for sure.

file: 2005/2005-08-21_easy news cahnnel_easy to gather_countries want to kill u.s._no phones_two middle aged white guys_they hate us_we are wonderful_buy book.gif
title: Dogbert's Lazy Easy News Channel

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good evening. This is the Dogbert Easy News Channel.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We bring you all the news that's easy to gather.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today's top story is about something that was first reported in a newspaper and later read by me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People in other countries want to kill us. The rest of the article is mostly names I can't pronounce.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We thought about asking them why they want to kill us, but they don't have phones.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So here's the next best thing: a debate between two middle-aged white guys who also don't know why people want to kill us.

transcript.speaker: Panelist 1
transcript.text: They hate us because we are so wonderful.

transcript.speaker: Panelist 2
transcript.text: Buy my book or you will all die!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next on Easy News, our panelists will discuss dumb crooks who keep getting stuck in chimneys.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excellent.

setting: Dilbert's living room, watching a TV news broadcast anchored by Dogbert
situation: Dilbert watches Dogbert anchor the Easy News Channel, which only covers stories that take minimal effort to gather. Dogbert reads a newspaper story, skips asking foreign people why they are hostile because they lack phones, and instead hosts a debate between two clueless middle-aged pundits. The pundits offer a self-flattering explanation and a book plug before the show teases a silly story about crooks stuck in chimneys.
punchline: The joke satirizes lazy, shallow cable news by showing a news show that does zero real reporting, relies on uninformed pundits who promote their books, and ends by cheerfully moving on to trivial fluff that Dilbert happily prefers.
summary: A news anchor dog builds a broadcast entirely from effortless material, including clueless pundits hawking books, then pivots to chimney-stuck burglars.

title: Copyrighting All Stupid Opinions

transcript.speaker: Bald man
transcript.text: And so that's why...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Excuse me. You're not entitled to your opinion.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I copyrighted all of the stupidest opinions in the universe so they can never again be uttered.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hey! I just realized that I no longer need to drink!

setting: A bar, with patrons standing at the counter
situation: A bald man is holding forth to a woman at a bar when Dogbert, sitting at the counter with a computer, interrupts to say the man isn't entitled to his opinion. Dogbert explains he has copyrighted all of the stupidest opinions in the universe so nobody can utter them again. The woman, who had been stuck listening to the man, realizes she no longer needs to drink.
punchline: If all stupid opinions are banned, bar bores can no longer talk, so the woman's reason for drinking to endure them disappears.
summary: A scheming dog silences a barstool windbag by claiming legal ownership of every foolish viewpoint, leaving a listener delighted to be spared.

title: Bribes Disguised as Consultant Fees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Elbonians are demanding bribes, or else they won't do business with us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hire them as overpaid consultants and don't ask them for anything. That way, it's all legal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And by legal you mean won't get caught?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Po-tay-to, po-tah-to.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the Elbonians will only do business with the company if they are paid bribes. The Boss suggests hiring them as overpaid consultants without giving them any work, so the payments look legitimate. Dilbert points out that this just means not getting caught, and the Boss shrugs it off.
punchline: The Boss treats 'legal' and 'unlikely to be caught' as the same thing, showing a casual disregard for ethics in disguising a bribe as a consulting contract.
summary: A manager launders a foreign partner's bribe demand by labeling the payoff as consulting fees and brushes off the ethical difference.

file: 2005/2005-11-17_gullible world_magazine_cover story_shed pounds_yell at children_eat your way_be a better parent.gif
title: Gullible World Magazine Cover Stories

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My new magazine is called "Gullible World."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This month's cover story is "Shed pounds by yelling at your children."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next month will be "Eat your way to being a better parent."

setting: Dilbert's office or home, with Dogbert at a desk computer
situation: Dogbert sits at a computer and announces he is publishing a magazine called "Gullible World." He reads out the absurd cover stories for this month and next while Dilbert stands nearby holding a mug, listening.
punchline: Dogbert's magazine openly targets gullible readers with nonsensical self-help headlines that swap cause and effect, presumably profiting from people who will believe anything.
summary: A scheming dog launches a publication aimed at the easily fooled, previewing ridiculous parenting and weight-loss headlines.

title: Dogbert's Deadly Advice for Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm afraid that my boss will try to kill me because I know about his malfeasance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend that you ask to meet him alone at an abandoned warehouse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was a mistake to name you the beneficiary on my life insurance policy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember to insult his goons.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert sitting on the couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he fears his boss may try to have him killed because he knows about the boss's wrongdoing. Dogbert, acting as adviser, suggests the most dangerous possible course of action: meeting the boss alone at an abandoned warehouse. Dilbert realizes he made Dogbert the beneficiary of his life insurance, but Dogbert just adds to the dangerous advice.
punchline: Dogbert gives deliberately lethal advice because, as the life insurance beneficiary, he stands to profit from Dilbert's death.
summary: A worried employee seeks counsel from his dog, who steers him toward certain doom to collect the payout.

title: Alice Interrogates a Lying Skull

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Habitual liar

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you sticking with your story that you're still alive?

transcript.speaker: Skull
transcript.text: I feel terrific!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm running a marathon later today.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Low priced cremations while you wait!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm a genie in a bottle! Make a wish!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

setting: Office or cubicle, with a sign advertising cremations on the wall
situation: Alice holds a skull and questions it about its claim that it is still alive. The skull insists it feels terrific, then makes a string of outlandish claims, including that it is running a marathon and is a genie in a bottle. Alice is horrified by the final claim and recoils from the desk.
punchline: The skull is a dead 'habitual liar' that keeps telling absurd falsehoods, since a skull obviously cannot feel terrific, run a marathon or be a genie, and its lies escalate until even Alice can't take it.
summary: A woman grills a skull that stubbornly insists it's alive and keeps spinning ever wilder tall tales until she screams.

title: Dilbert Predicts Vendor's Broken Promises

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll build your software with all the features you want plus a few extras.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe you'll start late and claim there's no way to do everything by the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then you'll say that the unfinished features aren't important and you're losing money on the deal.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I can't hear you.

setting: Conference room during a vendor negotiation
situation: Dilbert, apparently acting as the software vendor, sits across the table from a client and begins by making the usual optimistic promises. He then candidly predicts how the client will behave: starting late, blaming the deadline, and dismissing unfinished features. The client responds by covering his ears and refusing to listen.
punchline: The client won't listen to a realistic forecast of how the project will go wrong, showing that both sides already know the pattern of broken promises and are willfully ignoring it.
summary: A software vendor lays out the entire doomed project timeline in advance, and the customer simply plugs his ears.

title: Drunken Art Critic Insults Rat's Painting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Art Bar

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That painting is dreadful. It looks as if a rat created it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lucky guess. I'll ask you again at midnight.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that night

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Ah wan shix of ose an shum bar nuts!!!

setting: Dogbert's Art Bar, a cocktail bar displaying framed art
situation: A man in a red jacket at Dogbert's bar sneers that a framed painting looks like it was made by a rat. Dogbert, who runs the bar, says the guess was lucky and he'll ask again at midnight. Later that night the now-drunk customer slurs his words as he points at the same painting and orders some of those and bar nuts.
punchline: After a few drinks the snobbish critic's taste collapses, and he drunkenly wants to buy the painting he mocked earlier.
summary: A pretentious bar patron dismisses a painting as rat-made, then after hours of drinking slurringly tries to buy it.

title: Dogbert's Couch Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert works for the cable company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If your picture is fuzzy then get new glasses.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: If my glasses are the problem, why does the couch look perfectly clear?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good question. Please hold while I transfer you to couch tech support.

setting: Cable company call center and a customer's home
situation: Dogbert, working as a cable company support rep, tells a caller with a fuzzy TV picture to get new glasses. The customer points out that his couch looks perfectly clear, undermining the advice. Dogbert responds by cheerfully transferring him to a nonexistent 'couch tech support'.
punchline: Rather than admit his advice was wrong, Dogbert deflects with a absurd transfer, mocking how tech support dodges responsibility by passing callers along.
summary: A cable company rep blames a customer's eyesight for a blurry TV, then sidesteps a smart objection by redirecting him to a ridiculous department.

title: Boss Brings Asok as Luggage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm flying to Los Angeles for a meeting and I want you to join me.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gasp

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am honored. This feels like an important milestone in my burgeoning career!

transcript.speaker: Gate Agent
transcript.text: We'll begin by pre-boarding anyone who...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Coming through!

setting: Office, then an airport boarding gate
situation: The Boss invites Asok to fly with him to Los Angeles for a meeting, and Asok eagerly gushes about what an honor it is and how it advances his career. At the airport gate, the Boss barges ahead of the line to pre-board while carrying Asok over his shoulder, wrapped up like luggage or cargo.
punchline: Asok's excitement about a career milestone is undercut by the fact that the Boss only wants him along as something to carry, so he can jump the queue as if he were a passenger with a disability or small child.
summary: A young employee is thrilled to be chosen for a business trip, only to discover he's being used as a prop to get his boss early boarding.

file: 2005/2005-03-01_elbonian culture class_elbonian businessman_card_eat card_spit_dueling yak bones.gif
title: Elbonian Business Card Etiquette Class

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonian culture class

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: When an Elbonian businessman gives you his card...

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Crumple it up and put it in your mouth. Chew it slowly then spit it toward his forehead.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: This leads me to my next topic: dueling with yak bones.

situation: An Elbonian instructor in a tall dark hat teaches a culture class on how to react when an Elbonian businessman hands you his business card. His advice is to chew the card and spit it at the man's forehead. He then moves on to the next topic, dueling with yak bones, while the Boss and Dilbert sit and listen.
punchline: Elbonian business etiquette is so bizarre and hostile that exchanging business cards inevitably leads to a fight, making a lesson on yak bone dueling the logical next step.
summary: A cultural trainer explains an absurdly rude card-exchange custom, which naturally segues into weapons combat.

file: 2005/2005-01-11_stock - picking software_more feauture_make hair grow_bald guys_test on rat_butticks.gif
title: Testing Hair Growth Software on Rat

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My stock-picking software needs more features.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I'll add a module that claims to make hair grow on bald guys. I'll first test it on a rat.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I feel a new one on my buttocks!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's all the proof I need.

setting: Dilbert's kitchen table, then a computer desk
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert over breakfast that he wants to add a hair-growth module to his stock-picking software and will test it on a rat first. In the last panel Ratbert, sitting at a computer, reports feeling a new hair on his buttocks, and Dogbert declares that sufficient proof.
punchline: Dogbert treats a single, dubious anecdotal sensation from one rat as conclusive proof of efficacy, mocking the flimsy evidence behind miracle-cure products and the scams they feed.
summary: A scheming dog accepts one rat's embarrassing claim as full validation for his bogus baldness remedy.

title: Celebrity Lookalike Marketing Worked Too Well

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My marketing plan involved giving free samples of our cruddy product to celebrity lookalikes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The fact that it worked caused a steep decline in my respect for the intelligence of people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In conclusion, there's a fine line between marketing and hating.

setting: Conference room during a marketing presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a sales chart to two seated managers, explaining that his marketing plan was to give free samples of a poor-quality product to celebrity lookalikes. He points to a slide showing an ordinary person transformed into a celebrity lookalike and admits that the trick's success has lowered his opinion of people's intelligence. He concludes that marketing is close to hating the customers.
punchline: Dilbert's marketing success depends on consumers being fooled by lookalikes, so effective marketing is revealed to rest on contempt for the public's intelligence.
summary: A presenter confesses that a cynical stunt of handing out bad products to lookalike stars boosted sales and left him disillusioned about human gullibility.

title: Wally Reveals Procrastination Strategy Aloud

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, this is important, but you have a month to finish it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll start right away.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's smarter to wait until the last minute and then make a big show of how hard you're working to meet the unreasonable deadline.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You said that right in front of him.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It'll still work. That's the freaky part.

situation: The Boss gives Asok an important assignment with a month to complete it, and Asok eagerly promises to start immediately. Wally, holding his coffee mug, advises Asok to wait until the last minute and then put on a show of working hard to meet the deadline. Asok points out that Wally said this right in front of the boss.
punchline: Even when the boss hears the procrastination strategy spelled out in front of him, the trick will still work because he is too oblivious to notice.
summary: Wally openly coaches a coworker to fake a heroic last-minute effort, and cheerfully notes the clueless boss will fall for it anyway.

file: 2005/2005-03-19_forecast_predcit_pants so high_kill self with belt_statue erected_honor of blet_stupid towns people.gif
title: Alice Predicts Boss's Belt Death

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I predict that someday you'll wear your pants so high that you'll choke yourself to death with your belt.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And the townspeople will erect a statue to honor the belt.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stupid townspeople.

situation: The Boss demands a forecast from Alice immediately. Instead of a business prediction, she foretells that he will someday pull his pants so high that his belt strangles him. She adds that townspeople will build a statue honoring the belt, and the Boss reacts only by insulting the townspeople.
punchline: Alice turns a request for a business forecast into a gleeful prediction of the Boss's absurd death, and the clueless Boss only objects to the townspeople's stupidity rather than his own demise.
summary: Pressed for a forecast, Alice foretells her boss's fatal fashion mishap and the monument that will follow, while he misses the insult entirely.

file: 2005/2005-12-29_employee of the month_award_don't know my job_never listen_boss.gif

transcript.text: It's as if you've never listened to anything I've ever said.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're welcome!

situation: The Boss announces Tina as employee of the month but vaguely praises her for 'various work' because he doesn't know what she actually does. Tina, holding her award certificate, objects that his ignorance of her job makes the award meaningless and that he never listens to her. The Boss responds only with a cheerful 'You're welcome!'
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he proves Tina's point by failing to hear her complaint and taking her criticism as a thank-you.
summary: A clueless manager hands out a hollow award, then misreads the recipient's objections as gratitude.

title: Hired for Bullying Face

transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Grrrr...

setting: Job interview in a conference room or office
situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss interviews a job candidate, noting her experience as a boss's pet. He then asks her to demonstrate the scowling face she would use to bully his employees behind his back. She snarls with wrinkled forehead, and he hires her on the spot.
punchline: The boss's hiring criteria are bullying his own staff and sycophancy, and he openly selects a candidate for her ability to intimidate employees rather than for any legitimate skill.
summary: A manager auditions an applicant by having her practice her best intimidating scowl, then hires her for being a convincing bully who suits his favorites.

title: Sourpuss Mangles the Lemons Saying

transcript.speaker: Sourpuss

transcript.speaker: Sourpuss
transcript.text: You stupid lemon eater.

situation: Dilbert stands holding a coffee mug while Sourpuss, a gloomy rat-like coworker in a tie, delivers his own version of the "when life gives you lemons" saying. Across three identical panels he turns the optimistic proverb into a curse and then an insult. Dilbert says nothing throughout.
punchline: Sourpuss twists the cheerful lemonade proverb into a bitter insult, showing he cannot be optimistic even when quoting an optimistic saying.
summary: A perpetually bitter coworker turns a famously upbeat proverb into a string of nasty put-downs while Dilbert silently holds his coffee.

title: Feature Creep Proposes Civil Union

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper versus the Feature Creep

transcript.text: We need to add a keyword search function.

transcript.speaker: Feature Creep
transcript.text: That's nothing!

transcript.text: It should also search in different languages including Friulian, Kataang, Horpa and Wagi.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I like your style.

transcript.speaker: Feature Creep
transcript.text: That's nothing! I want to marry you in a civil union.

situation: Two men sit at a meeting table. One proposes adding a keyword search function, and the other keeps escalating the requirements, first demanding support for obscure languages. When the first man says he likes his style, the feature-creeper escalates even further by proposing a civil union.
punchline: Feature creep is so compulsive that the requirements-escalator can't stop even when being complimented, and one-ups the flattery by proposing marriage.
summary: A coworker who piles on ever-wilder requirements responds to a compliment by escalating it into a wedding proposal.

title: Secretary Can't Be Fired Without Form

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, you're the worst secretary ever. I have to let you go.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You can't fire me until you fill out the Involuntary Termination Form 904-B.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you get me one of those?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Yeah. I'll get right on that.

situation: The Boss tells his secretary Carol that she is the worst secretary ever and he has to fire her. Carol replies that he must first complete the Involuntary Termination Form 904-B, and he asks her to fetch the form. She cheerfully agrees to get right on it.
punchline: Carol is so bad at her job that the boss must rely on her to obtain the very form needed to fire her, so her incompetence protects her from being fired.
summary: A manager's attempt to dismiss his useless assistant stalls because the paperwork required to do it has to come from her.

title: Shafting Innocents Is Not Illegal, Right?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Our shareholders are suing us for misleading them about our financial problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Since when is it illegal to shaft innocent people for personal gain?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Don't put that in the minutes.

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: I'll see what I can do.

situation: At a board meeting, an executive reports that shareholders are suing the company for misleading them about its financial problems. The Boss responds with indignation, asking since when it is illegal to shaft innocent people for personal gain. Another executive quickly tells the note-taker to keep that remark out of the minutes, and the note-taker agrees to try.
punchline: The Boss openly admits to defrauding shareholders for personal gain while treating it as perfectly normal, and the only concern is keeping the admission out of the official record.
summary: Leadership shrugs off a fraud lawsuit with a candid confession of exploiting investors, then rushes to hide that confession from the paper trail.

file: 2005/2005-04-24_emailed file_accomplishments_entire month_open the file_down load_browser_upgrade broswer_operating system_upagrde_software_hard disk_view of file_engineering.gif

transcript.text: I tried to download the viewer from the internet but the web site didn't support my browser.

transcript.text: And I couldn't upgrade my browser until I upgraded my operating system!

transcript.text: That required me to upgrade all of my applications software, too.

transcript.text: So, then you got to view the file?

situation: At a monthly status meeting, Wally announces that his big accomplishment was opening an emailed file. punchline: An entire month of cascading upgrades, ending in a new computer, was spent just to view a throwaway joke email about a cat.
summary: A lazy employee justifies a month of effort by describing an absurd chain of software and hardware upgrades needed to open a single email attachment.

title: Everyone Good Has Already Quit

transcript.text: A-a-nyhoo.

He muses that all the good employees leave, then concludes that only wretched, incompetent, lazy people remain. Dilbert, the one staying, looks stunned by the insult as the Boss casually changes the subject.
punchline: The Boss obliviously insults the very employee he is talking to, since anyone still there must by his own logic be wretched and incompetent.
summary: A manager laments that talented staff always leave, then cheerfully insults the only person left listening without realizing it.

punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests the coworker patent his "way of helping," since his only contributions were insults and bad advice rather than any real inventive input.
summary: A colleague demands co-credit on an invention, but the emails he sent turn out to be nothing but put-downs and nonsense advice.

title: Vampire CEO Candidate Needs Dental

transcript.text: Dogbert's Executive Search Firm

transcript.text: He's not very effective during the day.

setting: Dogbert's executive search firm office, then a corporate boardroom
situation: Dogbert, running an executive search firm, offers a vampire sitting in a coffin the job of CEO of a major corporation with a $100 million annual salary. The vampire asks about the dental plan, and in the boardroom he is later shown as a smoldering, headless-looking figure at the table in daylight while Dogbert explains he is ineffective during the day.
punchline: The vampire CEO is literally incapacitated by daylight, which Dogbert dismisses as just a mild effectiveness problem, mocking how overpaid and ineffective some CEOs are.
summary: A pet-run recruiting firm places a coffin-dwelling vampire as a highly paid corporate chief, only for the board to find him smoking and useless whenever the sun is up.

title: Gullible World's Inflated Readership Claim

transcript.text: Wow!

situation: Dogbert pitches the Boss on buying ad space in his new magazine, claiming it has one to two billion readers. The impressed Boss is taken in. At home, Dogbert tells Dilbert over coffee that he has simply found a way to make three readers sound like a huge audience.
punchline: The Boss is so gullible that a mathematically technical but absurd claim of 'between one and two billion' readers convinces him, which makes the magazine's name "Gullible World" literally accurate.
summary: Dogbert dupes his boss into buying ad space with a wildly vague circulation claim, then admits to Dilbert the magazine barely has any readers.

file: 2005/2005-07-17_wrong budget_no probelms_unrealitic_failure_deceptive forecstas_believe the lie_deception_optimism_few hours_perfect budget.gif

transcript.text: This budget would only work if the project encountered no problems whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All projects have unexpected problems. Therefore, this budget is almost certainly wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leaders do not plan for failure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do leaders make deceptive forecasts and later act shocked when things don't work out?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A leader first makes himself believe the lie, thus turning deception into an inspiring form of optimism. Observe.

summary: A manager proves his unrealistic spending plan is sound by physically pounding the delusion into his own skull.

transcript.text: I can't get the marketing ones to stick. They keep sliding off.

setting: Office, with Catbert addressing employees from a stool and later a desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces that layoffs will be handled humanely. He reveals he hired a giant dung beetle to roll the poor performers into a ball and carry them out the door. In the last panel the beetle struggles with a lumpy ball of employees, complaining that the marketing people won't stick.
punchline: The 'humane' downsizing method is absurdly dehumanizing, and the beetle's complaint implies marketing staff are so slippery they evade even being swept away like dung.
summary: A scheming HR cat deploys an enormous insect to bundle up fired workers and roll them out of the building, but one department keeps slipping free.

title: Fortune Made From Incompetent Investing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I made a fortune by being an incompetent CEO. Everyone called me crazy when I put my entire personal wealth into pigs and garbage dumps.

transcript.speaker: Man at table
transcript.text: You invested all of your money in pigs and dumps?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Invested? Now that would have been a good idea too.

setting: Around a conference table at a business dinner or social gathering, with drinks
situation: Dogbert, holding a mug of beer at a table with two business associates, brags that he got rich by being an incompetent CEO and putting all his personal wealth into pigs and garbage dumps. One listener asks if he invested everything in those. Dogbert replies that investing would have been a good idea too, implying he spent the money rather than invested it.
punchline: Dogbert's fortune apparently came from sheer luck or absurd mismanagement, since he never actually invested the money in pigs and dumps, which would have been the smart move.
summary: A boastful canine executive reveals that his supposed brilliant bets were never investments at all, which would have been wiser.

file: 2005/2005-08-12_phishing_new hobby_fake banking emails_gullible executives_financial information_steal_password social security card.gif
title: Dogbert's Phishing Hobby Catches Boss

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have a new hobby. It's called phishing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I send fake banking e-mails to gullible executives. Then I find out their financial information and use it to steal the money they don't deserve.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dear Customer, This is your bank. We forgot your social security number and password. Why don't you send them to us so we can protect your money. Sincerely, I. B. Banker

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Looks legit.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: Dogbert sits at a computer and tells Dilbert that his new hobby is phishing: sending fake bank e-mails to gullible executives to steal their money. The final panel shows the fake e-mail asking for a social security number and password, and the Boss reading it and thinking it looks legitimate.
punchline: The e-mail is an absurdly obvious scam, yet the Boss, exactly the kind of gullible executive Dogbert targets, thinks it looks legit.
summary: A scheming dog explains his online con, and the very next victim falls for an obviously ridiculous message.

file: 2005/2005-01-23_change is good_triple pay_meeting_work for free_change can be bad_slogans_logic_business.gif
title: Change Is Good, Unless It's Pay

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You must learn that change is good.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Change is [smiley face]

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Who wants this one?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Why don't you triple our pay? That would be a change.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That would not be in the best interest of shareholders.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, why don't you work for free? That's a change that's good for shareholders.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or would it be better to admit that change can be very bad?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My favorite part was when he yelled, "Stop ruining my slogans with your logic!"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Snort. Hee-hee!!!

setting: Conference room during a management presentation
situation: The Boss lectures employees that change is good, using a slide with a smiley face. Dilbert volunteers to ask a question, suggesting the company triple everyone's pay as a change, then suggests the Boss work for free. The Boss gets angry, and afterward Wally gleefully recalls the Boss's outburst.
punchline: When Dilbert applies the Boss's 'change is good' slogan to pay and the Boss's own salary, the Boss cannot defend it and angrily blames Dilbert's logic for ruining his slogans.
summary: A manager's cheery pro-change slogan collapses when an employee applies it to salaries and the manager's own pay.

title: Eyebrows Hide Sleeping Wally

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What fresh hell is this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm letting my eyebrows grow out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I comb them over my eyes, no one can tell that I'm asleep.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're quiet today.

setting: Office hallway and a conference room meeting
situation: Alice reacts with alarm to Wally's unkempt, bushy eyebrows, and he explains he is growing them out on purpose. His plan is to comb them down over his eyes so coworkers cannot tell he is sleeping. In a meeting, Wally sits dozing behind his eyebrows while the Boss remarks that he is quiet today.
punchline: Wally's laziness has reached the point of engineering a disguise for sleeping at work, and the oblivious Boss falls for it, noticing only that he is quiet.
summary: A napping employee grows out his eyebrows into a curtain so he can doze through meetings undetected.

file: 2005/2005-08-27_stealth layoff_evil director_human resources_worthless employees_job no longer exists_business.gif
title: Stealth Layoff by Project Consolidation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I call it a stealth layoff.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We move all of the worthless employees to the same project. When it's done, we tell them that their jobs no longer exist.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't like the looks of this.

setting: Catbert's HR office, then a conference room
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains his scheme to the Boss: gather all the useless employees onto a single project and eliminate their jobs once it finishes. In the last panel, a group of employees sits around a conference table, and one of them nervously senses something is wrong.
punchline: The employees are being herded onto a doomed project, and one has the dawning suspicion that it's a trap, which it is.
summary: An HR villain reveals a sneaky method of firing people by quietly grouping the unwanted onto one temporary assignment.

file: 2005/2005-05-26_good advice_balance_personal life_zen approach_no freinds_no work_perfect balance_zen_faster.gif
title: Wally's Zen Work-Life Balance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one has any good advice on how I can balance my work with my personal life.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You didn't ask me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I take the Zen approach of having no friends and doing no work. Hence, perfect balance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where did you get that definition of Zen?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I used to read, but it's faster to make up stuff.

setting: Office break room table during lunch
situation: Dilbert complains over lunch that nobody has given him useful advice on balancing work and personal life. Wally offers his own 'Zen' philosophy of having no friends and doing no work, which supposedly yields perfect balance. When Dilbert questions the definition, Wally admits he just invents things rather than reading.
punchline: Wally's self-serving definition of Zen is simply laziness and isolation dressed up as philosophy, and he cheerfully admits he fabricates facts because it's quicker than reading.
summary: A colleague justifies his slacking and loneliness as a spiritual philosophy and then confesses he simply invents his information.

title: Year-End Budget Spending Wink Wink

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to use up my budget before the end of the year or else I'll get less next year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'll be flexible about approving expenses for a few days. Wink, wink.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice coffee-holding panda.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You should see the one that isn't pregnant.

situation: The Boss tells Wally that he must spend his remaining budget before year-end or risk a smaller budget next year, and hints that he'll approve questionable expenses for a few days. Wally then appears with a panda carrying a coffee mug on its head, and Dilbert compliments the panda.
punchline: Wally immediately exploits the boss's lax expense approval by expensing a panda, and implies he even bought a second, pregnant one, showing how use-it-or-lose-it budgeting encourages wasteful spending.
summary: Given a green light to burn through leftover funds, an employee promptly buys an absurdly impractical exotic animal.

title: Tech Support Survey Before Help

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please fill out the online customer satisfaction survey.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Um... but you haven't even tried to help me yet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like to base my help on how happy you expect to be.

situation: Dogbert, working a tech support phone line with a headset, asks a caller to complete a customer satisfaction survey before offering any assistance. The confused customer points out that no help has been provided yet. Dogbert explains that the level of help he gives depends on how happy the customer expects to be.
punchline: Dogbert reverses the usual order of customer service by tailoring his effort to the customer's predicted satisfaction, which lets him do as little as possible while gaming the survey results.
summary: A tech support dog demands a satisfaction survey up front so he can match his effort to the caller's expectations.

title: Pitching a Cable That Connects Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new product is a cable that doesn't attach to anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We hope to create demand via a series of commercials showing young people dancing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And then we'll all go straight to hell.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He didn't take the last round of budget cuts well.

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a new product to a meeting, a cable that connects to nothing, with a plan to build demand through commercials of young people dancing. The pointy-haired Boss blurts out that they will all go straight to hell, and a colleague explains away the outburst as a reaction to the last round of budget cuts.
punchline: The Boss's blunt, despairing remark is the honest assessment of a ridiculous product plan, and the colleague excuses it as budget-cut trauma rather than admitting he is right.
summary: A pointless product and a vague marketing plan are met by the boss's bleak prediction of doom, which a coworker brushes off as lingering stress from cost-cutting.

file: 2005/2005-05-30_[roducts name_means something bad_elbonian_pleasure from wedgie_thinking of trying_elbonia.gif
title: Product Name Means Wedgie Pleasure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've just been informed that our product's name means something bad in the Elbonian language.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It means "the intense pleasure derived from giving yourself a wedgie."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Thus was hatched the greatest prank ever perpetrated by Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I gotta try that.

situation: At a meeting, The Boss announces that the company's product name has a bad meaning in the Elbonian language, then reads out the definition: the pleasure of giving oneself a wedgie. A caption credits this as Elbonia's greatest prank, while the attendees, including Dilbert, sit thinking privately that they want to try it.
punchline: Instead of being embarrassed by the offensive meaning, everyone at the table is silently intrigued and wants to try giving themselves a wedgie.
summary: A meeting about a mistranslated product name turns into quiet curiosity about a bizarre Elbonian word for self-inflicted discomfort.

file: 2005/2005-07-09_managers elbow_patting yourself on back_prescription_leptard_cirque du soliel.gif
title: Manager's Elbow Needs a Leotard

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You've got a bad case of manager's elbow.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It's caused by patting yourself on the back and covering your butt at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I recommend that you join the Cirque du Soleil. I'm giving you a prescription for a leotard.

situation: The Boss sits half-undressed on an exam table while a doctor diagnoses him with 'manager's elbow.' The doctor explains it comes from simultaneously patting yourself on the back and covering your butt, then prescribes a leotard and suggests he join Cirque du Soleil.
punchline: Managers who constantly take credit and shift blame contort themselves like circus acrobats, so the only fitting treatment is a career as a contortionist.
summary: A physician mocks a manager's habit of praising himself while dodging blame by diagnosing a made-up ailment and sending him off to the circus.

title: CEO Bungee Jumps Into Volcano

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your CEO was underperforming, so I convinced him to bungee jump into a live volcano. Problem solved.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, he under-performed and he got punished.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pumiced, actually.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Evil, yet amusing.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that he dealt with an underperforming CEO by convincing him to bungee jump into a live volcano. Dilbert responds with a pun about the CEO being punished for underperforming, and Dogbert corrects him with an even better pun.
punchline: Dogbert corrects Dilbert's 'punished' pun with 'pumiced', a pun on pumice, the volcanic rock, and Dilbert admits the CEO's fiery death is evil yet amusing.
summary: After talking an underachieving chief executive into a fatal stunt over a volcano, Dogbert trades wordplay with Dilbert about the grisly result.

file: 2005/2005-05-31_hired a genius_faking british accent_ello bird_sexy sounds.gif
title: Genius Hire Fakes British Accent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought I hired a genius.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But he turned out to be an ordinary guy faking a British accent.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: 'Ello, bird. 'Ow 'bout a spot o' tea? Whot do you say, gov'nor?

transcript.speaker: Woman at computer (thought)
transcript.text: Who's making those sexy sounds?

setting: Office, including the boss's desk and a cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that the new hire he thought was a genius is just an ordinary guy putting on a British accent. The new hire then walks through the office speaking in an exaggerated cockney accent, offering tea, while a female coworker at her computer is charmed by it.
punchline: The fake British accent made the employee seem like a genius to the boss, yet it also works as a charm on a coworker, showing how people are swayed by accents more than by actual ability.
summary: A manager realizes his supposedly brilliant new employee is merely an average man with a put-on English accent, though the voice still enchants a coworker.

title: Boss Is The Moron Standardizing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the coding coming along?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem unless . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: . . . some moron tries to standardize on a new programming methodology in the middle of the project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if it's me instead of some moron guy?

situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's cubicle to ask how the coding is going. Dilbert says it's fine unless some moron tries to standardize on a new programming methodology mid-project. The Boss, who is likely planning exactly that, asks what if the moron is him.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly reveals he is the very moron Dilbert was warning about, and he hopes to be excused because he isn't 'some moron guy'.
summary: A manager checking on a developer's progress learns that mid-project process changes are the only danger, then wonders aloud whether his own meddling counts.

file: 2005/2005-04-06_new marketing camoaign_no budget_brave enough_bold project_worst job_hiding.gif
title: Volunteer for Impossible Marketing Campaign

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need a new marketing campaign but we have no budget for it whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who among us is brave enough to lead such a bold and risky project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, you're doing the worst job of hiding under the table.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that a new marketing campaign is needed but there is no budget. He then asks who is brave enough to lead the bold and risky project. In the last panel the employees have all ducked down so only their eyes and foreheads show above the table, and the Boss calls out how badly they are hiding.
punchline: The staff are so desperate to avoid volunteering for an unfunded, doomed project that they hide under the table, and even the oblivious Boss notices how poorly they are doing it.
summary: Faced with an unfunded and risky assignment, the whole team ducks below the conference table to dodge being chosen.

file: 2005/2005-05-25_balancing work life_job anger_destablizie_crush urges_punch something_will want kids.gif
title: Job Anger Crushes Maternal Urges

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm having trouble balancing my work life and my personal life. How do you do it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I use job anger to destabilize my hormonal balance and crush any competing urges.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That reminds me: I need to punch something today or I'll want to have kids.

situation: Dilbert asks Alice how she manages work-life balance while she pours coffee at the break area. Alice explains she deliberately uses job anger to disrupt her hormones and suppress other desires. She then adds that she must punch something today or she'll start wanting children.
punchline: Alice's coping strategy for work-life balance is cultivating rage to suppress her maternal urges, and she needs daily violence to keep them at bay.
summary: A coworker seeking advice on juggling career and home gets a darkly funny answer about weaponizing workplace fury against biology.

title: Alice Misreads Dilbert's Wedgie Discomfort

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He doesn't respect my work. I can tell by the way he's sitting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Two can play this game. I will hate you with the fury of a thousand suns!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Die! Die! Die!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rats. I sat down wrong and gave myself a wedgie.

situation: Alice sits at a meeting table and silently concludes from Dilbert's posture that he disrespects her work. She retaliates by glaring at him and mentally wishing him death. Dilbert, meanwhile, is simply uncomfortable because he gave himself a wedgie when sitting down.
punchline: Alice's furious interpretation of Dilbert's body language is completely wrong, since he is merely adjusting to an embarrassing wedgie.
summary: A seething coworker reads malice into a colleague's squirming, when he's just sitting uncomfortably.

file: 2005/2005-08-02_mordac_preventer of information_screen saver_modified_seconds of inactivity_head bobbing bird.gif
title: Mordac Versus the Drinking Bird

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac, the Preventer of Information Technology. I have modified your screensaver security to lock up after two seconds of inactivity.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Ha ha! Unless you touch the keyboard every two seconds you will be forced to log-in again!

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Dang your perpetually moving head-bobbing bird! Gaaa!!!

situation: Mordac, the IT security enforcer, announces to a seated coworker that he has set her screensaver to lock after only two seconds of inactivity, forcing constant keyboard contact or a fresh log-in. In the last panel she has rigged a toy head-bobbing bird to keep tapping the keyboard, defeating his policy and leaving him furious.
punchline: Mordac's petty, draconian security rule is beaten by a cheap novelty bird toy that keeps pressing the keys, leaving him impotently enraged.
summary: An IT security tyrant imposes an absurdly short screensaver timeout, only to be outsmarted by a bobbing desk toy that keeps the keyboard active.

title: Boss Marks Territory With Prototype Change

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I must mark my territory by insisting on a change to the prototype.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give it a wireless Internet option.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It already has one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What doesn't it have?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: An idiot designing it.

setting: Conference room during a prototype review meeting
situation: In a meeting, the Boss thinks to himself that he must assert his authority by demanding a change to the prototype Dilbert is holding. He asks for a wireless Internet option, but Dilbert says it already has one. The Boss then asks what it lacks, and Dilbert says it lacks an idiot designing it.
punchline: Dilbert's reply insults the Boss by implying that he is the idiot who would ruin the design, so the only thing the prototype is missing is his interference.
summary: A manager insists on altering a gadget purely to show who is in charge, and the engineer slyly insults him in reply.

title: Reward for Finishing: Newsletter Duty

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have completed all of my projects and I am ready for a new challenge.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can help Tina write the department newsletter.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But the newsletter job is only given to the most worthless employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And her assistant.

situation: Asok, an eager young employee, tells the Boss he has finished all his projects and wants a new challenge. The Boss assigns him to help Tina write the department newsletter. Asok protests that this job goes only to the most worthless employee, and the Boss adds that it also goes to her assistant.
punchline: The Boss casually confirms that Asok's reward for finishing his work is being labeled worthless, since the newsletter job goes to the worst employee and her assistant.
summary: A diligent worker seeking more responsibility is handed a task reserved for the company's least valued staff, and his boss cheerfully makes the insult explicit.

title: Boss Rewards Porpoise for Killing Lawyer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no law that says a porpoise can't kill a company lawyer, but it's still somewhat bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Officially, I have to give you a reprimand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Unofficially, do you like mackerel?

transcript.speaker: Porpoise
transcript.text: Squeak!

situation: The Boss sits at his desk talking to a porpoise that has killed the company lawyer. He says he must formally reprimand it, then privately offers it a treat of mackerel, and the porpoise squeaks happily.
punchline: The Boss's official disciplinary stance is a sham, since he secretly approves of the lawyer's death and rewards the killer with fish.
summary: A manager scolds a lawyer-slaying porpoise for the record, then quietly bribes it with seafood in thanks.

title: CFO Estimates Deadly Bungee Cord

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: It's good P.R. for the company when the CEO is a fearless adventurer.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Sounds dangerous.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Don't worry. I've asked your Chief Financial Officer to be in charge of safety.

transcript.speaker: Voice from balloon
transcript.text: Okay, who estimated the length of the bungee cord?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Oops

setting: Corporate office with a pedestal, then a hot air balloon over an erupting volcano
situation: A small egg-shaped CEO tells a bald executive that being a fearless adventurer is good publicity for the company. When the executive says it sounds dangerous, the CEO reassures him by saying the Chief Financial Officer has been put in charge of safety. In the last panel, the CEO dangles from a balloon on a bungee cord that has dropped him into a volcano and asks who estimated the cord's length.
punchline: Putting a finance executive in charge of safety leads to a bad estimate, so the CEO's bungee cord is too long and drops him into an active volcano.
summary: A chief executive chases publicity through extreme sports, entrusts safety to the company's money man, and ends up dipped into a lava crater by a miscalculated rope.

file: 2005/2005-11-06_quirky co worker_colossal waste_invented table_executive recruiter_leadership or crazy_wallet alone.gif

file: 2005/2005-12-18_buy insurance_whole life umbrella rider_read list_acts of god_wrong god_lighting strike.gif
title: Praying To The Right God

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to buy some insurance, but I don't know much about it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need my special indemnity casualty whole life umbrella rider binder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does it cover?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't answer that directly.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Just read that list of exclusions. Anything not in there is covered.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it cover acts of God?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, unless you pray to the wrong one.

Dilbert asks what it covers, and Dogbert dodges, telling him to read the exclusions. When Dilbert asks about acts of God, Dogbert says they are covered unless he prays to the wrong god, and suggests trying another god if lightning doesn't strike Dogbert.
punchline: Dogbert mocks insurance loopholes by making acts-of-God coverage depend on guessing the right deity, with the only test being whether Dogbert himself gets struck by lightning.
summary: A dog selling a convoluted insurance policy explains that divine-disaster coverage fails if the buyer worships the wrong deity.

file: 2005/2005-05-28_tech support_bad computer_designed to be slower_unrelaible_defragment_disk drive.gif
title: Dogbert Offers False Hope Defragmenting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have a bad case of computer rot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your computer is designed to become slower and more unreliable over time so you have to upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if you'd like some false hope, I can tell you how to defragment your disk drive.

setting: Dogbert's tech support desk, wearing a headset in front of a computer
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support line with a headset, diagnoses a caller's computer with 'computer rot'. He explains that computers are deliberately designed to degrade so customers must buy upgrades, then offers to share a defragmenting tip purely as false hope.
punchline: Dogbert cynically admits that hardware is built to fail so you'll buy new equipment, and that the usual fix, defragmenting, is just a placebo.
summary: A candid tech support dog tells a customer that planned decline is built into computers, then hands over a pointless maintenance tip for comfort.

file: 2005/2005-03-18_conference call_success_set up_15 people_forgot to call in_mute buttons_spinning story.gif
title: Conference Call Success By Spin

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The conference call was a huge success.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Three out of 15 people were available and only one of them forgot to call in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So it was a phone call between two people?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It would have been if they hadn't used the mute buttons.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: An employee reports to The Boss and a colleague that a conference call was a huge success. He then reveals that only three of fifteen people were available and one forgot to call in. The Boss concludes it was just a call between two people, and the employee responds with a twisted excuse involving mute buttons.
punchline: The employee spins a near-total failure as a success, and even his defense admits the call was only productive if nobody had muted themselves, which is a nonsensical rationalization.
summary: A staffer proudly labels a conference call a triumph despite almost nobody participating, then deflects the boss's blunt assessment with a flimsy excuse.
